text:
PHYSICIAN: Come on in, Geraldine. So you were just discharged on Friday, right? How're you holding up?
PATIENT: Yeah, um, honestly I'm doing okay. The blood pressure thing seems like it's settling down now, so I'm not as worried about that anymore. I mean, I'm taking my stuff every day.
PHYSICIAN: That's great to hear. And which medications are you on right now?
PATIENT: So I've got the carvedilol, the 6.25 mg tablets, and I'm taking those twice a day like you said. Haven't skipped a single one. But then there's the other one—the allopurinol—and, um, I'll be honest, I've missed a couple doses here and there. Life's been kind of chaotic.
PHYSICIAN: Allopurinol at 300 mg, yeah? It's okay, these things happen. But let's circle back to that in a minute. Have you noticed anything else going on since you left the hospital?
PATIENT: Well, I've had this dizziness that comes and goes, but it's not really any worse than before. Like, it's the same annoying thing. And then, um, my head's been hurting since like Monday? Not like crazy bad, but it's definitely bothersome and it won't go away.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, the dizziness is stable at least. And this headache started Monday—is it constant or does it come in waves?
PATIENT: It's like, I don't know, pretty much there all day? It's moderate. I take some ibuprofen and it helps a little bit but then it comes back. I haven't seen any, like, weird vision stuff or anything, so that's good.
PHYSICIAN: Good catch on the vision—nothing blurry going on, no double vision or anything like that?
PATIENT: No, my eyes are fine, actually. It's just the headache and the dizziness. Oh, and sometimes I feel really tense, you know? Like my shoulders get all tight and I can't relax. Do you think that's weird? My mom says I'm just anxious, but I don't know if that's actually a thing or just me being dramatic.
PHYSICIAN: That's not weird at all. Actually, I want to ask you more about that—do you find yourself worrying a lot, even about stuff that's probably fine? Or having trouble sleeping because your mind won't shut off? And there's the hypertension to think about too. We should also keep the blurred vision on our radar.
PATIENT: Um, yeah, actually. Like I'll lie in bed and just think about random things forever. And like, sometimes I think about my grandmother—she had alzheimer disease and died a few years ago—and I get like this weird panic thinking about whether I'll get it too, you know? Which is silly because I'm nineteen.
PHYSICIAN: It's not silly at all. That kind of worry, especially when it's affecting your sleep and relaxation, can definitely be a sign of generalized anxiety disorder. We're not confirming anything today, but I want to keep an eye on that. Have you had any thoughts about a referral to someone who specializes in that kind of thing?
PATIENT: I mean, maybe? I don't know. What do you think I should do?
PHYSICIAN: Let's start with getting some bloodwork done to rule out anything physical—sometimes thyroid problems or blood sugar stuff can mimic anxiety. And I'm also thinking we should get you to pulmonology since you mentioned some breathing stuff before you were discharged. Remember that?
PATIENT: Oh yeah, right. The shortness of breath thing. Okay, so what do I need to do for the bloodwork? Do I go to the lab or...?
PHYSICIAN: Yep, you'll schedule that at the front desk on your way out. They'll give you the orders. And for the pulmonology appointment, I'll put in a referral today, and they should call you within a week or so. In the meantime, we're also going to adjust your allopurinol dose up a bit since you've been missing some doses and we want better coverage. Let's go to 300 mg once daily, but we might bump it up after we see how you're doing.
PATIENT: Wait, I'm already on 300 mg though. Do you mean like, increase it?
PHYSICIAN: Oh, you're right—my mistake. We'll keep it at 300 mg for now, but the big thing is trying not to miss those doses. Set a phone reminder if that helps.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay, I can do that. So just to make sure I have it straight—bloodwork, pulmonology, and keep taking everything the way I'm doing it now?
PHYSICIAN: Exactly. And Geraldine, don't hesitate to call if that headache gets worse or if you're feeling more anxious. We're going to check in with you again after the bloodwork comes back.

PHYSICIAN: So Adalynn, you mentioned on the phone that you've been having some chest pain—is that what's been bothering you the most lately?
PATIENT: Well, yeah, it started yesterday. It's not terrible or anything, but it's there, you know? Kind of just a dull ache that won't go away. But honestly, I think what's more concerning is my legs have been really swollen since Monday.
PHYSICIAN: The leg swelling—that's new for you? And it's been about the same since Monday or getting worse?
PATIENT: Pretty much the same. Maybe a tiny bit better in the mornings, but by the afternoon it's back. Um, and then on top of that, I've been getting these spells where I feel really lightheaded. Like, walking up the stairs or even just standing up from the couch, and suddenly the room starts spinning.
PHYSICIAN: When did that start?
PATIENT: Over the weekend, I guess. That's actually what scared me a little bit and made me call you guys.
PHYSICIAN: That's definitely worth having checked out. So we know you have hypertension—have you been keeping up with your medications like usual?
PATIENT: Um, well, mostly. I mean, the naproxen, 500 mg, I take that twice a day and I've been really good about that. The albuterol is—wait, actually, I'm supposed to do 2 puffs, right? No, wait, no—it's 1 puff as needed. Sorry, I always mix that up. But yeah, I've been taking it, though I'll admit I've missed a few doses here and there recently.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, so you've been consistent with the naproxen but spotty with the albuterol. Do you remember when you last used the albuterol?
PATIENT: Probably this morning? Or maybe yesterday morning. It's honestly hard to say. I've been kind of distracted with the swelling and feeling dizzy.
PHYSICIAN: I get it. And with the gastroesophageal reflux disease—that acid reflux stuff—have you had any flare-ups recently, or is that pretty stable on what you're taking? Let me get the albuterol down: 1 puffs, as needed, and you're missed a few doses lately.
PATIENT: Oh, that's been fine actually. I mean, I get it sometimes if I eat too late, but nothing crazy. The chest pain I'm having now doesn't feel like the reflux, you know? It's different.
PHYSICIAN: That's good information. Let me pull up your recent labs here—I'm seeing your fasting glucose came back at 96, which is still in the normal range but we'll keep an eye on that.
PATIENT: 96? Is that okay? I've been trying to watch my diet and all that.
PHYSICIAN: It's fine for now, yeah. So given everything you're experiencing—the chest pain, the lightheadedness, the swelling—I want to get you set up for a follow-up visit pretty soon, maybe next week if we can. But I'm also thinking we should consider a referral to cardiology just to rule out anything serious with your heart.
PATIENT: Cardiology? Like, do you think something's wrong with my heart? That's kind of scary.
PHYSICIAN: I don't want to jump to conclusions, but with the combination of symptoms, it's worth having them take a look. It's probably nothing, but better safe than sorry. Does that sound okay to you?
PATIENT: I guess so, yeah. When would that happen? And I can do the follow-up visit?
PHYSICIAN: We'll schedule you for both. The follow-up visit with me would be our baseline check-in, and we'll get the cardiology referral rolling so they can fit you in. My nurse will have the appointments set up before you leave today.
PATIENT: Okay, thank you. I was really worried it was something serious, so I'm glad I came in.

NURSE: Okay Delilah, so I got your weight here—212 pounds—and I'm seeing your blood pressure's still running a little high today. Can we talk about how things have been going with your hypertension? Have you noticed anything different lately?
PATIENT: Well, that's actually kind of why I'm here. I mean, I've been managing okay but—um—I noticed starting three days ago I've had to go to the bathroom, like, way more than usual. Frequent urination, I guess you'd say? And I'm not totally sure what's up with that.
NURSE: Okay, that's helpful to know. And has that been getting worse, or is it staying pretty much the same?
PATIENT: No, it's—it's been about the same, honestly. Not super bothering me, just noticeable. But then this morning, yeah, I woke up and I'm just—I'm really thirsty. Like, unusually thirsty. I've been drinking so much water and I'm still dry. Increased thirst, you know? That one's definitely more bothersome than the bathroom thing.
NURSE: That's important information. And have you felt okay otherwise? Any other changes?
PATIENT: Um, well, I had some fatigue starting yesterday, but honestly it's getting better already. Nothing major. I think I'm just tired because work's been insane lately—we've got this whole project deadline and I've been staying up too late.
NURSE: I hear you. Let's look at your meds for a second. You're on escitalopram, right? The 20 mg?
PATIENT: Yeah, I've got that one. Um, full disclosure though—I think I missed a dose or two over the past month or so. Life gets crazy and I forget sometimes, but I've been pretty good about it overall.
NURSE: No judgment—it happens. And you're also on duloxetine for the anxiety side of things, the 60 mg once a day?
PATIENT: Right, that one too. And yeah, I'll be honest, same thing—I've skipped it here and there. But I'm trying to be better about it. I know I need both of those to keep my head on straight, especially with everything going on.
NURSE: Totally makes sense. Now, the dapagliflozin—the 5 mg—you've been doing really well with that one, right? No missed doses on that?
PATIENT: Oh no, I haven't missed a single one of those. That one I'm really careful about. I remember taking it every morning with breakfast.
NURSE: That's great, actually. But given everything you're experiencing right now—the thirst, the urination—I think we need to adjust your dapagliflozin dose. We might go a little higher to help manage things better. But first we'll need to run some bloodwork to get a full picture of what's happening.
PATIENT: Okay, so like, higher dapagliflozin? I'm fine with that if you think it'll help. And bloodwork is no problem, I can do that—I'm used to having labs done at this point.
NURSE: Perfect. We'll get you set up before you leave today. And then I'm going to have you come back in for a follow-up visit in about four weeks so we can see how you're doing on the new dose and review those results with you.
PATIENT: Four weeks sounds good. Should be fine with my schedule, wait—no, actually let me check my calendar. But yeah, I can make that work. And this should help with all this thirst business?
NURSE: That's what we're hoping for, yeah. Your body's been giving us some signals, so let's listen to them and dial things in. We'll get the bloodwork back, adjust the medication like we talked about, and then reassess at your follow-up visit. Sound okay?
PATIENT: Sounds good to me. I really appreciate you taking the time to go through all this today.

NURSE: Hey Maxwell, come on back. Looks like it's been a couple months since we last saw you. Let's get your vitals real quick before we chat.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. Um, I've actually been dealing with some stuff. The heartburn has been really brutal the last three days or so—like, I can barely get through dinner without feeling like my chest is on fire, you know?
NURSE: Okay, heartburn for three days, got it. Let me grab your temperature here... alright, you're running a slight fever—100.4. And your BP is up a bit today. We'll keep an eye on that. But first tell me more about this heartburn. Has anything changed with your diet or your meds?
PATIENT: No, no, nothing different. I mean, I've been taking the doxycycline like you said, 100 mg twice a day, but—wait, actually I'm not totally sure I've been consistent with it. Some days I remember, some days I kinda forget. And then I've got the muscle aches on top of it all, started maybe a week ago, and they're not going away.
NURSE: Muscle aches since around your last visit? Okay. Are they in your legs, arms, everywhere? And we should probably talk about maybe adjusting that doxycycline dose if you're having side effects.
PATIENT: Yeah, kind of all over, to be honest. But that's not even the worst part. I've been getting these dizzy spells, you know, really dizzy, and it started maybe two weeks ago. It's actually gotten worse since then, which freaks me out a little.
NURSE: Dizziness that's worsening—that does warrant some attention. Any shortness of breath with it? Chest pain? Or is it more room-spinning type of dizziness?
PATIENT: Um, it's like the room kind of tilts, and my head feels like it's floating. Not so much chest pain, but with the high blood pressure—the hypertension, I mean—I'm worried it's related somehow. And I do have a slight headache, but that's actually getting better, so I'm not too concerned about that one.
NURSE: Good that the headache's improving. Let's circle back to your current meds for a second. You're taking the atenolol every morning, 25 mg, right? And how's that going?
PATIENT: Yeah, I take that one as prescribed, no problems. And the amitriptyline at night, the 25 mg, I'm good with that too. Those two I don't miss.
NURSE: Okay, so you're reliable with those two. Got it. Your hyperlipidemia and the high blood pressure have been pretty stable on the atenolol, but given this dizziness and some of the other symptoms, I think we need to get you referred to pulmonology to make sure there's nothing going on with your lungs that could be contributing. And we'll definitely need to adjust the doxycycline dosing, maybe try a lower frequency or lower amount.
PATIENT: Wait, pulmonology? Like a lung doctor? I'm not having trouble breathing though...
NURSE: It's just to be thorough with the dizziness and the overall picture. We want to rule out anything we might be missing. Trust me, it's routine in cases like this. And your brother, he's got type 2 diabetes mellitus, right? That's something we keep in the back of our minds with your cholesterol and blood pressure situation.
PATIENT: Oh yeah, he was diagnosed a few years back. I always wondered if that stuff runs in the family, you know? But anyway, so you're saying I should do the pulmonology thing?
NURSE: Yes, I'm going to get that referral set up. And one more thing—I want you to try walking more. Just even a ten-, fifteen-minute walk a few times a week. It'll help with the blood pressure, help you feel better overall. Can you commit to that?
PATIENT: Walking more, yeah, I can do that. My knees aren't great, but I can handle a short walk. So to recap, you're adjusting the doxycycline, sending me to pulmonology, and I gotta get moving more. Got it.
NURSE: Exactly. We'll try dropping the doxycycline to once a day and see if that helps with the muscle aches and the heartburn. And seriously, get that walking in—it's going to make a difference. Come back in four weeks and we'll see how you're doing.
PATIENT: Sounds good. Thanks for actually listening to all this. I was pretty nervous coming in today.
NURSE: That's what we're here for, Maxwell. We'll get to the bottom of this dizziness and get you feeling better. Let the front desk know if you have any questions about the pulmonology referral.

CARE_COORDINATOR: Gloria, sorry I'm running about five minutes behind. Let me just grab your chart here. How've you been doing since we last saw you in March?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, same old same old. Well, not exactly. My knees have been killing me more than usual. The osteoarthritis, I guess—just doesn't want to cooperate some days.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I hear you. Are the knees what brought you in today, or is there something else going on?
PATIENT: No, actually, it's more that I'm just not feeling like eating much. Like, my poor appetite has been a real thing since, um, I want to say since my last visit? And then on top of that, I've been—well, I'm getting out of breath easier than I used to.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, the shortness of breath—how would you describe that? Is it about the same as it was, or is it getting worse?
PATIENT: No, it's definitely getting worse. Like, I'll be making the bed or walking up the stairs and I just feel like I can't quite catch my breath. It's bothersome, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's important to know. Given your coronary artery disease, we want to keep an eye on that. When did you first notice it worsening?
PATIENT: Mm, the past week or two, maybe? Oh, and I also had this tiredness hit me on Monday. Fatigue, I guess—though that's actually getting a little better, so I'm not too worried about that one.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Glad that's improving. Let me check your vitals real quick. Your heart rate is running at 58, which is on the slower side but not alarming. Let me ask—are you still taking your atorvastatin?
PATIENT: Um, well... honestly, I stopped taking that one. The 40 mg. I just—it was one more pill, and I was having a hard time keeping track. I know I'm supposed to, but...
CARE_COORDINATOR: I'm glad you told me. We need to get you back on that. It's important for protecting your heart, especially with the coronary disease. Let's set up a pill organizer or something that makes it easier. Are you still taking your insulin glargine at bedtime?
PATIENT: Oh yes, that one I don't forget. I do my 20 units every single night. Haven't missed a dose on that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. Actually, speaking of the insulin glargine, I want to bump up your dose a bit. We'll go to 22 units at bedtime and recheck things in a few weeks. But first, I want to get some fresh bloodwork done to see how your kidney function is looking.
PATIENT: Kidney function? Is something wrong with my kidneys?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Not necessarily wrong, but given some of what we're seeing, I want to take a closer look. The bloodwork will tell us. And if we do see something, I'm going to refer you over to nephrology—that's our kidney specialist—just to make sure we're on top of it.
PATIENT: Oh, okay. That makes sense, I guess. You know, my neighbor just got shingles—poor thing, she's miserable. I was worried I might get it too, but knock on wood, so far so good.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Well, shingles isn't contagious in the way some people think, but I'm glad your neighbor's doing okay. Anyway, back to you—the shortness of breath is the thing I want us to focus on. We'll get your bloodwork done this week, adjust your insulin glargine as we talked about, and get you set up with nephrology. And please, restart that atorvastatin 40 mg once a day. Can you do all that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can. I'll get the pills back on track. I just need to be better about keeping up with it all, right?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Exactly. We're going to make it simpler. And Gloria, let's not wait too long on this. I want to see you back in four weeks to go over those results and see how you're feeling.
PATIENT: Okay, I'll be here. Thank you for listening to all this.

PATIENT: So I've been having this chest pain that's like, really bad, and I wasn't sure if I should wait to see you or just go to the ER, you know? But my friend said to call first, so here I am.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, let's start there. When you say it's really bad—when did it start, and is it constant or does it come and go?
PATIENT: Um, it started this morning, actually. It's not like, every second, but it's been lingering. And then on top of that I've noticed I'm getting a little bit short of breath, which is new. Like, just this morning too.
PHYSICIAN: Short of breath—even just sitting or when you're moving around?
PATIENT: Both, kind of. More when I'm moving, but honestly it's been bothering me. And the weird thing is, I've also been getting these dizzy spells, like lightheadedness? I mentioned it last time I was in, and it seemed to be getting better, but today with everything else it's just—it's a lot.
PHYSICIAN: Got it. So the lightheadedness has been improving since your last visit, but the chest pain and the shortness of breath are brand new as of this morning. I want to make sure we're tracking your peripheral artery disease carefully, especially with these symptoms popping up. Have you noticed anything with your vision—any blurriness or anything like that?
PATIENT: No, my vision's been fine, actually. That's the one thing that hasn't been weird.
PHYSICIAN: Alright, that's good. Let me ask you about your medications. You're on apixaban for the blood clots—how's that been going? Are you taking it regularly?
PATIENT: I'm supposed to take it twice a day, right? So the 5 mg? I've been mostly doing that, but I'll be honest, I skipped it a couple of times. Life gets busy and I just... forgot. But I've been trying to be better about it.
PHYSICIAN: I appreciate the honesty. We need you on that consistently because of the peripheral artery disease. What about your other diabetes medications—the canagliflozin and the dulaglutide?
PATIENT: Um, the canagliflozin—the 100 mg one—I'm taking that, but like, I'm not totally sure how consistent I've been with it. Some days I remember, some days I'm running out the door and I don't know if I took it or not. And the dulaglutide, the 1.5 mg injection? I stopped doing that a while ago. I know I probably shouldn't have, but it was just another thing and I was already dealing with the major depressive disorder stuff, and I just kind of dropped it.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, I hear you. The depression is real and it's hard to juggle everything, but we need to think about getting you back on the dulaglutide. Right now let's focus on what's happening today. On a scale of zero to ten, where would you put this chest pain?
PATIENT: I'd say 6 out of 10. It's not crushing or anything, but it's definitely there and it's uncomfortable.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. We're going to get some bloodwork done today just to check where you're at, and I want to get your fasting glucose to see where that's sitting. When was the last time we checked that? I do want to make a note of the blurred vision while we're at it. Just to confirm — the dulaglutide, that's 1.5 mg once a week, and it sounds like you've been stopped taking it.
PATIENT: I think like a month ago? And you said it was 96, so like, not terrible?
PHYSICIAN: Right, that 96 was reasonable for fasting. Let's see what it is now with everything going on. Given the chest pain and the new shortness of breath, I'm going to refer you to cardiology so they can do a more detailed workup. We can't mess around with that, okay?
PATIENT: So cardiology like, a heart specialist? Am I having a heart attack or something?
PHYSICIAN: We don't think so—your vitals look stable right now—but we need to rule things out. The cardiology team will run tests and make sure everything's okay with your heart, especially with your peripheral artery disease and the symptoms you're having.
PATIENT: Okay. Yeah, that makes sense. I'm a little nervous, but I get it.
PHYSICIAN: That's normal. I'm also going to need you to check your blood pressure at home—do you have a cuff?
PATIENT: I think I do, yeah. It's in a drawer somewhere. My mom gave me one.
PHYSICIAN: Great, dig it out and start monitoring. Write down what you get each day and bring it to your cardiology appointment. And before you leave, we'll get that bloodwork done, get you set up with the referral, and we'll get you a follow-up appointment here in about two weeks so we can see how you're doing and talk about getting back on some of these medications.
PATIENT: Sounds good. And should I like, go to the ER if the chest pain gets worse?
PHYSICIAN: Yes. If it gets significantly worse, or if you have new symptoms like fainting or severe shortness of breath, don't wait—go to the ER. Otherwise, let's get you in with cardiology and see what we're dealing with.

CARE_COORDINATOR: Ivy, we've got you in for a follow-up today. I see it's been, what, about three weeks since discharge? How are you feeling overall?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, it's been a mixed bag. I've been trying to stick to everything, but—um, I actually wanted to ask about something that started happening on Monday. My feet have this weird numbness, like pins and needles almost, and it's getting worse, not better.
PHYSICIAN: Numbness in the feet—when you say it's getting worse, does it go up your leg at all, or is it pretty localized to just your feet?
PATIENT: No, it's mostly the feet. Both feet. It's like, um, kind of a fuzzy feeling? I don't know if that's the right word. And I woke up this morning and I couldn't feel the tile on the bathroom floor as well as I normally do.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's definitely something we want to keep an eye on. Have you noticed anything else that's been off? Any changes with your vision or energy levels?
PATIENT: Well, my vision's been a little blurry. Like, not terrible, just—I'll be reading and the words get a little fuzzy for a second. Oh, and I've been thirstier than usual. Like, I'm going through my water bottle so fast. Started around when I came in last month, and it's kind of ramping up.
PHYSICIAN: Increased thirst and some blurred vision—we'll definitely want to circle back to that. But let me ask you something: have you had any night sweats? Waking up soaked through?
PATIENT: No, actually I haven't. My sheets have been totally fine. I sleep pretty decent, so that's one thing I can say is going okay.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's good. And you're managing the type 2 diabetes mellitus, right? How's that been for you day-to-day?
PATIENT: I mean, yeah, it's—well, it's been keeping me on my toes with all the medication. But I'm taking everything like I'm supposed to. I haven't missed my insulin glargine at bedtime, not once since I got home. And I take my rosuvastatin every morning with breakfast, same time every day.
PHYSICIAN: Good adherence there. Are you getting the 30 units of insulin glargine every night, or have you had to adjust it at all?
PATIENT: No, same 30 units every night. I do it right after my amitriptyline, actually. I take the amitriptyline, which is 25 mg, and then I do my insulin shot. Been really consistent with the amitriptyline too—helps me sleep.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And the rosuvastatin—40 mg, correct? You're not having any side effects from that?
PATIENT: No, 40 mg, and nope, no problems. I take it every day like clockwork.
PHYSICIAN: Let me get a heart rate here. Just relax your arm for me. Okay, I'm seeing 58. That's actually quite good—nice and steady.
PATIENT: Oh good, because I was worried something might be off with the heart, you know, with everything else going on.
PHYSICIAN: Your heart rate is solid. Now, I want to talk about your osteoarthritis—the joint pain. How's that been treating you?
PATIENT: It's, um, it's okay some days and not okay others. Today it's probably about 6 out of 10, if I'm being honest. My knees are the worst, and my right shoulder's been cranky.
CARE_COORDINATOR: With the osteoarthritis flaring up, have you been able to think about moving around more? We'd talked before about walking more, and that can really help with both the joint pain and the blood sugar management.
PATIENT: I know, I know. Walking more would probably be good. I've been a little hesitant because of the knee, but maybe I could do some shorter walks? Like, just around the block kind of thing?
PHYSICIAN: That's a great starting point. You don't have to go out for an hour. Even a couple of ten-minute walks can make a difference. And since you've got these new symptoms—the numbness and the thirst—I'd like you to check your blood pressure at home, okay? Can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I have a cuff at home. Um, wait—I actually haven't checked it since I got home. Should I be doing that regularly?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We'd like you to check it every couple days, morning and evening if you can. Just keep track of the numbers and bring them to your next appointment, or call us if anything looks really off.
PATIENT: Okay, I'll do that. Morning and evening. Got it. And I'll try to start walking more—maybe just in the evenings when it's cooler out.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. And we're going to keep a close eye on that numbness in your feet and the vision changes. If either of those gets worse, don't wait—call us right away.
PATIENT: Will do. Thank you. I appreciate it.

NURSE: Aaron, let's just check a few things real quick before we dive in. How're you doing today?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, hanging in there. My daughter drove me over—she's right outside parking the car. But I gotta tell you, I've been so thirsty lately. Like, unusually thirsty. Started just yesterday and it's gotten worse, not better.
NURSE: That's definitely something we want to keep an eye on. Let me jot that down. So you're noticing the increased thirst is pretty bothersome?
PATIENT: Yeah, it's annoying. I'm drinking water constantly and I still feel parched. And while we're at it, um, the frequent urination—remember I mentioned that last time?—well, it's actually getting better, thank God. That was really bothering me for a while there.
NURSE: That's good to hear about the urination piece. And these symptoms together with your coronary artery disease, we just want to make sure everything's stable. Have you been keeping up with your medications?
PATIENT: Mostly, yeah. I take the sacubitril-valsartan twice a day—well, I try to. Sometimes I forget to take it at night, to be honest. And then there's the, um, what's it called... the one for sleep?
NURSE: The amitriptyline?
PATIENT: That's it. Yeah, I'm supposed to take 25 mg at bedtime. I do most nights, but I'll admit I've skipped it a couple times when I forget or I'm not home.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: Dad, you also said you were tired lately, remember? You mentioned that when we were having breakfast yesterday.
PATIENT: Oh right, yeah. I mean, the fatigue is pretty mild, nothing crazy. Been going on maybe a month now? And like I said, that seems to be getting better too, so I'm not too worried about it.
NURSE: So the fatigue started around a month ago but it's improving—that's reassuring. With your heart condition, we definitely want to track these things. Now, we also need to talk about your LDL cholesterol. It came back at 156, which is higher than where we'd like to see it.
PATIENT: 156? That doesn't sound great. But my diet's been okay, I thought. I've been eating pretty well.
NURSE: It's good that you're conscious of that. We might want to look at your statin dose or possibly adjust your other meds. First thing is we're gonna need to get some bloodwork done. Can we order that for you today?
PATIENT: Yeah, sure, go ahead. When would you need it?
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: And I'm thinking, Mom—I mean, you know how to check your blood pressure at home, right? We got you that monitor.
PATIENT: Yeah, I have it at home. Haven't been using it much, if I'm being honest.
NURSE: Let's make that part of the plan, okay? I want you to check your blood pressure at home maybe three or four times a week, and keep a little log so we can see what's going on.
PATIENT: Okay, I can do that. So with the sacubitril-valsartan—97 mg twice daily—is that still the right dose, or is something gonna change?
NURSE: We'll likely keep you on that for now. But let's see what the bloodwork shows first. And speaking of which, we should probably schedule a follow-up visit so we can go over the results with you and talk about next steps.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: How soon can he come back in? I want to make sure we don't just let this slide.
NURSE: We can shoot for two to three weeks out. That should give us time to get the labs back and reviewed. Does that work for you, Aaron?
PATIENT: Two to three weeks sounds fine. And you're gonna remind me about taking my medications, right? I know I'm not great at remembering.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I'll help you with that. Maybe we set a phone alarm or something.
NURSE: That's a really good idea. Setting reminders can make a big difference, especially with the 25 mg of amitriptyline at night and making sure you don't miss doses of the other one. So to sum up: we're ordering bloodwork, you're gonna monitor at home with your blood pressure, and we'll get you back in for that follow-up visit to talk about where we go from here.
PATIENT: Got it. But I'm still concerned about this thirst thing. Should I be worried?
NURSE: The increased thirst combined with the frequent urination that you had before makes me want to check a few things on the bloodwork, so we'll definitely look into it. In the meantime, keep track of whether it's getting worse and let us know at your follow-up visit.

NURSE: Alright Julie, come on back. How are you feeling since we sent you home? I see you've got some swelling going on with your legs.
PATIENT: Yeah, um, honestly not great. Like, the swelling started over the weekend and it's just gotten worse. It's really bad, like, I can barely get my pants on this morning.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Walk us through what's been going on since discharge. Any fevers or anything like that?
PATIENT: No, no fevers. I've been keeping an eye on that. I'm not having any of those night sweats or anything—just the leg swelling that's driving me crazy.
NURSE: And how's the incision healing? Any pain there, or mostly just the leg issue?
PATIENT: Oh, the incision pain is still pretty bothersome, to be honest. Like, it started a couple weeks ago and it's just... it's not getting any better. It's moderate, you know? Not unbearable, but it's there.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Has anything else been going on? Any lightheadedness, shortness of breath?
PATIENT: Well, I've had some dizziness, which has actually been improving, so that's good. But between that and the leg thing, I've been pretty worried.
NURSE: Let me check your blood pressure real quick. And just to back up—we were treating you for the cellulitis, that infection in your leg tissue, right? And you also have anemia we've been monitoring.
PATIENT: Yeah, the cellulitis thing, the skin infection. My friend actually just had to have surgery because of gallstones, so I'm like, everything that can go wrong is going wrong, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Let's get you on the monitor. Julie, are you taking your medications like we discussed?
PATIENT: Um, mostly? I'm taking the torsemide, the 20 mg once a day. But, wait—the chlorthalidone, the 25 mg one, I forget that pretty regularly, honestly. Like, maybe half the time?
NURSE: Okay, and the albuterol? The rescue inhaler?
PATIENT: I take it as needed, 1 puffs when I feel like I need it. I'm not totally sure how often I've actually been using it—maybe not as much as I should be.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We'll help you set up better reminders for that chlorthalidone. But Julie, I'm looking at your blood pressure here and it's... it's really elevated. That's concerning, especially with the leg swelling getting worse.
PATIENT: How high? Is that bad? Like, is that because of the anemia or—
NURSE: It's high enough that we need to get you seen by cardiology right away. This needs escalation. We're going to send you over there today if they have an opening, or we might need to get you to urgent care to get this checked out immediately.
PATIENT: Like, today? Oh my gosh. Okay, um, should I be worried about driving?
CARE_COORDINATOR: I'll call ahead and see what they can do. In the meantime, we're definitely going to need updated bloodwork from you. That's non-negotiable at this point.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. Will they check on the anemia and all that with the bloodwork?
NURSE: Yes, we'll get comprehensive labs. Your fasting glucose was 96 when we checked it, which is fine, but with everything else going on we need the full picture.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And we'll get you scheduled for a follow-up visit with your primary once cardiology weighs in. But first things first—we need to get that blood pressure situation handled.
PATIENT: Alright. So I'm going to cardiology today, get bloodwork done, and then we'll schedule a follow-up visit? That's a lot happening.
NURSE: I know it's a lot, but this is important. And we're going to work on getting you consistent with those medications—especially the chlorthalidone and the torsemide. That's part of managing this.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah. I'll do better. I just... I hope this leg thing isn't something crazy.
CARE_COORDINATOR: The cardiology team will help us figure that out. Let me get you checked in with them, and we'll have you back in the office soon.

PATIENT: Yeah, so I woke up this morning and I just couldn't catch my breath. It's been getting worse all day and I'm kind of worried about it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, let's slow down a second. When you say you're having shortness of breath—is this something new that started today, or have you been dealing with this for a while?
PATIENT: Just today. This morning. I was lying in bed and just—like, I couldn't get enough air. And it's been really bad, um, getting worse as the day goes on.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's definitely something we need to pay attention to. Have you noticed any other symptoms—like maybe a cough or anything like that?
PATIENT: Actually, yeah. I've had this cough that's been bothering me. It's not terrible, but it's definitely there and it seems to be getting worse too. It's, um, kind of annoying when I'm trying to sleep.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I hear you. So between the breathing trouble and the cough, you're having a rough time. Let's talk about where things stand otherwise. How's your energy level been?
PATIENT: Oh, the fatigue is just—it's really bad. I mean, I'm already tired all the time with the sleep apnea, you know, the obstructive sleep apnea makes everything harder. But lately it just seems the same, honestly. Like, I can barely get through the day.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That must be exhausting. And I know you also deal with migraines. How's that been going?
PATIENT: Oh, the migraine headaches, yeah—they've been about the same. Nothing new there, thank God. I mean, they're still a pain, but at least they're not worse.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, small blessings. Let me ask you—have you noticed any swelling in your legs at all? Any puffiness or anything like that?
PATIENT: No, no leg swelling or anything. My legs look the same as always. Thank goodness, because my mother had that and it seemed really uncomfortable.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good to know. Now let's go through your medications real quick. You're still on the potassium chloride, right?
PATIENT: Yes, but—wait, I'm supposed to be taking that, um, 20 mEq, is that right? Yeah, once a day. Though I'll be honest, I forget it sometimes. Maybe once a week or so.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's helpful to know you're skipping it occasionally. We'll want to talk about that. What about your asthma inhaler? The one with the fluticasone-salmeterol in it?
PATIENT: Oh, I use that one. I think it's like, 1 puffs twice a day? But honestly, I can't remember exactly if I'm doing it right. Sometimes I use it twice, sometimes I'm not sure. It's confusing.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We'll clean that up before you leave. So your last lab work came back—your A1C was 7.8, which is in okay shape but we'd like to see it a little better.
PATIENT: Seven point eight. Um, is that good or bad? I'm not really sure what that number means.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's a measure of your blood sugar control over the last few months. Could be tighter, but it's not alarming. That said, given what I'm hearing today and with your kidney function, I think we need to get you in with nephrology to make sure everything's on track there.
PATIENT: Nephrology? That's the kidneys, right? Is something wrong with my kidneys?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Nothing alarming, but it's good to have a specialist take a closer look, especially with the shortness of breath you're having today. And we're going to adjust your potassium chloride dose too—hold off on that until you see nephrology, because the kidneys affect how your body handles potassium.
PATIENT: Okay, so I should stop taking it, or just wait? I'm a little confused. And yeah, I'm okay with seeing the kidney doctor. I just want to figure out why I'm having so much trouble breathing today.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: No, keep taking it for now, just like you have been. We'll call nephrology this week and get you scheduled, and they'll tell us if anything needs to change with the potassium chloride. In the meantime, I want you to keep an eye on that shortness of breath. If it gets worse or you start having chest pain, I want you to go to the ER. Deal?
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. That makes sense. I'll keep watching it. And I'll try to remember my meds better too. You know me, I'm not great with keeping track of things.

NURSE: So, Arianna, I'm seeing you came in this morning because of some chest and breathing issues — is that right?
PATIENT: Yeah, um, it's been really bad since like early this morning when I woke up. The chest pain is pretty severe, honestly, and I can barely catch my breath. I've been trying to stay calm but it just keeps getting worse.
NURSE: Okay, we're going to get to the bottom of this. Do you remember when the chest pain started exactly, and has it been constant or does it come and go?
PATIENT: This morning, like around seven or so. And it's kind of constant but — wait, no — actually it's been improving a little bit over the last couple hours, I think? But the shortness of breath is still really there, you know? That part feels like it's actually getting worse.
NURSE: The shortness of breath is getting worse, got it. Have you felt any fluttering in your chest or irregular heartbeats at all?
PATIENT: No, nothing like that. No palpitations or anything. Just this heaviness and I can't breathe properly. Oh, and I've been feeling kind of dizzy too, like lightheaded? That started this morning as well.
NURSE: Lightheaded on top of everything else — that's important. Okay, I need to ask about your medical history. I'm looking here that you had atrial fibrillation before, but that's been resolved, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, that was like last year sometime. They treated it and it got better. But I also have hyperlipidemia — high cholesterol, basically — and they've been managing that, or trying to anyway.
NURSE: Right, so we're dealing with the high cholesterol. Walk me through your current medications because that matters a lot here.
PATIENT: Um, okay, so I'm taking azithromycin, 250 mg once a day. I haven't missed that one. And then there's the naproxen, 250 mg twice a day, and I've been pretty good about that too, didn't miss any doses. But, um, I stopped taking the doxycycline — the 100 mg one I was supposed to take twice a day. I just kind of stopped a few weeks back because I wasn't sure I needed it anymore.
NURSE: Okay, so we need to talk about that doxycycline, but first let me finish the picture here. You mentioned earlier your leg swelling — when did that start? And there's the lightheadedness to think about too.
PATIENT: Oh yeah, that's been going on for a couple weeks or so. It's actually getting a little better now, which is good, but it was pretty puffy at first.
NURSE: Good that it's improving. So we ran a peak flow test and I got 240 L/min, which I want to keep an eye on. And your A1C came back at 9.2, which tells me your blood sugar control hasn't been where we'd like it.
PATIENT: Oh, wow. Is that bad? I mean, I knew my numbers weren't great, but 9.2 sounds pretty high.
NURSE: It's something we need to address, yeah. So here's what I'm thinking — first, I want you to check your blood pressure at home. Can you do that regularly, like once a day in the morning?
PATIENT: I can do that, yeah. I have one of those cuffs at home. So should I just, like, write down the numbers or something?
NURSE: Write them down or take a picture — whatever works for you. Also, we're going to consider a referral to nephrology just to make sure your kidneys are doing okay with everything that's going on, especially given the numbers we're seeing and the leg swelling.
PATIENT: Um, nephrology — that's the kidney doctor, right? Is that serious? Like, should I be worried?
NURSE: It's really just a precaution at this point. We want to make sure nothing's slipping through the cracks, especially with your blood sugar and the swelling. But right now, let's focus on getting you stabilized and having you be more consistent with your meds — including restarting the doxycycline, okay?
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, I can do that. I feel a little better actually just knowing what's going on. The chest pain is way less now than it was this morning.
NURSE: That's good to hear. Keep monitoring how you feel, get that blood pressure log going, and we'll set up that nephrology appointment. Any questions before you head out?
PATIENT: No, I think I got it. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

NURSE: Alright Andrew, let's just go through how you've been feeling since you left the hospital. Any issues with that leg, or—?
PATIENT: Yeah, so my leg's still pretty swollen but like, it's getting better I think. Been going down over the past few days at least.
NURSE: That's good to hear. And the leg swelling—is that uncomfortable or just bothersome when you're moving around?
PATIENT: It's like, moderate I guess? Like I notice it, especially at the end of the day, but it's not like I can't walk or anything.
NURSE: Okay, got it. Now, they told you you have a pulmonary embolism, right? That blood clot in your lung? Have you had any chest pain or shortness of breath since yesterday?
PATIENT: No, nothing like that. But um, I've just been really wiped out. Like, fatigue is pretty bad right now, honestly. Started yesterday and I just can't get energy.
NURSE: When you say you can't get energy, is that all day or more in the afternoons?
PATIENT: It's like, it comes and goes, but yeah, mostly I'm just worn out. I barely made it through breakfast this morning.
NURSE: Mmhm. Have you noticed any night sweats at all? Like, waking up in the middle of the night drenched?
PATIENT: No, actually I haven't. Sleep's been okay on that front—nothing weird going on at night.
NURSE: Alright. So let's talk about your meds real quick. I know you're on a couple of things. You're taking the empagliflozin, that's the 25 mg once a day—are you remembering to take that?
PATIENT: Um, yeah, well—to be honest I stopped taking that one. I wasn't sure if I was supposed to keep going with it after everything, so I just kind of quit.
NURSE: Okay, we'll talk about restarting that. What about the pioglitazone? The 15 mg in the morning?
PATIENT: I think I'm taking it? I mean, I've tried to, but I'm not gonna lie—some mornings I forget. It's sitting there but like, I'm not always great about it.
NURSE: Understandable. And the azithromycin, the antibiotic—you got that one filled, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, I got that. It's the 250 mg, one a day. Wait, no—actually I think it was 500 mg. Let me think... yeah, 500 mg. Sorry.
NURSE: No worries. And are you taking that pretty regularly?
PATIENT: Um, probably not as consistent as I should be, if I'm being honest. Some days I remember, some days I don't.
NURSE: We got a quick oxygen check when you came in—you're sitting at 93%, which is good. Okay so here's what we're gonna do. We need to get some bloodwork done to see how things are progressing, especially given the pulmonary embolism and make sure your clotting markers are where they need to be. Sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's fine. I can do that.
NURSE: Great. And I want you to check your blood pressure at home, just once a day in the morning if you can. We have a monitor we're gonna send home with you. Can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. And then I come back here for the bloodwork, or do they do it at my regular doctor?
NURSE: We'll get you scheduled here. I'll give you the appointment before you leave. Any other questions or concerns right now?
PATIENT: I don't think so. I mean, just... when can I go back to normal stuff? Like working out or whatever?
NURSE: Let's see how you do over the next couple weeks. Once we get that bloodwork back and know you're stable, we can talk about it. For now, take it easy and keep an eye on that leg.

CARE_COORDINATOR: Brooklyn, thanks for coming in this morning. The clinician is just finishing up with another patient, so we've got maybe two minutes. How are you feeling today?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, same old same old. Actually, wait—I've been wanting to mention this. My feet have been acting up. Like, really bad numbness in the feet, and it wasn't like this when I saw Dr. Martinez last time.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Got it. That's good to flag. We'll definitely make sure the clinician knows. Let me just pull up your vitals real quick. You've been keeping up with your medications okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah. The levothyroxine—that's the thyroid one, right?—I take it every single day. No misses there. And the other one, the colchicine, 0.6 mg, I haven't skipped a dose either.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Morning, Brooklyn. I'm Lisa, the nurse practitioner. Okay, so I'm looking at your chart and I see we're following up on your type 2 diabetes mellitus, plus your hypothyroidism—your thyroid thing. How've you been feeling overall?
PATIENT: Oh, better actually. My energy's come back a lot. The fatigue was pretty rough for a while, like I couldn't even get through my yoga class, but that's improved. So that's good.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's really good to hear. But I want to dig into what care_coordinator mentioned—this numbness in your feet. When did that start?
PATIENT: Uh, maybe three weeks? It's not like pins and needles exactly. It's more like... my whole foot feels kind of distant, you know? My friend was telling me about her carpal tunnel syndrome the other day—completely different thing—but it got me thinking about nerve stuff.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. Yeah, different issues, but I'm glad you brought it up. We should definitely look at your blood sugar control more closely, because that can affect your nerves. That's actually something I want to address today. We might need to tweak your levothyroxine as well—your TSH numbers from last month were a little high.
PATIENT: Wait, so you're gonna change my thyroid medicine? I thought I was doing okay on the, um, the 100 mcg dose.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Just a small adjustment. Sometimes with hypothyroidism, you need to dial it in just right. The fatigue you had could've been related to that. So I'd like to bump your levothyroxine up slightly, and then we'll recheck your levels in about six weeks.
PATIENT: Okay, that makes sense. And what about my feet? Should I be worried about that?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We'll keep a close eye on it. That numbness in the feet can sometimes come with your type 2 diabetes mellitus if your glucose levels drift up. That's why I want to get some fresh bloodwork done to see where you're at. That'll tell us a lot. Let me get the levothyroxine down: 100 mcg, once a day, and you're taking it every day.
CARE_COORDINATOR: So we'll be ordering bloodwork, Brooklyn. That'll probably go out tomorrow, and you can get it done at the lab near you. It's just a quick finger stick usually.
PATIENT: No problem. I've done it a million times. Um, and you said you're changing the levothyroxine, so do I just start that right away, or—
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: The care coordinator will send you the updated prescription today. Same time of day, same way—just the new dose. Keep taking your colchicine, 0.6 mg, exactly like you are now. No changes there. You're doing great with your adherence.
PATIENT: Good, good. I'm kind of religious about my meds. My sister always forgets hers, drives me crazy, but I'm not like that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's excellent. And we'll get that bloodwork order to your email by end of day. Try to get it done within the next week or two, okay? Then come back in about six weeks to see how everything's looking.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And Brooklyn, if that numbness gets worse, or if you feel anything else weird—tingling going up your leg, trouble with balance—you call us. Don't wait.
PATIENT: Will do. Thanks, Lisa. So I pick up the new levothyroxine at my pharmacy?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Yep, same place as always. You're all set. See you in six weeks!
PATIENT: Perfect. Oh, and tell my doctor hello from Brooklyn—wait, that's you! Sorry, I'm being silly. Thanks again.

NURSE: Ava, good to see you back. I've got your vitals here and we need to go over a few things before you leave today.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. I'm just... I've been feeling pretty tired lately, like, the past couple weeks I just can't get going in the morning, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: That fatigue you're describing—has anything changed with your sleep schedule or your mood?
PATIENT: Well, my major depressive disorder, it's been a little harder to manage recently, if I'm being honest. Some days are just harder than others. But the tiredness is different, it's like a heaviness.
NURSE: And we checked your blood pressure just now—it came in at 158/86, which is running a bit higher than we'd like to see.
PATIENT: Oh no, really? Um, I've been taking my lisinopril, 20 mg, every morning, I haven't missed a single dose. I'm really good about that one.
CARE_COORDINATOR: You're doing all the right things there. But I want to circle back—you mentioned feeling tired for a couple weeks. Have you noticed any shortness of breath, or maybe a cough that's been bothering you?
PATIENT: Oh my God, yes, actually! The cough started like last week and it's getting worse, like really bad. I thought maybe it was allergies or something, but it just keeps going.
NURSE: Is it a dry cough or are you bringing anything up when you cough?
PATIENT: Mostly dry, I guess, but it's pretty intense. And now I'm getting a little dizzy, which started just a few days ago, and um, that's worsening too, honestly.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, so we've got the fatigue, the cough, and now some dizziness that's getting worse over the past few days. Any swelling in your legs at all?
PATIENT: No, no leg swelling, thankfully. My legs feel normal, just my energy that's all messed up.
NURSE: We're going to look into a few things here. One concern is whether we might be dealing with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, though we're not certain yet. That's why we want to get you to pulmonology to rule out other possibilities with that cough.
PATIENT: Heart failure? Wait—no, I mean, is that... what does that mean exactly?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's a condition where the heart doesn't pump as efficiently as it should. But let's not get ahead of ourselves. First we need the pulmonology consult to see if there's something going on with your lungs causing these symptoms. That's the most pressing thing right now.
PATIENT: Okay, um, so I go to pulmonology? How soon would that be? And I'm still taking my canagliflozin, the 300 mg once a day, that hasn't changed, right?
NURSE: Keep taking that exactly as you have been. I'll get the referral going to pulmonology today, and they usually get people in within two to three weeks. We can also discuss scheduling a follow-up visit with your doctor in the meantime if you want to check in before the specialist sees you.
PATIENT: Yeah, maybe a follow-up visit would be good. At least to see if anything's different by then, I guess. Oh, and I'm also still on naproxen, 250 mg twice a day for my joint pain, and I haven't missed those either.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good, you're staying on top of your medications. We'll want to keep an eye on your blood pressure, especially with everything else going on. Any questions before we set up those appointments?
PATIENT: I don't think so, just... hopefully it's nothing too serious with the heart thing. The cough and the dizziness just came on so fast, you know?
NURSE: We're going to get you the answers you need. One step at a time.

text:
PHYSICIAN: Greyson, I see here you were discharged about two weeks ago—let me just touch base and see how you're managing at home.
PATIENT: Yeah, well, I'm okay mostly, but my legs have been really puffy, you know? Like, swelling I can't get down. It's been going on for a month now, maybe longer, and honestly it's getting worse not better.
PHYSICIAN: The leg swelling you're noticing—that's something we need to pay attention to, especially with your deep vein thrombosis diagnosis. When exactly did you start noticing it getting worse?
PATIENT: Oh, um, past couple weeks maybe? I mean the swelling's been there longer, but in the last—I dunno, week and a half?—it's really picked up. And I gotta tell you, I've been feeling kind of winded. Like just walking from the bedroom to the kitchen and I'm catching my breath.
PHYSICIAN: How long has that shortness of breath been going on?
PATIENT: Three days, maybe four. Not sure exactly when it started, but I noticed it Tuesday or Wednesday. It's annoying, Doc. I don't like feeling like an old man, wait—I mean, I *am* an old man—but you know what I mean.
PHYSICIAN: I do. Let me get your blood pressure and pulse real quick. Here we go—124 over 78, and your heart rate's running at 104. That's a little elevated. Now, let's talk about your medications. I want to make sure you're staying on top of them. You're still taking the amlodipine?
PATIENT: The amlodipine—yeah, I mean, I'm *pretty sure* I've been taking that, the 10 mg once a day. But honestly I haven't been... um, super consistent, if I'm being straight with you. Some days I remember, some days I'm not sure.
PHYSICIAN: That's useful to know. What about the losartan we talked about before—are you taking that still?
PATIENT: No, actually I stopped that. I was taking it for a while, the 50 mg, but then I just kinda quit. I don't remember exactly when. Figured I had enough pills to keep track of, you know?
PHYSICIAN: Alright, we're going to need to get you back on the losartan—your kidney function with the chronic kidney disease stage 3 needs that support, and your blood pressure situation makes it important too. So 50 mg once daily, and let's set you up with a pill organizer or something so you're not missing doses. Sound good? Your blood pressure came back at 124/78.
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I can do that. A pill organizer might actually help. My daughter's been getting on me about this stuff anyway.
PHYSICIAN: Good. One more thing—I noticed in your chart it says you have a drink or two most nights. How accurate is that?
PATIENT: Ah, well, yeah, I have my whiskey before bed usually. Maybe a beer with dinner sometimes. Why? Is that a problem?
PHYSICIAN: With your kidney situation and the fact that your blood pressure's up and your heart rate's elevated right now, I really think you should cut back on alcohol. Can you do that—maybe bring it down to just a couple times a week instead?
PATIENT: I mean... okay. I'll try. It's my ritual, but I get it. I haven't been gaining any weight at least—still the same as I was, so that's something.
PHYSICIAN: That's good there's no weight loss happening. One more thing though—your dad, did he have any heart problems you know about?
PATIENT: Oh, my father? Yeah, he had some kind of heart rhythm thing—atrial fibrillation, I think they called it. He had to take medication for it most of his later years. Why, you think I might get that?
PHYSICIAN: It's just something to monitor, especially with the symptoms you're describing. We'll keep an eye on things. So here's what we're doing: you're back on the losartan, you're going to keep the amlodipine and actually stay consistent with it—use that pill organizer. You're going to cut back on alcohol. And I want you to watch that leg swelling and your breathing. If either one gets worse, you call us right away, okay?
PATIENT: Okay, Doc. I'll do my best. And I'll get my daughter to help me stay on track with the pills and the drinking thing.
PHYSICIAN: That's a good plan. We'll check in in a couple weeks and see how you're doing. Any questions before you go?
PATIENT: No, I think that covers it. Thanks for seeing me today.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So Elaine, it's been what, about three weeks since you got out? How are you managing at home?
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, I mean—I'm trying, but honestly I've been pretty exhausted. Like, I woke up Monday and just hit a wall with the fatigue, and it's been really bad ever since. I can barely get through the day.

PATIENT: Like this? *blows* How'd I do?
PHYSICIAN: 320 L/min. That's solid. Now, let's talk about your meds. You're still on the chlorthalidone, right? The blood pressure one?
PATIENT: Yeah, 25 mg every morning. I haven't skipped a single dose—I've got it set up with my pill organizer so I don't forget. And I'm taking that amoxicillin you gave me for the sinus infection thing. 875 mg twice a day, and I've been really consistent with that one too, actually.
PHYSICIAN: Good, that's really good adherence. How about the ibuprofen for aches?
PATIENT: Um, the 200 mg? Honestly, I've been kind of hit or miss with that. I missed a couple doses last week and then forgot about it again yesterday because with all this other stuff going on, I kind of lost track of it.
PHYSICIAN: That's okay, it's only as needed anyway. But with the symptoms you're having—the chest pain especially—I want to bump you up on the amoxicillin. Let's go 875 mg three times a day now, so we make sure we're staying ahead of any infection that might be contributing.
PATIENT: Three times? Okay, so I take it with breakfast, lunch, and dinner kind of thing?
PHYSICIAN: Exactly. And honestly, I'd also like to get you in with pulmonology—the lung specialists—just to make sure nothing's brewing there with the shortness of breath. It's probably nothing, but better safe.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, I can do that. Um, and—do I need to come back here for a follow-up visit with you, or should I wait and see what the pulmonology people say?
PHYSICIAN: Let's plan on a follow-up visit here in about three weeks, after you've seen the lung team. That way we can compare notes and see where you're at. In the meantime, if things get worse—like if you can't catch your breath or the chest pain gets sharper—you're going to want to head to the ER or call 911. Don't tough it out.
PATIENT: Got it. I will. I appreciate you taking this seriously.

NURSE: Roger, come on back. We're running a couple minutes behind today, but I'm gonna get you all set. How're you doing?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, hanging in there. Been a rough couple days if I'm being honest. Started noticing yesterday I just don't have much appetite, which is weird for me.
NURSE: Mm-hmm. Poor appetite—is that something new, or has it been going on for a while?
PATIENT: Just since yesterday. Nothing crazy, it's just kind of... I dunno, mild. Like, I'll look at food and think, 'eh.' Not like I'm sick or anything.
NURSE: Got it. Any other changes in how you've been feeling? Sleep any different?
PATIENT: Yeah, actually, my sleep has been getting worse—wait, no. Um. It just started yesterday, like the appetite thing. Difficulty sleeping, I guess. It's not too bad though, just tossing around more than usual.
NURSE: Okay, so both the appetite and the sleep thing are new as of yesterday. Let's circle back to that. First, let me just get your weight. Step on the scale for me.
PATIENT: Sure thing.
NURSE: All right, you're coming in at 204 pounds today. And I see here you've got heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and gastroesophageal reflux disease on your problem list. How are you managing with all that lately?
PATIENT: The reflux thing—you mean the acid reflux? Yeah, I mean, it's been okay. I take the Tums when I need to, you know? As for the heart thing, uh, it's scary to think about still sometimes, but I'm trying to stay on top of it.
NURSE: Right. And your medications—let me check where you're at. Are you still taking the acetaminophen, 500 mg, when you need it?
PATIENT: Oh, um, no actually. I stopped taking that a while back. I don't know, I just kept forgetting it, and then I figured my back wasn't bothering me as much anyway, so I just... stopped picking it up.
NURSE: Okay, no problem. What about the prednisone? That's supposed to be 10 mg once a day. How's that going? Let me get the acetaminophen down: 500 mg, as needed, and you're not taking it anymore.
PATIENT: Um, the prednisone... I mean, I'm on hold with that one right now. But honestly I can't remember if I'm supposed to take it every day or what. I know I have the bottle somewhere.
NURSE: All right, we'll clarify that in a sec. And the lisinopril, the 40 mg—how's that one?
PATIENT: Oh, that one I take every morning without fail. I remember that one. Every single day.
NURSE: Excellent, that's really good to hear. Before we move on, I want to get a blood pressure on you right now, just to check.
PATIENT: Sure, go ahead.
NURSE: Hmm. Roger, I'm getting a reading of 178 over 115. That's quite high. I need to get you to the emergency department to make sure everything's okay. This isn't something we can manage just here today.
PATIENT: Wait, really? Like, am I okay? Should I be worried?
NURSE: I want you to get checked out right away, just to be safe. With your heart failure history and this reading, we need to make sure nothing's happening. I'm gonna call over and let them know you're coming. But before you go, let me just say—once you're stable, it's really important that you check your blood pressure at home regularly, okay? We need that data.
PATIENT: Okay, okay. I can do that. I have one of those cuffs at home already.
NURSE: Perfect. And after the ED visit, you're going to need some follow-up bloodwork to look at your cardiac enzymes and your metabolic panel. We'll set that up. We're also gonna get you a referral to endocrinology because we need to evaluate your metabolic status, especially given everything else going on. But the emergency department visit is first priority.
PATIENT: All right. Thanks for catching that. I'm ready to head over.
