text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Hey Eva, how're you feeling since you got home? Any issues we should talk about?
PATIENT: Um, okay, so—well, I woke up this morning and I just feel like completely wiped out, like, really exhausted. I don't know if that's normal or not. I mean, I was fine yesterday.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Got it. Fatigue can happen in the first week or two after discharge, but let's dig in a bit. How's the incision looking otherwise?
PATIENT: The incision's... it's sore. Like, it started bothering me over the weekend, and it's getting a little better now, but it's still pretty tender if I touch it. Should I be worried?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That timeline sounds reasonable. Incision pain usually peaks around day three, four, and then starts to ease. You keeping it clean and dry?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I am. I shower and—oh, and um, another thing. I've had this weird dizziness, like, not super bad, but it's there. Started about a week ago, maybe a little before I got home. It's getting better though, I think.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Mild dizziness in that timeframe is pretty common too. Let me ask you something though—have you noticed any headaches? Any head pain that feels different from your normal headaches, maybe pounding or one-sided?
PATIENT: Hmm, actually, now that you mention it, I did have this really bad headache yesterday. Like, the back of my head was killing me, and I felt kind of nauseous with it. Do you think that's a migraine? I don't usually get those.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Could be. We'll keep an eye on that. But here's what I'm more concerned about right now—you mentioned fatigue this morning. And I want to check: have you been sweating a lot at night, like, waking up drenched?
PATIENT: No, no, nothing like that. My sheets are fine. I don't have night sweats or anything. But honestly, I've been feeling short of breath. Like, just walking to the kitchen I get a bit winded, and it's gotten worse over the past few days. That worries me a little bit.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, that's something I want to take seriously. Let me listen to your lungs real quick.
PATIENT: Is it the blood clot thing again? Because I thought that was all resolved—the deep vein thrombosis is gone, right? I was so worried about that when I was in the hospital.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: The deep vein thrombosis resolved, yes, but I want to make sure we're not seeing any other complications. Your shortness of breath combined with the other symptoms is worth investigating. Let me check your peak flow—come on, I want to see what you're putting out.
PATIENT: Okay, um... *blowing* ... how is that?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You're at 320 L/min, which is actually decent, but not as strong as I'd like to see. We need to figure out what's driving that shortness of breath. By the way, are you taking your medications consistently?
PATIENT: Well, I'm taking them, but I'll be honest—I'm not, like, super disciplined about it. The metoprolol succinate, I'm supposed to take 100 mg once a day, and the atenolol at 50 mg, and I do take them most days, but sometimes I forget or I'll skip a day. Is that bad?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Yeah, that's actually pretty important right now. Both of those need to be every single day—no skipping. That inconsistency could be contributing to what you're feeling. And I want to pull some labs to get a full picture. We should do some bloodwork to see where you're at.
PATIENT: Like, more blood tests? Okay. Um, also—my grandfather, he had colon cancer, so I guess that's something to keep in mind? Or does that matter?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We'll definitely note that family history of colon cancer. We can talk screening down the line. But right now let's focus on what's going on. We checked your hemoglobin a1c at your last visit and it came back at 8.6, which is higher than we want. That could be related to how you're feeling.
PATIENT: Oh, wow. So that's... not good? I mean, I thought I was managing that okay.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's something we can work on together, especially with consistent medication and maybe some lifestyle tweaks. But listen, I'm going to refer you to cardiology to rule some things out. I want a fresh set of eyes on what might be causing the shortness of breath and your other symptoms.
PATIENT: Cardiology? Like a heart specialist? That sounds kind of scary. Do you think it's my heart?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I'm not saying there is something, but given your history and what you're reporting, it makes sense to have them take a look. Better to be sure. The referral to cardiology will get you in within a couple of weeks, and in the meantime, stick with those meds every single day without fail. Deal?
PATIENT: Yeah, okay, I can do that. And I'll get the bloodwork done?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Yep, I'll have the lab order ready for you before you leave. And if anything gets worse—if the shortness of breath suddenly spikes or you develop new symptoms, you call me or head to urgent care. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, I will. Thank you.

PHYSICIAN: Hey Raymond, good to see you again. I've got your chart here from the last couple months. So tell me, how have things been going with your breathing since we last touched base?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, mostly better actually. Like the shortness of breath that I was dealing with before—that's definitely improving. But I gotta be honest, I've been feeling some chest tightness that's been kind of bugging me, and it's been going on since maybe right after my last visit.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, chest tightness—that's worth paying attention to. On a scale of zero to ten, where would you put it pain-wise?
PATIENT: I'd say it's a 5 out of 10, so it's there but not like debilitating or anything. More annoying than anything else.
PHYSICIAN: Alright, that's helpful. And the shortness of breath—you're saying that's trending better? Any pattern to when it happens?
PATIENT: Yeah, definitely better. I mean, I notice it less when I'm just walking around, you know? Oh, and I've been dealing with fatigue—well, actually that just started yesterday, so it's getting worse. No wait, I mean—sorry, I'm confusing myself. It started yesterday, so I can't really say if it's getting worse or not yet, you know?
PHYSICIAN: No worries, that makes sense. So fatigue kicked in just yesterday. Have you noticed any weight loss at all, or are you stable with that?
PATIENT: No, I haven't lost any weight. Pretty much staying where I was, which is good I guess.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Now let's talk about your medications. You're still on the doxycycline, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, I'm taking it. The 100 mg twice a day—I'm pretty good about that one. I take it every single day, no problem.
PHYSICIAN: That's excellent adherence. What about the aspirin? How's that going? And there's the check your blood pressure at home to think about too.
PATIENT: Um, the aspirin—I mean, I've got it, I'm taking it. The 325 mg once a day, but honestly, I'm not super consistent. Some days I remember, some days I don't. I know I should be better about it.
PHYSICIAN: I hear you. That's actually something we might want to adjust anyway. Before we get there, is there anything else going on? Any health stuff running in your family we should keep an eye on?
PATIENT: Well, my mom—she's got type 2 diabetes mellitus, so that's always been something I think about, especially with my lifestyle and all. That's probably why you had me on all this stuff in the first place, right?
PHYSICIAN: Yeah, that family history is definitely part of the picture. Okay, so here's what I'm thinking with the aspirin—I'd like to adjust that dose for you. And given everything, I really want you to try to cut back on alcohol, okay? How much are you typically drinking?
PATIENT: I mean, I don't go crazy or anything, but I probably have a few drinks a couple times a week. I can definitely cut back on alcohol. That shouldn't be too hard.
PHYSICIAN: Good, I'm glad you're open to that. And one more thing—I'd like you to start checking your blood pressure at home. We can get you a home monitor, or if you already have one, use that. Can you do that regularly, like a few times a week?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. I've got one at home actually, so I'm good there. How often were you thinking—like, same time every day?
PHYSICIAN: Morning and evening is ideal, or at least a couple times a week if that's easier for you. Just so we have a sense of how you're tracking. We'll follow up on all this in about four weeks, and we'll see how the chest tightness is doing too. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds good. Thanks, doc. I'll definitely work on those things.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So I pulled up your labs from last week, Leah. Let's walk through some of them together—starting with your blood sugar, which came back at 124 when you were fasting. That's a little higher than where we want to be.
PATIENT: Oh gosh, really? I thought I was doing better with my diet. Um, you know, I cut back on sweets and everything.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You're definitely putting in the effort. But what really jumped out at me was your hemoglobin a1c—that's your three-month average—and it came in at 9.2, which tells me we need to get a better handle on things.
PATIENT: Nine point two? Hmm. Is that... that's not good, is it? Sorry, I get confused with all these numbers.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Not great, honestly. We want to see that lower. But before we talk about adjustments, tell me—how are you feeling day-to-day? Any symptoms bothering you lately?
PATIENT: Well, that's why I wanted to come in. I've had this dizziness that started maybe two weeks ago, and it's really quite bad, you know? Like, some mornings I stand up and the room just spins. My daughter actually said I should go to the emergency department after one bad spell, but I didn't think it was that serious.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, that's important. We're going to need to figure out what's going on there. How often is this happening?
PATIENT: Maybe a couple times a week? And, oh, I've also been getting these headaches that just won't quit. They're not terrible, but they're bothering me, especially in the afternoons. And—wait, no, let me think—the muscle aches I had are actually getting better, so that's one thing going right.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright, so we've got the dizziness as the main thing, then these headaches that are worsening. Let's talk about your medications. You're on the torsemide, the water pill—20 mg once a day. How's that going?
PATIENT: Oh, I take that every single morning, no problem. I don't forget that one. It's the other stuff I sometimes mix up.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good, consistency is huge with that one. Now, I'm looking back and you used to take metoprolol tartrate, 25 mg twice a day for your blood pressure. Why'd you stop that?
PATIENT: Um, I think—didn't you say something about side effects, or was I having trouble remembering to take it? No wait, I remember now. You said it could lower my blood pressure too much, and honestly, I was tired of taking so many pills. So I just... stopped.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We probably should revisit that with the dizziness you're describing. But first, the naproxen situation. You're supposed to be on it for inflammation, 250 mg twice a day, but I'm not sure how consistent you've actually been with it lately.
PATIENT: Yeah, I take it when I remember, but not like clockwork. My coworker Sarah just got diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome and she's been complaining about it constantly, which made me realize I should probably be more regular with my own pain stuff. So, um, what do we do?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Let's adjust that dose down. We might try 250 mg once instead of twice, and see if you tolerate it better. Consistency matters more than the amount anyway. Also, I want to circle back to the other thing—your gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD as people usually call it. How's that?
PATIENT: Oh, that's been okay actually. I've been watching what I eat more carefully.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. And speaking of diet, one thing that could really help with the blood sugar and your blood pressure is if you could cut back on salt. That's going to be important for us.
PATIENT: Okay, I can do that. I know I use the salt shaker more than I probably should.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright. I also want to get some fresh bloodwork done in the next month or so to see where we're at. We'll probably do labs again and reassess. Given everything you're experiencing, especially that severe dizziness, I think we should get you checked out at the emergency department today just to make sure there's nothing urgent going on.
PATIENT: The emergency department? Like, right now? Oh wow, okay. I wasn't expecting that, but if you think it's necessary. Should I have my daughter drive me?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Yeah, that's a good call. Let them know about the dizziness, the headache, and the fact that your blood pressures have been variable since you stopped the metoprolol tartrate. They'll get to the bottom of it. We'll touch base after their workup.

CARE_COORDINATOR: Hey Elliott, the doc's about five minutes behind but just wants to make sure we get your meds sorted out today — you doing okay in the waiting area?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I'm fine. Though honestly, I've been having some pretty bad chest pain the last couple weeks, like really bad. I wasn't sure if it was something to worry about or just, I dunno, indigestion or something.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, we'll definitely have the doctor check that out. Let me just flag that in here. And how are you feeling otherwise?
PATIENT: Well, um, my legs have been swelling up pretty bad this morning. Like my ankles especially. It's been getting worse as the day goes on, which is weird because I just woke up with it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Got it. And is there any shortness of breath happening at all?
PATIENT: Yeah, actually, that started this morning too. It's pretty much stayed the same since I got up, just kinda lingering there. Nothing's really getting better or worse with the breathing.
PHYSICIAN: Elliott, hey. Sorry for the wait. So I'm seeing you today for medication reconciliation and cardiovascular follow-up. Let's talk about your transient ischemic attack, okay? How are you doing since that episode?
PATIENT: Oh, you mean the TIA? Yeah, I'm... I mean, I'm managing. But I gotta ask, are these new symptoms connected? The swelling in my legs, and I can't catch my breath like I usually can.
PHYSICIAN: Could be, that's why I want to go through everything with you today. Quick question — you're not feeling queasy or nauseous or anything like that?
PATIENT: No nausea, thankfully. I mean, I feel pretty crummy, but at least my stomach's okay. The chest pain though — that's what's really bugging me. It started after my last visit with you, and it's just been sitting there, you know, same intensity.
PHYSICIAN: Alright, let's get into the meds then. You're on type 2 diabetes mellitus medications, and we've got you on a couple other things too. Walk me through what you're actually taking and how often.
PATIENT: Okay, so there's... um, what's the one for gout? Allopurinol? Yeah, 100 mg, I'm supposed to take that every day. But honestly, I miss it sometimes, like maybe once a week I'll space it and forget.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And the dabigatran — that's your blood thinner. How's that going?
PATIENT: Same story, you know? I take it, but I forget. It's 150 mg twice a day, so I'm supposed to do morning and night, but I'll miss one here and there. Then there's azithromycin, which is — wait, no, actually I'm not totally sure how often I'm supposed to take that one. Is it every day? I thought it was, but it's just 250 mg and I just... I can't quite remember the schedule.
PHYSICIAN: That's the azithromycin — let me look that up. Okay, so that's a daily medication, 250 mg once daily. We need to get you some clarity on the dosing schedule. And we talked about cutting back on the alcohol at your last visit, right? How's that been going?
PATIENT: Yeah, I agreed to cut back on alcohol. I've been doing better, like I'm not going out as much on the weekends anymore. Still might have a couple beers now and then but nothing like before.
PHYSICIAN: That's good to hear. Now, because we're managing your type 2 diabetes mellitus and you've had a transient ischemic attack, we want to get a nephrology referral in place. It's important to have someone look at your kidneys given everything going on.
PATIENT: Nephrology? That's... the kidney people, right? Is that because of the diabetes or like, the leg swelling? I'm trying to understand what's connected to what here.
PHYSICIAN: Both, actually. Diabetes can affect the kidneys over time, and your kidney function helps us manage everything else — your blood pressure, fluid balance. The leg swelling could be related to kidney function too, so we want to get that checked out.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We'll get that nephrology referral submitted today, and they should contact you within a couple weeks to schedule. In the meantime, let's make sure you've got written instructions for your meds, okay? Especially the azithromycin so there's no confusion.
PATIENT: Yeah, please. That would help a lot. Oh, um — one more thing. This chest pain, like, should I be worried? Is that something that happens with the TIA or is that separate?
PHYSICIAN: The chest pain — we need to monitor that. Since it started after your last visit and hasn't changed, it's not acutely getting worse, which is reassuring. But given your cardiac history and the leg swelling and shortness of breath all starting this morning, I want to be cautious. We should get an EKG done today just to be safe.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah. Yeah, that makes sense. I appreciate that. So is there anything else I should be doing? Like with lifestyle stuff?
PHYSICIAN: Beyond what we talked about — the alcohol reduction, which you're doing well with — I want you to try to be more consistent with the medications. Maybe set phone reminders or use a pill organizer for dabigatran and allopurinol, since you're missing those. And definitely get that nephrology appointment scheduled as soon as they call.

PHYSICIAN: Alright Serenity, so it's been what, about three weeks since you left the hospital? How are you actually doing at home?
PATIENT: Well, I've been okay, but honestly I'm just so tired all the time. Like, I'll get up in the morning and by lunch I'm exhausted. This fatigue is just relentless, you know?
PHYSICIAN: That's something we need to dig into. When you say exhausted, is this different from how you usually feel, or has this been going on for years?
PATIENT: No, this is new—well, I mean, it got worse when I got sick. Um, the hospital people said my heart isn't pumping the way it should. They called it heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which terrified me, to be honest.
PHYSICIAN: I hear you. That sounds scary. But we're going to work through this together. Have you noticed anything else—maybe like you're running out of breath doing things you used to do?
PATIENT: Yes, actually. I walked to the mailbox yesterday and I got so winded. This shortness of breath started just a few days ago, and I wasn't expecting it to hit me like that.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, we're definitely going to monitor that closely. No lightheadedness though, right? You're not feeling like the room is spinning or anything?
PATIENT: Oh no, I haven't had any dizziness. My daughter asked me the same thing last week and I told her the same thing—I feel steady on my feet, at least.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Now let me ask about your medications. Are you taking everything the way we discussed?
PATIENT: Um, mostly. So I'm taking the valsartan—the one that's 160 mg—every single morning, I'm very consistent with that one. And the sitagliptin, that's 100 mg, I'm taking that every day too.
PHYSICIAN: Great. How about the other ones we talked about? Just to confirm — the amitriptyline, that's 10 mg at bedtime, and it sounds like you've been not taking it anymore. Your blood pressure came back at 124/92.
PATIENT: Well, the metoprolol tartrate, the 25 mg that I was supposed to take twice a day? I actually stopped that one. It was making me feel weird and I didn't like it, so I just decided not to take it anymore.
PHYSICIAN: I appreciate you being honest about that. We do need to talk about restarting it, because it really helps your heart. But first, what about the amitriptyline for sleep?
PATIENT: Oh, I'm not taking that anymore either. I took it for a few days but it made me groggy in the mornings, so I stopped. Is that a problem?
PHYSICIAN: It's not ideal, but we can adjust. Let me get your blood pressure here real quick. Okay, I'm getting 124 over 92. That's a bit high.
PATIENT: Is that bad? I haven't really been watching it at home or anything.
PHYSICIAN: That's actually something we want you to start doing. I want you to check your blood pressure at home, maybe every few days, and keep a little log for me. We have a home monitor you can borrow.
PATIENT: Okay, I can do that. My daughter has one of those gadgets, so maybe she can help me get the hang of it.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. Also, about the medications—we're going to adjust your sitagliptin dose, bring it up a bit to help your blood sugar. And we really do need to get you back on the metoprolol tartrate, even if you're not excited about it.
PATIENT: Hmm, I was hoping we could skip that one. But I guess if my heart needs it... Do you think once I start it again, the weird feeling will go away?
PHYSICIAN: Sometimes it takes a few days to adjust, yes. We're also managing your high cholesterol—your hyperlipidemia—and that's part of why the whole medication plan matters. It all works together. You with me?
PATIENT: Yeah, I think so. It's a lot to keep track of, but I understand the point. I really don't want to end up back in the hospital.

text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright Jeffrey, I see here you were in last week with that chest stuff going on. What's been happening since then?
PATIENT: Yeah, so the tightness—like the chest tightness—it started like three days ago and it was pretty bad, you know, really bad. But honestly, um, it's getting better now. I was kind of freaked out at first, not gonna lie.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, that's good it's improving. And when you say it was severe—on a scale of one to ten, where did it max out?
PATIENT: I'd say like an eight. Maybe eight-and-a-half. I couldn't really do my normal stuff for the first couple days, and then, wait—no, actually the wheezing thing started too, that was like Monday or so. That's still happening a little bit.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: The wheezing's lingering then. And we talked about the community-acquired pneumonia last time—how are you feeling otherwise? Energy level okay?
PATIENT: Um, I mean, I've been pretty tired, which I know is partly the anemia thing, the low blood count or whatever. I get winded easier than I used to. Oh, and I've had that heartburn stuff acting up. The reflux, I mean—gastroesophageal reflux disease, that's what my doctor called it before—it's been bothering me, especially at night.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Right, so the reflux is flaring. We're managing that. Let me ask you about your meds real quick—are you taking the nebivolol like we talked about?
PATIENT: Yeah, mostly. I mean, it's the 5 mg one, and I'm supposed to take it every day, but honestly sometimes I just forget. Like, I'll miss it a couple times a week. Is that bad?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Consistency matters with that one, so try to set a reminder on your phone or keep it by your toothbrush. What about the semaglutide—how's that going?
PATIENT: Um, that one's actually on hold right now. We decided to pause it, and like, I'm not even totally sure I was taking it right before that anyway. It was supposed to be 1 mg once a week, but I probably missed doses. I don't think I was super consistent with it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, that's fine—we'll sort that out. And I see you were on the glipizide for a bit. Are you still taking that? Just to confirm — the glipizide, that's 10 mg once a day, and it sounds like you've been not taking it anymore.
PATIENT: No, actually I stopped that. The 10 mg one, right? I just kind of, um, decided to stop taking it a while back. I probably should have told you, sorry.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We do need to talk through med changes, but let's circle back on that. I want to get your peak flow—go ahead and use the meter real quick.
PATIENT: Sure. Okay, um, 360 L/min. Is that normal or...?

PATIENT: Not really palpitations today. I mean, with the AFib, my heart does that irregular thing sometimes, but today it just feels like pressure. Oh, and my legs—both of them—they're a little swollen, but like, only since Monday, and they're already getting better. At least I think they are.
NURSE: Leg swelling since Monday—have you noticed any changes overnight, is it worse in the morning?
PATIENT: Um, it's mild swelling, really not that bad. But now that I think about it, yeah, it seems a little less puffy than it was yesterday. Could be nothing.
NURSE: We'll keep an eye on that. Any headaches been going on with all this?
PATIENT: No, thankfully I don't have a headache. That's one thing I'm not dealing with today, which is nice. Oh, but I should tell you—my dad, he had breast cancer years back. I don't know if that matters for anything, but I always mention it just in case.
NURSE: Thanks for sharing that. It's good to have that in your history. Now let's talk about your medications. Are you taking your torsemide regularly?
PATIENT: Yeah, the 10 mg—I take that every single day, no problem. I've never missed it. And then there's the insulin aspart that I do with meals, 4 units, and I haven't skipped any of those either.
NURSE: Good. What about the levothyroxine for your thyroid?
PATIENT: Um, okay so that one is the 100 mcg, right? I take it most days, I'm pretty sure, but honestly I can't remember exactly how often I'm supposed to take it or if I miss it sometimes. I think I'm doing it though.
NURSE: Let's make sure you're clear on that—it should be daily just like the others. I'll send you a reminder card. For now, let's talk about monitoring at home. Can you check your blood pressure at home? Do you have a cuff?
PATIENT: I do, actually. My daughter got me one. So yeah, I can definitely check my blood pressure at home and keep track of it.
NURSE: Perfect. Do that daily and bring those readings with you next time. We should probably get some bloodwork done to see how you're doing with all your conditions—the AFib, diabetes, and thyroid. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, sure. When would you need the bloodwork done?
NURSE: We can set that up before you leave today if you want, or you can go to the lab in a day or two. Either way works. But given these symptoms today, sooner is probably better.
PATIENT: Okay, I'll do it today then. Better to get it over with, right?

PHYSICIAN: So Kingston, how've you been feeling since we last saw you a couple months back?
PATIENT: Um, not great to be honest. I've been having these episodes where I get really dizzy, like the room's spinning and everything. It started maybe a week or so after our last visit, and it's gotten pretty bad.
PHYSICIAN: That's concerning. Have you noticed if there's anything that triggers it, or is it pretty random?
PATIENT: It's like, it'll just happen when I stand up sometimes, or even just sitting there. And—oh, I've also been nauseous a lot lately. Like, it's been bugging me more and more, you know? Not like vomiting or anything, but just this gross feeling in my stomach that won't go away.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. And when did the nausea start getting worse?
PATIENT: Maybe the last week, two weeks? And then on top of that, I got this heartburn thing going on. That just popped up like three days ago, and honestly it's just kind of sitting there, not really getting better or worse.
PHYSICIAN: Let me ask you something—are you still taking your medications regularly? We talked about your hypothyroidism and your type 2 diabetes mellitus management when you were here last time.
PATIENT: Oh yeah, so here's the thing. The dapagliflozin—I was taking it, the 5 mg once a day, but honestly I kinda stopped a couple months ago. I don't know, I just forgot about it and then wasn't sure if I needed it anymore.
PHYSICIAN: You stopped the dapagliflozin? Okay, we're gonna need to talk about that. What about the omeprazole for your stomach?
PATIENT: Um, I've been taking that one—the 40 mg, right? Though I gotta be honest, I can't really remember if I'm taking it once a day like you said or if I'm doing it more or less. I just kind of take it when I think about it.
PHYSICIAN: So it's not on a regular schedule. That could be contributing to the heartburn. I also want to ask about your energy levels. How's your fatigue been? Just to confirm — the dapagliflozin, that's 5 mg once a day, and it sounds like you've been stopped taking it.
PATIENT: Dude, I'm exhausted all the time. Like, I wake up already feeling tired, and by afternoon I just want to crash. It's really bad, honestly—I can barely get through work some days.
PHYSICIAN: That's a significant complaint. And the dizziness you mentioned—on a scale of 0 to 10, how bad is it bothering you?
PATIENT: Oh man, I'd say it's a 6 out of 10. It's not like I'm falling over or anything, but it's definitely interfering with my day.
PHYSICIAN: Alright. Here's what I'm thinking. First, we need to restart you on the dapagliflozin, but we're going to adjust the dose—maybe go higher given how your numbers have been trending. We also need to get your omeprazole on a proper schedule, 40 mg every morning with food. And because of the dizziness and the fatigue with your diabetes, I want to get you set up with nephrology to make sure your kidney function is where it should be.
PATIENT: Wait, nephrology? Like, that's the kidney doctors, right? Do you think something's wrong with my kidneys?
PHYSICIAN: We're not saying something's definitely wrong, but with type 2 diabetes mellitus and these symptoms, it's smart to have them take a look. It's just a precaution. Do you feel okay about that plan? And we're adjusting the dapagliflozin to get your blood sugar better controlled.
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, that makes sense. So I start the higher dose of dapagliflozin again, take the omeprazole every day—got it. And I'll go to nephrology whenever they can fit me in.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. The referral will go out today, and we'll call you with the appointment. Come back and see us in about a month so we can check in on how you're doing on the new plan.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Hey Parker, come on in. I see you're here for a med check—how're you doing with everything since we discharged you?
PATIENT: Um, honestly, it's been rough. I've been pretty tired all the time, like, I can barely make it through work. And then yesterday out of nowhere I got really dizzy, like, super bad. It's getting better now but it was kind of scary.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That dizziness sounds like it came on pretty sudden. When exactly did it start, and what were you doing?
PATIENT: Yeah, I was just sitting at my desk at like three in the afternoon and the room started spinning. I had to grab onto my desk. But it's better today, so... I dunno, maybe I just didn't eat enough or something.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We'll keep an eye on that. Let's circle back to the fatigue though—how long has that been going on?
PATIENT: Like, I dunno, couple weeks? It's just constant. I thought it was because of my heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, you know, the... the condition I have. But I'm not sure.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's definitely something that can contribute. Now let me ask about your meds—walk me through what you're actually taking day to day.
PATIENT: Okay so like, I'm taking the warfarin, the 5 mg tablet, and I've been pretty good with that one. I don't miss it. But then there's, um... the dabigatran? I think it's 150 mg twice a day? But honestly I'm not totally sure how often I'm supposed to be taking it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Yeah, dabigatran is definitely twice daily. Can you tell me about the pravastatin?
PATIENT: Oh, the pravastatin... yeah, I stopped taking that one. It was 40 mg and I just, I dunno, I got busy and then I just, wait—no, actually I think I just forgot about it for a while and then I didn't know if I should restart it, so I just... didn't.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Got it. We need to restart that—the cholesterol management is important with your type 2 diabetes mellitus. Your LDL came back at 102, which is okay but we want to optimize it. Let's actually bump your pravastatin dose up a bit.
PATIENT: So like, higher than the 40 mg? Is that... is that gonna be a problem?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: No, you should be fine. We'll go to 60 mg once a day. Your hemoglobin a1c is at 6.8, which is actually pretty decent, but we want to make sure we keep tightening that up. I'm going to refer you to endocrinology so they can really dial in your diabetes management.
PATIENT: Oh okay. Um, my dad actually had a stroke, so like, I guess I should be paying attention to all this stuff more, huh?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's really good context to bring up. Family history of stroke definitely puts you on notice. That's exactly why we need to stay on top of your blood pressure and your cholesterol and your diabetes control.
PATIENT: Yeah, I get it. So what do I need to do?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, so number one: I need you to check your blood pressure at home. Can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I have a cuff. My mom has one too, so I can borrow it if mine doesn't work. How often?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Once a day, same time if you can. Write it down or use your phone. And restart pravastatin at the new dose. Those are your main things. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, that makes sense. So back on the pravastatin, and keep taking the dabigatran twice a day, and the warfarin like I've been doing?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Exactly right. You nailed it. We'll see you in like four weeks and go from there. And when endocrinology gets you scheduled, make sure you show up—they're going to be key for managing all of this.

text:
CARE_COORDINATOR: Bella, thanks for coming back in. I know the drive here can be a hassle—how are you holding up since you got home from the hospital?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, it's been okay. A little tired, but I'm managing. My daughter's been helping me get the groceries and stuff. Um, but actually there's something kind of weird that started a few days ago. My feet have this weird sensation—like, numbness in the feet, if that makes sense? It's mostly at night, and I wasn't sure if I should call or just wait.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's definitely worth mentioning. Can you tell me a bit more about when it started? Was it sudden, or did it kind of creep up on you?
PATIENT: It was like three days ago, I think—yeah, Thursday evening. And also my vision got a little blurry, which was weird. But that one's actually getting better already, so maybe it was nothing. The feet thing though, that's the one bothering me.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Got it. And besides those two things, anything else feeling off? Any changes with your thirst, your energy, any of that?
PATIENT: Well, now that you mention it... I've been drinking a lot more water. Like, I'll have a glass and then twenty minutes later I'm thirsty again. It's just this mild increased thirst, but it's been going on for maybe a month now and it's kind of getting worse, to be honest. I thought maybe it was just the heat.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, we'll want to keep an eye on that. So between your obstructive sleep apnea—the sleep apnea that we talked about before you were discharged—and the chronic kidney disease stage 3, or the chronic kidney disease that's in stage 3, we really need to make sure we're monitoring your blood sugars and kidney function closely. That's why I want to order some fresh bloodwork for you.
PATIENT: More blood tests? I feel like I just got them done. But okay, if you need to. Um, my fasting glucose was, what did the nurse say... it was 152, I think? Is that bad?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's higher than we'd like. That's actually one of the reasons we want to look at your dulaglutide. You're on that once a week, right? The injection?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah. Wait—actually, I'm kind of confused because I've been taking it every day. Is that wrong? I thought maybe since I was having trouble remembering stuff I'd just do it daily instead of trying to remember which day it was supposed to be.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Ah, okay, so you've been taking it more often than prescribed. The dulaglutide is supposed to be once a week—so 0.75 mg once weekly—not daily. But that's good information. We might actually adjust the dulaglutide dose anyway to help bring that number down, so let's talk about that option and see what makes sense for you.
PATIENT: Oh gosh, I really messed that up. I'm sorry. And I'm also not super great about the aspirin, to be honest. I know I'm supposed to take it every day, the 325 mg, but I can't remember exactly how often I actually do. Some days I forget, some days I take it... it's been kind of hit or miss.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We can work on that—maybe we set up a pill organizer or you use your phone to remind you. But given your heart situation, the aspirin is pretty important. Actually, speaking of that, I want to get you set up with a cardiology appointment as well. Just to make sure everything's looking good there and to coordinate your care.
PATIENT: You mean a heart doctor? I haven't seen one of those before. Is that because of the kidney thing, or... I'm a little nervous about what that means.
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's just part of managing everything together. You've got a lot going on—the sleep apnea, the chronic kidney disease stage 3, your glucose control. Cardiology will help us make sure your heart's staying strong through all of this.
PATIENT: Okay, well, if you think it's necessary. When would that be? And will they do more tests, or...?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We'll get you on the schedule and you'll get a call with an appointment. They might do an EKG or an ultrasound, just to get a good picture of what's happening. But we'll get the bloodwork done first, and then we can all work from the same page. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds fine. Um, and those feet—should I do anything about that, or just keep an eye on it like I'm doing now?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We'll monitor it, especially since you also had the blurred vision at the same time. Keep tracking it—write down if it gets worse or if anything else shows up. And definitely mention it at the cardiology visit too. For now, let's get that bloodwork scheduled and we'll see what we're working with.

NURSE: Hi Max, I'm Sarah, one of the nurses here. Let's get your vitals first, alright? I'm going to take your blood pressure.
PATIENT: Yeah, sure. Though I gotta say, I woke up this morning and my whole body just feels like, um, I don't know—just terrible. My muscle aches are really bad. Like, I can barely move my arms.
NURSE: Oh, that sounds uncomfortable. When did that start?
PATIENT: Like I said, this morning. And it's getting worse as the day goes on. I'm worried it might be something.
NURSE: We'll definitely keep an eye on that. Okay, got your blood pressure here—146 over 88. That's a little elevated. And your heart rate is at 84, which is good. So let me just ask, have you been having any problems with your vision at all? Like anything blurry?
PATIENT: No, no, my eyes are fine. Can't complain there.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Max, I'm James, the care coordinator. I want to walk through your medications with you today because we also need to talk about some of these new symptoms you're mentioning. Can you tell me—are you still taking your heart medication, the sacubitril-valsartan?
PATIENT: Oh yeah, I take that one no problem. Twice a day, 49 mg each time. I'm really good about that one. Never miss it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Great, that's excellent to hear. What about your cholesterol med—the atorvastatin, the 20 mg tablet?
PATIENT: Um, well... I stopped taking that one a couple weeks ago, actually. I ran out and just, you know, forgot to refill it.
NURSE: Okay, we'll get that refilled today. And the aspirin? You're still on the 325 mg once a day?
PATIENT: Yeah, I take that every day. Never missed one of those either. But listen, I also been feeling kind of nauseous, like just this—wait, what day did that start? Yesterday, I think? And it's not terrible, but it's getting worse.
CARE_COORDINATOR: So you've got the nausea since yesterday that's worsening, and these muscle aches that came on this morning. Have you also been feeling dizzy at all, or lightheaded? I do want to make a note of the dizziness while we're at it. I do want to make a note of the blurred vision while we're at it. Your blood pressure came back at 146/88.
PATIENT: A little bit, yeah. Been kind of bothersome, but honestly, it's actually getting better than it was earlier. So that's good, I guess.
NURSE: That's good that that one's improving. Given your anemia and everything else going on, these symptoms together are something we need to take seriously. Has anything felt different with your reflux disease—your gastroesophageal reflux disease, I mean?
PATIENT: Hm, well, the heartburn's been okay. Not really worse than usual.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Alright. So here's what we're thinking, Max. We want to schedule a follow-up visit with you in about two weeks so we can recheck everything and make sure these new symptoms settle down. Does that work for your schedule?
PATIENT: Yeah, two weeks is fine by me. I can do that.
NURSE: Perfect. And we're also going to refer you to endocrinology because we want to get another set of eyes on your overall metabolic picture, especially with the anemia and these symptoms popping up.
PATIENT: Endocrinology? What's that for?
CARE_COORDINATOR: They specialize in hormones and metabolism, so they can help us figure out if something's going on with your overall system. It's just a specialist we want to bring in to help manage everything together.
PATIENT: Okay, okay. Makes sense. So I'll get the atorvastatin refilled, and we'll get that follow-up visit on the books. What else?
NURSE: Just keep an eye on those muscle aches and the nausea—let us know if either one gets significantly worse before your next visit. And definitely continue taking the sacubitril-valsartan and aspirin like you have been. You've been doing great with those.
PATIENT: Will do. Thanks for seeing me today.

CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay Mariah, so I'm looking at your chart here and I see you came in because of some symptoms that started around Monday? Walk me through what's been going on.
PATIENT: Yeah, um, so honestly I've been feeling these weird fluttery things in my chest, like my heart's just going crazy sometimes. It's been really intense, kind of scary actually. And then my legs, they feel a little puffy? Like my socks leave marks when I take them off.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, so the palpitations started Monday and they're still pretty bad, is that fair to say?
PATIENT: Yeah, they're about the same. Not getting better or worse really. But the leg swelling—at least that's been improving a tiny bit, I think.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: She woke me up Saturday—I mean Monday—because she was just holding her chest and saying something felt wrong. I knew we needed to get her in.
PATIENT: My mom's being dramatic, but yeah, it was scary. And you know, with my history, I'm always worried about—I had that transient ischemic attack a few years back, remember? So when I get chest stuff I don't mess around.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right, I see that in here. The TIA. That makes total sense why you'd want to come in. Now I also see you've got type 2 diabetes mellitus and we've got some labs from about a month ago. Your hemoglobin a1c came back at 8.1, which is—
PATIENT: Wait, is that bad? I always forget what that number means.
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's a little higher than we'd like it to be. Ideally we want it under 7, so yours at 8.1 means your blood sugar's been running a bit high on average. We can definitely work on that. But let me also ask about your gastroesophageal reflux disease—the acid reflux stuff. Has that been flaring up?
PATIENT: Oh God, the heartburn's been there but nothing unusual. I mean, I get it most days anyway, so I can't really tell if it's worse.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, got it. So you're on your pravastatin, 40 mg, every day—are you still taking that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I take it every morning with breakfast. No problem there. I'm pretty good about that one.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. And the azithromycin, 250 mg, for the respiratory thing you had—you taking that consistently?
PATIENT: Um, mostly. I think I missed it maybe twice? I just kind of forgot one day and then, you know, life got busy.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: She's been skipping it more than she thinks. I told her she needs to set a phone reminder.
PATIENT: Mom, come on—okay fine, yeah, maybe I've been a little inconsistent. But I'm trying.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Well, it's better to take it every day like it says. By the way, my coworker actually came in yesterday with a case of shingles, so I'm already wound up about catching things—but that's not relevant to you. Your LDL cholesterol came back at 142, though, and combined with everything else, I think we need to bump up your pravastatin dose.
PATIENT: So like, a higher dose? That's fine. I don't have any side effects from it now.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good to know. And one more thing—given your diabetes and now these cardiac symptoms, I want to get nephrology involved to check your kidney function. That okay with you?
PATIENT: Nephrology, so a kidney doctor? Yeah, I mean, if you think I need it. This is all just... a lot, you know?
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: When can we get that appointment scheduled?
CARE_COORDINATOR: I'll send the referral to nephrology today. They usually get back to us within a week. In the meantime, Mariah, let's be really careful about getting that azithromycin on schedule every single day, okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, I'll set something up on my phone. And so the pravastatin changes, when do I start the new dose?
CARE_COORDINATOR: You'll get a new prescription before you leave today. Any other questions?
PATIENT: I don't think so. Just, um, should I be worried about that leg swelling coming back if it's improving?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Keep an eye on it and let us know if it gets worse instead of better. But right now the fact that it's getting a bit better is a good sign.

NURSE: Stella? We got your EKG back from last week, and I wanted to touch base with you about a couple things before the provider comes in. How are you feeling overall?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, pretty good most days. Though honestly I had this weird dizzy spell last month, lightheadedness kind of out of nowhere, but actually it's been getting better. So I'm not too worried about it anymore.
NURSE: Good to hear that's settling down. Have you noticed any chest pain or anything uncomfortable in your chest at all?
PATIENT: Um, yeah, actually—I got this chest pain over the weekend that's been hanging around. It's not terrible, nothing sharp or anything, just like a dull thing, you know? It's been about the same since it started.
NURSE: Okay, we'll definitely keep an eye on that. I know you were diagnosed with atrial fibrillation a while back—how are you managing with all of that?
PATIENT: Right, my heart condition. Yeah, well, I take my tramadol like I'm supposed to, 50 mg as needed whenever I have pain. That's not a problem. But the other one—wait, what is it—the torsemide, the water pill—I think I've been okay with it but I'm honestly not super consistent. Like sometimes I forget.
NURSE: The torsemide at 20 mg once a day. That's really important for managing your heart rhythm, so we want to make sure you're taking that every single day. Can we set up a time that works for you?
PATIENT: Yeah, um, maybe with breakfast? I'm better about that than I am at night. Oh, and I take the amitriptyline at bedtime—25 mg—and I do that pretty much every night, so that one's fine.
NURSE: Great, consistency with that one is good. Now, you also have hyperlipidemia, the high cholesterol, and gout—how's the gout been treating you?
PATIENT: The gout, ugh, it flares up every couple months in my foot. But no, I don't have blurred vision or anything like that going on. My eyes are fine.
NURSE: Good. We did a peak flow test last visit and you were at 240 L/min, which is reasonable. And your hemoglobin a1c came back at 6.8, so your sugar control is looking pretty stable.
PATIENT: Oh okay, so that's good? I wasn't sure what those numbers meant, to be honest.
NURSE: Yeah, both of those are in a good range for where you want to be. But with your atrial fibrillation and the chest pain you mentioned, we're going to want you to check your blood pressure at home. Do you have a monitor at home?
PATIENT: I have one somewhere, yeah. I can dust it off. How often should I be doing that?
NURSE: A few times a week is good, maybe keep a little log so we can see the numbers at your follow-up visit. Speaking of which, we'll get that scheduled before you leave today.
PATIENT: Okay, that works. And do I need anything else, like more tests or something?
NURSE: The provider might want to order some bloodwork to check your lipid panel again and make sure your electrolytes are holding up with the medications you're on. We can talk about that when she comes in.
PATIENT: Fair enough. Oh, but—wait, is the chest pain something I should be worried about, like should I go to the ER or something?
NURSE: If it gets worse or you start having shortness of breath with it, absolutely call 911. But given your history with atrial fibrillation and the fact that it's been stable since the weekend, the provider wants to send you over to cardiology for a quick evaluation just to be thorough. That's routine for us.
PATIENT: Okay, so like a heart specialist will look at me? Alright, I can do that. When would that be?
NURSE: We'll get them coordinated on that today, and you should hear from their office within a few days with an appointment time. In the meantime, keep tracking those blood pressures and don't hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

NURSE: Regina, come on in—I see from your chart we need to go over those lab results from last month. How've you been feeling overall?
PATIENT: Well, I've been, um, okay mostly, but I gotta tell you I've had this headache that just won't quit. Really bad, you know? And it's not getting any better—been like this for weeks now.
NURSE: That severe headache—when did it start? Has anything else been going on that's different?
PATIENT: Oh, and I've been tired. Really tired. Like, I go to bed and I wake up exhausted still. This fatigue has been bothering me since, well, since I was here last time. Just drags on and on.
NURSE: I hear you. Fatigue that's sticking around like that—that matters. Anything with your stomach or digestion?
PATIENT: Actually, yes! Starting on Monday I started feeling, I dunno, queasy? Not like I'm gonna throw up, but there's this nausea that comes and goes. Nothing major, just annoying.
NURSE: Got it. Let's talk about your medications for a minute. You're on the spironolactone, right? The 12.5 mg tablet?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I take that one every morning. Haven't missed a single day—I have it with my breakfast so I remember.
NURSE: Perfect. That's excellent adherence. And the rosuvastatin—the 40 mg—how consistent have you been with that one?
PATIENT: Um, honestly? I'm not—I mean, I think I take it most days, but sometimes I'm not totally sure if I took it or if I took it yesterday, you know? Life gets busy.
NURSE: That's actually pretty common. We should talk about some ways to help you keep track of that. Your lipid levels came back a little high, which is why the rosuvastatin is so important—you've got hyperlipidemia, high cholesterol basically, and we're trying to keep that under control.
PATIENT: Right, right, the high cholesterol thing. Wait—I had a question. Sometimes at night I worry I'm sweating through my sheets, but actually no, that's not happening. I don't have any of those night sweats. I was worried about that but it's not going on.
NURSE: Good to know. So your type 2 diabetes mellitus is what we're tracking here too, and with these new symptoms—especially the nausea and the fatigue—we want to make sure nothing's shifted with your blood sugar control.
PATIENT: Oh gosh, is that—I mean, should I be worried? I've been trying to eat okay, but with all this tiredness it's hard to stay on top of things.
NURSE: Not worried, just careful. But I do want to refer you over to pulmonology because we want to rule out anything respiratory that might be contributing to all this fatigue and that headache. Have you had any shortness of breath?
PATIENT: Oh, pulmonology—that's the lung doctor, right? Um, not really shortness of breath, but I guess I get winded easier than I used to. Yeah, if you think I should see them, I'll go.
NURSE: I think that's the right move. I also want you to check your blood pressure at home regularly—couple times a week. We'll get you a good cuff, and just write down what you see. Can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, absolutely. I've got one at home actually. My daughter bought it for me. So I'll check my blood pressure at home like you said and write it down. What about my anxiety? I know I have that generalized anxiety disorder, and with all this stuff going on I'm extra nervous.
NURSE: We're going to keep you on what you're on for that unless you feel like it's not helping. But let's see what pulmonology says first—sometimes when we get the physical stuff sorted, the anxiety settles down too.
PATIENT: Okay, okay. So I'm gonna see the lung specialist and keep track of my blood pressure, and I'm gonna try to remember my cholesterol pill.
NURSE: Exactly. And call me if that headache gets worse or if the nausea changes. We'll touch base after pulmonology sees you.

NURSE: Hey Randy, come on back. We're running just a couple minutes behind but let's get you roomed. How're you doing today?
PATIENT: Um, honestly? I've been pretty wiped out the last few days. Like, worse than usual. I don't know if it's just work stress or what, but this fatigue is just... it's really bad, you know?
NURSE: When you say wiped out, are we talking you can barely get out of bed, or more like you're just tired?
PATIENT: No, it's worse than tired. Like, I got through work yesterday and I just collapsed on the couch. Couldn't even get dinner going. The fatigue just hit different this time.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Randy, I'm Sarah, the care coordinator. Good to see you again. Let me just double-check a couple things while we're here. So with your heart failure with reduced ejection fraction—how's that been sitting with you lately?
PATIENT: Yeah, well, some days are better than others. I mean, I don't really think about it that much anymore, but lately I've noticed I get a little short of breath, you know, just walking up stairs or something. It started maybe a month ago, just a little bit of shortness of breath, nothing crazy.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Is it getting worse or about the same as when you first noticed it?
PATIENT: About the same, I'd say. Mild. Doesn't stop me from doing stuff, but it's there.
NURSE: And any nausea? Stomach bothering you at all?
PATIENT: No, actually, my stomach's been fine. No nausea or anything like that. It's really just feeling completely drained.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, good. We did your labs last month and I'm looking at your hemoglobin a1c—it came back at 8.6, which is a little higher than where we want to be, but we're on it. Have you been taking your medications like you're supposed to?
PATIENT: Um, mostly? I mean, I take the rosuvastatin, 20 mg—I skip it maybe once or twice a week, but not on purpose, just like, I forget or I'm running late or whatever. And then the ezetimibe... wait, no—I actually stopped taking that one. I don't even remember when, maybe a few months ago?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Why'd you stop the ezetimibe, 10 mg? Did something happen with it?
PATIENT: I don't know, honestly. I think I ran out and just... didn't refill it? I wasn't sure I needed it anymore.
NURSE: And what about the blood pressure medication, the losartan? Okay, so rosuvastatin at 20 mg, once a day; and you're forgets it now and then, good.
PATIENT: Yeah, I'm taking that one. I mean, I think I'm taking it pretty regularly. I don't know exactly how often, like, some days I remember and some days... honestly, I'm not great about it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: The losartan at 100 mg really helps with your heart condition and your kidneys, so that one we want to be consistent with. Speaking of kidneys, we're looking at your recent creatinine numbers and I'm wondering about chronic kidney disease stage 3. We're not saying that's definite yet, but we want to keep an eye on that, especially given your anemia and everything else going on.
PATIENT: Wait, anemia? I have anemia?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Yeah, we found that in your bloodwork. That's actually connected to your fatigue that you're experiencing right now, and possibly related to what's happening with your kidneys. It all kind of ties together.
PATIENT: So like, my blood doesn't have enough iron or something?
NURSE: Not exactly iron in this case—it's low red blood cells, low hemoglobin. But the anemia could explain why you're feeling so drained. And with the kidney thing, we want to follow up pretty closely on that.
PATIENT: So what do I do about it? I mean, there's got to be something...
CARE_COORDINATOR: First thing is we want to make sure you're consistent with your medications. Also, we've noticed you stopped your escitalopram—the antidepressant—a few months back?
PATIENT: Oh yeah, that one too. I just felt like I was doing better so I figured I could stop it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I get it, but given everything you're dealing with, we might want to either get you back on escitalopram or at least discuss adjusting the dose. We'll figure out what works. But that's something we can talk through.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. I mean, I do feel kind of overwhelmed lately, so maybe that's not helping.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Alright. So here's what we're thinking: we want to get you scheduled for a follow-up visit in about two weeks so we can recheck your labs, especially looking at that kidney function and your hemoglobin levels. Sound good?
PATIENT: Two weeks? Yeah, I can do that. Should I be worried about any of this?
NURSE: Not worried, but definitely engaged. Get back on your meds, take the losartan consistently, and we'll see what your numbers look like at the follow-up visit. We'll figure out the next steps from there.
