text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Hey Maverick, come on back—I see here we've got some things to go over from your last visit. How are you feeling today? Any new things going on?
PATIENT: Well, that's kind of why I'm here, you know? I've been just… really dragging. Like, I can barely get through the day. This fatigue, man, it's been going on for a good month now and honestly, it's not getting any better.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: A month—okay. And this is different from your normal baseline? Like, you're struggling to do things you'd normally do?
PATIENT: Yeah, exactly. I used to work in the yard, take walks, you know. Now I'm just… spent by lunchtime. And another thing—I've been thirsty all the time. Like, increased thirst out of nowhere. I'm drinking water constantly, but it started about a month ago too, same time as the fatigue.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Interesting that they started around the same time. Has the thirst gotten any worse, or is it kind of leveling off?
PATIENT: Actually, that's the one thing that's been improving a little bit. So that's good, I guess. But the tiredness? Not so much.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, good to know. Now, I'm also looking at your chart here and I want to circle back to something. You've been dealing with the hyperlipidemia—the high cholesterol—and we've talked about managing that. How are you getting along with your medications?
PATIENT: Um, so I'm taking the acetaminophen, 500 mg, pretty much every day for my aches. That's been fine. But the duloxetine—I actually stopped that a while back. Just wasn't sure it was helping, you know?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You stopped the duloxetine, the 30 mg. Alright, we can talk about that. What about your simvastatin—are you taking that one pretty regularly?
PATIENT: The 40 mg? Yeah, I mean, I think I am, but honestly I'm not always super consistent about it. Some days I remember, some days I forget. It's supposed to be once a day, right?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It is, and consistency really does matter with that one for your cholesterol control. We should talk about maybe putting it somewhere visible—like a pill organizer by your coffee maker or something. But before we dig into all that, have you been having any night sweats? Waking up soaked?
PATIENT: No, no night sweats. Thank God. I've heard people complain about that and it sounds miserable. I'm just… tired and my feet have been bugging me too.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Your feet—tell me more about that. Let me get the acetaminophen down: 500 mg, as needed, and you're hasn't missed any doses. Okay, so duloxetine at 30 mg, once a day; and you're not taking it anymore, good.
PATIENT: There's numbness in the feet, especially when I sit down for a while. It's like pins and needles, kind of annoying and bothersome. It's been about the same for the last month or so, not getting worse or better.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's helpful. Okay, so listen, given everything you're describing and your cholesterol numbers, we really need to get you in with endocrinology to make sure we're not missing something metabolic going on. Sound okay?
PATIENT: Endocrinology, yeah. Like a specialist for that stuff? I mean, if you think that's what I need, sure. How long is that usually gonna take to get in?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We'll get that rolling for you today. In the meantime, I want you to check your blood pressure at home, okay? We need to keep an eye on it. Can you do that—grab a cuff and log it a few times a week?
PATIENT: Yeah, I've got a cuff at home. Check my blood pressure at home—I can do that. Should I write it down or something?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That would be great. But Maverick, I need to ask you something important before you go. Have you had any chest pain? Any pressure, anything like that?
PATIENT: Wait, actually—yeah. Now that you mention it, I have had some pain in my chest. It's been kind of coming and going, but um, it's gotten worse the past few days. Like, this morning it was pretty bad, caught me off guard.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That concerns me. I don't want you to panic, but we can't just wait on that. I'm sending you to urgent care right now so they can get you checked out properly with an EKG and the whole workup. This isn't something to sit on. Can you head over there today?
PATIENT: Oh. Um, okay. Yeah, I mean—urgent care. Yeah, I can do that. Should I drive or, like—
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I'll let them know you're coming. If you feel worse on the way, any shortness of breath, any radiating pain down your arm—you call 911. Don't hesitate, okay? We're taking this seriously.

CARE_COORDINATOR: River, come on back—we're running a little behind but we can get you in. How are things going since your last visit?
PATIENT: Uh, yeah, good mostly. Though I gotta say, my feet have been weird lately. Like, I've had this numbness in the feet for maybe three days now? Wasn't there before.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, that's something we'll definitely look at. Any idea when that started happening?
PATIENT: Three days ago, maybe Wednesday? And also—I don't know if this is related, but my vision's been really off. Like, blurred vision, you know? Started over the weekend and it's just... it's not getting better. Kind of freaking me out about it, honestly.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He mentioned that to me at dinner last night. I told him he should definitely bring it up today.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Smart. We want to know about this stuff. And the blurred vision—is it about the same as when it first started, or has it changed?
PATIENT: Um, pretty much the same. Maybe even a tiny bit worse, I'm not sure. It's been consistent since Saturday or Sunday, whenever it kicked in.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Got it. Let me ask you about something else—have you noticed any changes with thirst? Like, are you drinking more than usual?
PATIENT: Oh, yeah, actually now that you mention it, I have been a little more thirsty than normal. But like, not a ton—just, you know, slightly more. I figured it was just summer.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He's been going through water bottles faster, now that I think about it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. So we're looking at the numbness, the vision issue, a bit of extra thirst. Let's talk about your medications because I want to make sure you're taking things the way they're supposed to work. You're on glipizide, 5 mg—how's that going?
PATIENT: Um, yeah, I take that one. Although, wait—I missed a couple doses recently. Life got busy, you know? But I've been trying to get back on track with it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That happens. Just so you know, that one really does need to go every day if we're going to keep things stable. What about the dabigatran? The 110 mg you take twice a day?
PATIENT: Oh man, okay so... I take it, but honestly, I can't remember if I'm actually taking it twice a day like I'm supposed to or like, I don't know, once a day sometimes? I should probably be more careful.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I've noticed he grabs it in the morning for sure, but I'm not always there in the evening. Let's not forget about the increased thirst either. Okay, so tramadol at 50 mg, as needed; and you're been really consistent with it, good.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's really helpful to know. So the dabigatran is important to take both times—morning and evening, 110 mg each. And then you've got spironolactone too, 25 mg once a day. Are you still on that one?
PATIENT: Actually, no—I stopped taking that one, um, a while back. Like, I don't know, a month? It's been sitting there and I just... I don't know, I felt fine without it so I didn't refill it or anything.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, we're going to restart that. It's important for your heart and kidneys, and especially now with what's going on. We'll get that dialed back in. You're also on tramadol for pain—the 50 mg when you need it?
PATIENT: Yeah, that one I actually haven't missed. I take it like once, twice a week maybe when my back acts up.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good consistency there. So here's what I want to do. First, we're going to get some bloodwork ordered—that's going to help us figure out what's going on with the numbness, the vision, the thirst, all of it. We want to check your blood sugar especially, given the symptoms. Sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, that makes sense. How soon?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We can get you scheduled this week if you're available. And I'm going to adjust your spironolactone dose when we restart it—we'll bump it back to the 25 mg, but I want to check in after the bloodwork to make sure that's the right move. And we need to talk about getting you back on track with both the glipizide and making sure you're really nailing the dabigatran twice a day. Could you do a pill organizer or set phone reminders?
PATIENT: Oh, a pill organizer might actually help. My coworker Marco—he's got carpal tunnel syndrome and he was telling me how he has to be super organized with his stuff because his hands hurt. Made me think I should probably get more organized too.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I can help you set reminders on your phone too if you want.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's great. Let's get you that bloodwork and we'll see what we're dealing with. Also, I know you had coronary artery disease in the past—that's been stable for a while now, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's all resolved now. Been doing good on that front, thankfully.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Excellent. Okay, so we'll get that bloodwork in, get you back on the spironolactone, and I'm going to follow up with you in about two weeks to see how you're feeling and review the labs. Does that work?
PATIENT: Two weeks sounds good. Hopefully this stuff clears up soon.

CARE_COORDINATOR: Hi Amanda, come on in. We're running about five minutes behind, but your chart is all pulled up. How've you been doing since we saw you last, oh, couple months ago?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, same old same old. Well, not entirely. My feet have been acting up lately—there's this numbness in the feet that's been kind of bothering me. It's not terrible, but it's there, you know? And—oh, this is weird—yesterday I noticed I was just so thirsty all the time. Like, couldn't get enough water. Though it's gotten better, thank goodness.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, we'll definitely look into that. The numbness and the thirst—both good things to track. And the thirst is already improving? That's good. Let me ask, have you noticed any changes with your vision at all? Like blurriness, or anything like that?
PATIENT: No, no, my eyesight's been fine. I can see the TV just great still, which is more than I can say for my hearing at this age! *laughs* But vision-wise, no complaints there.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good to hear. Now, let's talk about how you're managing with your medications. You're on the simvastatin—that's your cholesterol medicine, the one that helps with your hyperlipidemia—and I see you're taking 10 mg once a day. Are you staying on top of that one?
PATIENT: Oh yeah, that one I don't miss. I take it every morning with my breakfast. No trouble there.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. And the glipizide, the 5 mg once a day—how's that going?
PATIENT: Um, the glipizide... I mean, I'm taking it, but honestly, I can't quite remember if I'm supposed to be taking it once a day or—wait, is it twice? I take it, but I'm not totally sure I'm doing it the right number of times. My daughter keeps telling me I need to use one of those pill organizers.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's actually a really smart idea. The glipizide is once a day, so we can work on that—maybe we'll get you set up with something to help keep you organized. What about your blood pressure medication, the hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg?
PATIENT: That one I'm doing good with. Every morning, same time as the simvastatin. My neighbor at work—well, she used to work with me before I retired—she takes something for sciatica, and she's always complaining about trying to remember her medications, so I figured I'd better get my act together. At least I'm more reliable than she is.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's great adherence with those two. And speaking of how you're feeling overall, I want to check in on your mood. How are things going for you mentally? Any feelings of sadness, or like things are kind of hopeless, or you're not enjoying things you normally would? We should also keep the blurred vision on our radar.
PATIENT: Oh, well... I mean, you get a little down sometimes at my age, right? But I don't know. Some days I just feel tired, you know? Like, really tired. And I'm not always sure if I want to do the things I used to like. But it's not like I'm crying all day or anything. Is that... is something I should be worried about?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We want to make sure we're not missing anything. What you're describing—the fatigue, losing interest in activities—those are things we sometimes see with major depressive disorder, but they can also come with other stuff, like how your blood sugar's been running, or even just stress. We're not jumping to any conclusions, but I'd like to keep an eye on it. Have you felt like this for a while, or is it something recent?
PATIENT: Hmm, maybe the last few weeks, I guess? It's hard to say. Some days are better than others. I still get out, still see my friends—well, I try to. Sometimes I cancel because I'm just exhausted.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We're going to address a few things here. So first, with the numbness in your feet and the increased thirst that you had—those are things we want to have an endocrinologist take a look at, especially because of your blood sugar management. I'm going to refer you to endocrinology and we'll get that set up. They'll do a more detailed workup.
PATIENT: Okay, so another specialist? How many doctors is that now? *laughs* Just kidding. If I need to go, I'll go.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I know it feels like a lot, but they're going to help us dial in your medications better, especially the glipizide situation. Also, I want to ask—do you drink alcohol at all?
PATIENT: Oh, just a glass of wine sometimes. Maybe a couple times a week? I'm not a big drinker or anything.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's good to know. One thing that could help with some of what you're experiencing—the fatigue, the mood stuff—is if you wanted to cut back on alcohol, even a little. It can really affect how you feel. Not saying you have to, but it's worth trying if you're open to it.
PATIENT: I could do that. I mean, it's not like I can't live without it. I'd try anything if it might help me feel a bit better. And you'll have the endocrinologist look at my feet and the thirst thing?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Absolutely. We'll get you an appointment within the next month or so, and in the meantime, we're going to work on getting your meds organized—especially that glipizide—and I want to see you back here in six weeks to check in on the mood piece and see how everything's going. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds good. Thank you for actually listening and not just, you know, rushing me out the door like some doctors do.

CARE_COORDINATOR: —so the discharge paperwork mentioned you were having some real trouble with heartburn when you left the hospital. How's that been sitting with you?
PATIENT: Oh man, it's been terrible. Severe heartburn, honestly. It started a couple weeks ago and just... it's not getting any better. Some days it wakes me up at night.
CARE_COORDINATOR: A couple weeks ago—that tracks with your discharge date pretty closely. And you haven't noticed it improving at all, or is it just about the same day to day?
PATIENT: Pretty much the same. Maybe slightly worse if I eat anything spicy or too late. I've been trying to be careful, but the severe heartburn just won't quit.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Got it. We'll definitely want to address that. Before we dive into the heartburn piece, I want to just check in on a few other things. You haven't had any fever, right?
PATIENT: No fever, thank goodness. I've been checking my temp because I had that cellulitis thing cleared up last year and I'm always paranoid it's coming back, but no—nothing like that. My coworker actually just got diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome, so I've been hearing all about it, but thankfully that's not something I'm dealing with.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That cellulitis is behind you now, so that's good. But I did want to ask about any other symptoms—have you been noticing any dizziness?
PATIENT: Yeah, I have actually. Mild dizziness—it started about a month ago. But honestly it's getting better, so I haven't been too worried.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's encouraging that it's trending the right direction. Any idea what might be triggering it when it does happen?
PATIENT: Mostly when I stand up too fast, or like, when I first get out of bed in the morning. Nothing that's really... um... what's the word I'm looking for... debilitating? No, it's just sort of fleeting.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That makes sense. Orthostatic kind of thing. Okay, let's talk through your medications because I think that might be part of what we're managing here. Are you still on the naproxen?
PATIENT: Yes, I am. 500 mg twice daily, like you prescribed. I haven't missed a single day, every single day I take it as prescribed.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's really good compliance. So here's the thing—we've been thinking about your hypertension control, and the naproxen at that dose can work against us a bit. I'd like to adjust naproxen dose, bring it down from twice daily to once daily. How does that feel?
PATIENT: Oh, okay. I mean, if that's going to help with the hypertension and maybe even help with some of this heartburn business, I'm game. I can definitely do that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. And you're taking the ibuprofen as needed?
PATIENT: I am, though I'll be honest—I've missed some doses. Sometimes I just forget, you know? Life gets busy. But yeah, 200 mg as needed when something really hurts.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I hear you. Let's keep that the same for now—200 mg as needed. That can stay as your backup. Now, the amlodipine—you're on 10 mg once daily for the hypertension. How's that been going?
PATIENT: Um, not sure, honestly. I don't remember if I've been totally consistent with it. I take it, but I couldn't say whether it's been every single day or if I've... you know, skipped some mornings.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's okay, these things happen. The good news is we can refill it and I'd encourage you to set a reminder—maybe tie it to something you do every morning like brushing your teeth or having coffee. Does that sound doable?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. My coffee maker's right next to my sink anyway.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect anchor. So we'll arrange a refill for the amlodipine 10 mg once daily. Now, I do want to circle back to that dizziness and some other things. Can you tell me how you've been feeling energy-wise? Any unusual fatigue?
PATIENT: Now that you mention it, yeah, I've been more tired than usual. I figured it was just stress from being in the hospital, but it's been a few weeks and I'm not quite back to normal.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Mm-hmm. That, combined with the mild dizziness, makes me want to rule out anemia. It's probably nothing, but I'm not convinced yet that we can write it off completely. We got your hemoglobin a1c at 6.2 %, which is good, but we should check your full blood count to be thorough.
PATIENT: Okay, so you're saying my blood might be... off? Wow, at this rate I'm falling apart—severe heartburn, dizziness, and now maybe my blood is misbehaving too. It's like a used car that's starting to need warranty work.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Ha, I like that image. But honestly, we're just making sure we're not missing anything. Oh, by the way, how much do you weigh right now? Have you noticed any changes?
PATIENT: I weigh 172 pounds. I think that's been pretty steady.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good, that's stable. Alright, so here's what I'm thinking: we adjust naproxen dose like we talked about, we monitor blood pressure at home—do you have a cuff?
PATIENT: I do, actually. My sister bought me one.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Great. Monitor blood pressure at home and keep a little log if you can. We'll get the blood work done to check on that anemia question, and then I want to schedule a follow-up visit with you in about three weeks to touch base on how the heartburn's doing and see those results.
PATIENT: Three weeks, okay. Yeah, I can do that.

NURSE: Okay, so I'm looking at your chart here from the discharge paperwork—it says you were sent home on torsemide and warfarin, the warfarin for the deep vein thrombosis. Is that all still making sense to you?
PATIENT: Yeah, I mean, the blood clot thing—yes, that's why I'm on those, right? I'm trying to keep track of it all.
NURSE: Right, that makes sense. And you're managing okay with the medications so far?
PATIENT: Well, the warfarin I'm taking exactly as prescribed, I haven't missed a single dose—2.5 mg once daily, every single day. But the torsemide, I'm not totally sure... I think it changed? The dose, I mean. I don't remember if I'm supposed to be taking the same amount or...
NURSE: Mm-hmm. Let me clarify that for you. The torsemide is actually coming down now—you're on 20 mg once daily now instead of what you were on before. The thinking there is blood pressure control, to help that come down a bit more gently. Does that ring a bell?
PATIENT: Oh. Oh, okay, so 20 mg once daily—yes, that sounds... I think that's what I've been doing, actually.
NURSE: Good. Good. Now, what's been going on with how you've been feeling?
PATIENT: Honestly, I've been pretty tired. Like, moderate fatigue, it started yesterday and... I mean, it's actually getting a little better now, but it was rough when it first came on.
NURSE: Moderate fatigue starting yesterday. And you said it's starting to improve?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah. A bit.
NURSE: Alright. Anything else you've noticed?
PATIENT: Well, I haven't had night sweats or anything like that—I want to be clear about that. But I have noticed I'm not eating as well. Mild poor appetite, really, but it's gotten worse, or like, steadier... it started a couple weeks ago and it's just kind of lingering.
NURSE: Okay, so no night sweats—good to hear that's not part of it. And the poor appetite's been mild but worsening since a couple weeks ago. Are you having any trouble keeping food down, or is it just not wanting to eat?
PATIENT: Just not wanting to, I think. Nothing physically... I can eat if I make myself, but I'm just not feeling hungry.
NURSE: And how's your sleep been?
PATIENT: That's been rough. I have severe difficulty sleeping—like, I've had that for about a month ago now, and it's just... it's not getting better or worse, it's just kind of staying the same. Stuck. Some nights I'm up until two, three in the morning just lying there, you know?
NURSE: A month of that already. That's significant. And the severity's been consistent?
PATIENT: Yeah, pretty much every night at this point.
NURSE: I do want to circle back to something. With the fatigue and the poor appetite and the sleep issues, sometimes what we see with deep vein thrombosis—the blood clot—is that it can also show up as anemia, where your blood isn't carrying enough oxygen. Have you felt shortness of breath at all?
PATIENT: No, I don't think so. Nothing I've really noticed. Although my brother-in-law actually just had a stroke a couple months back, and he was complaining about shortness of breath, but that was... I mean, that was a stroke, so that's different, right?
NURSE: Right, that is different. That's his stroke, separate thing entirely. But for you, no shortness of breath to report?
PATIENT: No.
NURSE: Any pain anywhere?
PATIENT: Um, yeah actually. In my left leg where the... where the clot is, I guess. It's an 8 on the pain scale when I've been standing too long, or walking. It settles down when I rest.
NURSE: An 8. That's significant pain. So that's related to the leg swelling and the DVT itself. That makes sense. And the anemia could be contributing to that fatigue you're feeling on top of everything else.
PATIENT: Right. I didn't really make that connection before, but... yeah, okay.
NURSE: Alright. So here's what I want to suggest. We should monitor your blood pressure at home—do you have a cuff?
PATIENT: I do, yes.
NURSE: Good. Can you monitor blood pressure at home for the next 4 weeks and keep a log of those readings? That way we can see how the torsemide adjustment is working.
PATIENT: Okay, yes, I can do that.
NURSE: And we're going to schedule a follow-up visit with the provider in 3 months to reassess all of this—see how you're tolerating the medications, check on the anemia, and see if the fatigue's staying under control. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yes, that sounds good to me.
NURSE: One more thing. I know I'm asking a lot, but we also want you to reduce alcohol over the next 3 months. That can affect blood pressure, your clotting, and your sleep quality too. Can you work on that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can try. I mean, I don't drink a ton anyway, but I'll cut back.

PHYSICIAN: Hi Cooper, this is Dr. Mendez calling from cardiology. Is this an okay time to talk for a few minutes?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I'm home. What's going on?
PHYSICIAN: I wanted to circle back on your chest pain and go over your medications. You had that moderate chest pain since my last visit, and I want to make sure we're managing it right.
PATIENT: Well, it's still there. I mean, it's not... it's not getting worse or anything, but it's definitely still happening.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. And the palpitations—are you still experiencing those?
PATIENT: Yeah, on and off. Sometimes it's like my heart's racing and I don't know why. Especially in the afternoon.
PHYSICIAN: I see. Let me ask you about your medications. You're on aspirin 325 mg once daily for your coronary artery disease, and I need to know—are you taking that consistently?
PATIENT: Uh, well... not really. I mean, I'm not taking it. I stopped taking it a couple weeks ago because I read something online about it, and it made me nervous.
PHYSICIAN: That's really important to tell me. The aspirin is crucial for your coronary artery disease. We're going to address that, and I want to refill it for you. But first, let's talk about your hypertension control. Your blood pressure at the clinic last month was 134/86—that's higher than we want it.
PATIENT: I know, I know. I've been stressed with work and I haven't been... well, I haven't been doing great with my diet.
PHYSICIAN: Let's focus on what we can control right now. The carvedilol 6.25 mg twice daily—how are you doing with that one?
PATIENT: Oh, that one I'm good with. I take it as prescribed. Every morning and every evening. Haven't missed a single dose.
PHYSICIAN: That's excellent. So you're consistent with the carvedilol. Given your blood pressure and the chest discomfort, I think we need to make some adjustments. First, I'm arranging for you to refill the aspirin 325 mg once daily, and we need to talk about your dosing on that. But also—
PATIENT: Wait, when you say adjust, do you mean... higher?
PHYSICIAN: Possibly. We'll need to discuss that. What I want to focus on now is making sure you understand why the aspirin matters. Without it, you're at higher risk for an event, especially with your coronary artery disease active. So yes, we're going to adjust aspirin dose, and we're also going to work on other things. One thing that will really help—you should cut back on salt. That'll help bring your blood pressure down over the next three months.
PATIENT: Cut back on salt. Yeah, okay, I—I mean, I know I use too much. How much less are we talking about here?
PHYSICIAN: General guideline is less than 2,300 milligrams a day, ideally lower. That means less processed food, no added salt at the table. It's one of the bigger levers you have right now.
PATIENT: Alright. I can try to do that.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Now, your chest pain—I want you to be very clear on something. If you develop worsening chest pain, or if it radiates into your arm or jaw, or if you can't catch your breath, you need to go to the emergency department. Don't wait, don't call me first. You go to the emergency department.
PATIENT: Should I... like, right away? How bad does it have to be?
PHYSICIAN: If it's worsening chest pain and it feels different from what you've been having, or if it's more intense, then yes—emergency department immediately. I'm being direct about this because your coronary artery disease means you're at risk.
PATIENT: Okay, I got it. Emergency department. Got it.
PHYSICIAN: And we also need to schedule a follow-up visit. I want to see you in three months so we can check your blood pressure again and make sure these changes are working.
PATIENT: Three months. Yeah, that's... I can do that.
PHYSICIAN: I'm going to put that on the schedule for you. In the meantime, pharmacy will have the refill on the aspirin, and we'll discuss the adjusted dose with them. Your carvedilol stays the same—no change needed there since you're doing so well with it.
PATIENT: Okay. So to recap, I'm refilling the aspirin, the carvedilol stays the same, I cut back on salt, and if my chest gets really bad I go to the emergency department, and we talk in three months.
PHYSICIAN: That's exactly right. Does that make sense?
PATIENT: Yeah, it does. Thanks for calling.
PHYSICIAN: You're welcome. Take care of yourself, and we'll see you in three months.

PHYSICIAN: So you're about two weeks out from discharge now—how's the incision holding up?
PATIENT: It's been fine mostly, but lately it's been bothering me more. I'd say the incision pain is moderate, and honestly it's getting worse, not better like I expected.
PHYSICIAN: That's important to know. When did you first start noticing that the pain was picking up?
PATIENT: A couple weeks ago is when it started, really. The first week after I got home it wasn't bad at all, but then something shifted.
PHYSICIAN: And on a scale of zero to ten, where would you put it right now?
PATIENT: I'd say about a 4, but like I said, it's trending the wrong way.
PHYSICIAN: Got it. So beyond the incision, you mentioned on the phone that you've been dealing with some dizziness as well?
PATIENT: Yes, yesterday it got really bad suddenly. I was standing up from the couch and everything just spun. I was pretty scared actually. But the good news is it's been getting better since then.
PHYSICIAN: When you say it got really bad yesterday, was this severe dizziness? Did you almost fall, or did you have to sit right back down?
PATIENT: Severe is the right word, yeah. I had to grab the wall and just stand there for a minute. I didn't fall but I definitely could have if I hadn't caught myself.
PHYSICIAN: That must have been frightening. And it's easing up today?
PATIENT: It is, thank goodness. Still a bit lightheaded but nothing like yesterday.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. I want to circle back to something else—I know you've had some nausea too. Tell me about that timeline.
PATIENT: That's actually been going on longer. About a month ago it started, just occasional at first. But it's gotten worse, and now it's severe. Some days I can barely eat.
PHYSICIAN: A month—so that predates your hospitalization?
PATIENT: Right, it was happening before I went in. I mentioned it to someone in the hospital but nobody made a big deal out of it.
PHYSICIAN: I see. Let me pull up your discharge summary here and see what we're working with. I'll be honest with you—I'm not convinced yet that the nausea and the dizziness are just from the community-acquired pneumonia getting better. I want to rule out heart failure with reduced ejection fraction as one possibility we need to look at.
PATIENT: Heart failure? That sounds serious. What does that mean?
PHYSICIAN: It means the heart isn't pumping blood as effectively as it should be. In this case, 'reduced ejection fraction' means the chamber isn't contracting strongly enough to push blood out like it normally would. That's why I say I want to rule it out—make sure it's not what's causing your symptoms. We'll do some testing.
PATIENT: Okay, that makes sense. So what do we do?
PHYSICIAN: First let's talk about your medications. You're still on the rivaroxaban for the blood clotting risk from the pneumonia, right?
PATIENT: Yes, I'm taking that every single day, 20 mg once daily. Haven't missed a dose.
PHYSICIAN: Good, and we'll get that refilled today so you don't run out. What about the metoprolol tartrate—the 50 mg twice daily?
PATIENT: I haven't been taking that one. I stopped taking it a few days after I got home because I was tired all the time and it felt like it was making things worse.
PHYSICIAN: Mm-hmm. I understand why that felt that way, but let's just note that for now and not change course on it at this visit. And the aspirin, 81 mg once daily—you're keeping that up?
PATIENT: Yes, I take that as prescribed too, every morning.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, that's good. I want to schedule a follow-up visit in about a week. We'll likely get some imaging and lab work to look more closely at that heart function question. In the meantime, I do want to adjust rivaroxaban dose—we'll do that in 3 months once we have more data and see how you're responding. For now though, keep taking what you're on. One more thing: I know you mentioned having a drink or two some nights. I'd like you to reduce alcohol, at least while we're sorting through this.
PATIENT: Okay, I can do that. I wasn't drinking heavily anyway, just a glass of wine now and then.
PHYSICIAN: I appreciate that. Now, one thing I need you to watch for—this is important—if you develop signs of a blood clot, like sudden leg swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath that's new or different, I want you to get to urgent care right away. Don't wait. Do you understand?
PATIENT: Yes, I've got it. If I get any of that, I go in right away.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Let me have our care coordinator reach out to get that follow-up visit on the calendar and confirm the rivaroxaban refill. Any questions for me?
PATIENT: No, I think you've covered everything. I feel better knowing we're looking into this.

text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So I see we've got you down for a medication question today—let me just pull up your chart here. How are you managing at the moment?
PATIENT: Yeah, well, that's why I'm here. I've been noticing some things the past few days that are kind of... bothering me.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, tell me what's going on.
PATIENT: I've got this mild shortness of breath, started three days ago. And my legs, they're swelling up. Both of them. I'm not sure what that's about.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: How's the shortness of breath been—is it with activity, or pretty much all the time?
PATIENT: It comes and goes, mostly when I'm moving around. And I had this moderate lightheadedness too, over the weekend, but honestly it's getting better. But the legs... that worries me a bit.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Right, let me get some vitals and we'll talk through this. I'm checking your heart rate—that's 92. And I'm seeing your blood pressure's a bit elevated too, which makes sense given your hypertension. Let me also pull your labs from last month. Your hemoglobin a1c is 6.2%—that's actually pretty good.
PATIENT: Okay, that's... good? I think?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Yeah, that's solid. Now I want to talk about your medications. You're on atenolol 50 mg once daily for the blood pressure, atorvastatin 80 mg at bedtime, and sacubitril-valsartan 97 mg twice daily. Walk me through how you're taking those.
PATIENT: Well... I've got to be honest. I haven't been taking the atenolol. I stopped it about two weeks ago because it was making me feel sluggish, and with work and everything, I just... I wasn't taking it anymore.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, I appreciate you telling me that. That's important. The atenolol is really doing work for your heart, so we need to get you back on it. We'll refill it today, and maybe we can talk about the side effects you're experiencing. But let's not skip that one. What about the others?
PATIENT: The atorvastatin—I take that as prescribed. Every single day, haven't missed once.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good, that's the statin. And the sacubitril-valsartan?
PATIENT: Same thing. I haven't missed that either, taking it as prescribed, twice daily like you told me.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Perfect. So those two are locked in. Now—and this is important given what you're telling me about the swelling and the shortness of breath—the combination of the leg swelling and the mild shortness of breath and you coming off the atenolol... I'm wondering if we're seeing a bit of fluid buildup. Have you noticed your shoes fitting tighter, or waking up more puffy?
PATIENT: Yeah, actually, now that you mention it, my shoes have felt snug. And I've been sleeping a bit worse.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That fits with what I'm thinking. I want to get the atenolol back on board right away—we'll refill it. But I also want you to cut back on salt. That's going to help with the fluid retention.
PATIENT: Cut back on salt? Like, no salt at all?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Not no salt—you do need some. But watch the processed stuff, the canned soups, the takeout, the bread. Just be mindful. Does that seem doable?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. My neighbor's been dealing with some medical stuff too—actually just got diagnosed with migraine, keeps complaining about it—but anyway, yeah, I'll cut back on salt. That I can handle.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. And look, I also want to—well, next week or so, it might make sense to monitor blood pressure at home if you have a cuff. We can see how it settles once you're back on the atenolol, but it's something to think about.
PATIENT: I don't have a cuff, but I could get one if you think it's important.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's worth having on hand. But we'll see—let's get you in for a follow-up visit, get a fresh set of labs in a couple of weeks. How does that sound?
PATIENT: A follow-up visit, yeah. That sounds reasonable.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Great. So we're going to schedule a follow-up visit for you in about three weeks. In the meantime, restart the atenolol, keep on the other two, and cut back on salt. Your gout—is that flaring up at all, or is it stable?
PATIENT: Gout's been quiet, thankfully. No flare for months now.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Let's keep it that way. One other thing—you mentioned you work, yeah? What is it you do?
PATIENT: I'm in logistics, move around a lot. That's partly why the sluggishness from the atenolol was getting to me.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I hear that. Sometimes it takes tweaking the dose or the timing. Let's see how you feel once you're back on it, and we can adjust if needed at the next visit. But please restart it—that's the priority.
PATIENT: Okay, I will. And the hypertension—I get it, that's why I'm on all this stuff.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Exactly. You've got hypertension, and with the leg swelling and the shortness of breath, we're probably looking at some fluid retention on top of that. Getting back on the atenolol and cutting back on salt should help settle things down. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, sounds good. I'll do it.

CARE_COORDINATOR: Sorry I'm running a bit behind—had a patient call on an urgent matter. But let's get started. I've got your chart pulled up, Joshua. I'm looking here at your labs from last week and there's some things we need to adjust.
PATIENT: Mm-hmm.
CARE_COORDINATOR: First off, your blood pressure reading today is 128/82. That's actually fairly stable, which is good. How are you feeling with your poor appetite lately?
PATIENT: It's been pretty rough. Severe really, since Monday. But actually it's getting a little better now, thank God. For a while there I couldn't look at food without feeling—I don't know, just nothing sounded good. I was at my daughter's last week and she made this whole dinner and I just sat there moving it around the plate.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right, I hear you. Since Monday you're saying—so that's been about a week now. And you're noticing improvement?
PATIENT: Yeah, it's getting better.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. That's encouraging. Have you had any shortness of breath with all of this?
PATIENT: Well... no, actually. I haven't noticed anything like that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. And the muscle aches you mentioned on your symptom check—are those still there?
PATIENT: Oh yeah. They're moderate, and to be honest they've been getting worse since my last visit. My neck, my back, my knees mostly. The osteoarthritis just seems to be—it's just grinding at me, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Are you getting any numbness in the feet at all?
PATIENT: Actually, yeah. Some. Just in the last week or so.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. I'm going to note that. Now, let me go through your medications with you because your labs suggest we need to make some changes. You're on metformin right now—how have you been taking that?
PATIENT: Most of it I take. But I'll be honest, I've missed some doses here and there. Work gets crazy and sometimes I just forget.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I appreciate you being upfront about that. Based on your latest results, we're actually going to increase it. You'll be going up to 850 mg twice daily. The lab results are showing your glucose levels are running higher than we want, so that's why we're bumping the dose. Can you work with that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can try to be more careful.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's all we ask. Now, the insulin glargine—you've been on 30 units at bedtime. How's that been going?
PATIENT: To be honest, I haven't been taking it. Haven't been taking it for maybe two weeks now.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. Can you tell me what's going on there? Any particular reason?
PATIENT: I just... I was worried about my blood pressure dropping too low at night, honestly. I felt a bit dizzy once and I thought maybe it was that, so I just stopped.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's actually something worth looking into together. For blood pressure control specifically, we might want to adjust that insulin glargine dose anyway. Let me bring it down to something more modest. We'll work on that in a way that doesn't worry you, okay? We can start by bringing it down from 30 units at bedtime.
PATIENT: Okay, that sounds better.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Your carvedilol, though—that's the one keeping things steady. How are you managing with the 3.125 mg twice daily?
PATIENT: No, I'm taking that as prescribed. Haven't missed a dose. Every single day, morning and night.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's exactly what I want to hear. We're going to keep it exactly where it is. Now, I want to talk to you about anemia. Your hemoglobin's come back low again, and we need to address that. One thing that can really help is cutting back on salt in your diet. Less salt helps your kidneys work better, and that helps with the anemia.
PATIENT: Huh. I don't really put salt on things.
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's more the salt that's already in packaged foods, deli meats, that sort of thing. Can you commit to cutting back on salt?
PATIENT: Yeah, I'll try. I can do that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Great. I'm also going to refer you to nephrology. That's a kidney specialist. Your kidney function numbers tell me you could use a dedicated look, and they might have some insights for us. We'll schedule that at your next visit.
PATIENT: Okay. Do I need to do anything special before that?
CARE_COORDINATOR: No, just keep doing what you're doing. Now let's schedule a follow-up visit. How does two weeks from now work for you?
PATIENT: Two weeks is fine.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. I'll get that on the calendar. Any questions before we wrap up?
PATIENT: No, I think that covers it.

PATIENT: Here we go again—back in the chair. I swear I was just in here last month. My wife jokes that I'm keeping you folks in business.
NURSE: Well, we're glad to see you. Let's get your weight today. Can you step on the scale for me?
PATIENT: Sure thing. I think I'm around 152 pounds, though honestly I haven't checked in a couple of days.
NURSE: Perfect, that matches what you're saying—152 pounds. And I see on the chart here you mentioned some blurred vision. Can you tell me a little bit about that?
PATIENT: Yeah, it started this morning when I woke up. Just mild blurred vision, nothing too alarming. But the weird thing is it seems to be getting better as the day goes on, so I don't know if I should even worry about it.
NURSE: That's good information. Any other symptoms you've noticed? Any changes in how you're feeling otherwise?
PATIENT: Now that you mention it, I've been pretty exhausted. Like severe fatigue, really. Started three days ago, and honestly it's getting worse, not better. I'm just dragging myself through the day.
NURSE: That's concerning. And how's your appetite? Any weight changes besides what we measured today?
PATIENT: Funny enough, I have noticed some moderate weight loss, but it just started yesterday. It's been about the same since then though, not really changing day to day.
NURSE: Let me document that. The doctor's going to want to see you about this cluster of symptoms. I'm going to let them know you're here, and I'll be right back.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Hey there. I'm Sarah, one of our care coordinators. I see in your chart you've got the blurred vision coming on this morning, and you're dealing with some pretty severe fatigue that started a few days back. Walk me through what's going on with your medications—are you taking everything the way we discussed?
PATIENT: Well, most of it. The semaglutide—I'm supposed to take 0.5 mg once weekly—but I'll be honest, I've missed a couple of doses recently. Work's been hectic. My doctor mentioned bringing the dose down anyway for my blood pressure, so I've kind of been all over the place with it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, that's important to know. And the sitagliptin—the 25 mg once daily tablet—how have you been with that one?
PATIENT: Honestly? I'm not sure. I take something most days, but I couldn't say if I'm taking it exactly right. I don't remember the details off the top of my head.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's helpful to say out loud. We're going to keep that sitagliptin at 25 mg once daily—same as you're on now, no change there. And the dulaglutide, the 3 mg once weekly injection—how's that been going?
PATIENT: That one I've been good with. I take the 3 mg once weekly as prescribed, and I haven't missed any doses on that one. Every time the calendar says it's time, I do it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's excellent. We can get that refilled for you today. Now, tell me—and this is important—have you ever had any kind of fainting episode? Any time you've lost consciousness or felt like you were about to pass out?
PATIENT: No, nothing like that. I mean, I feel tired and kind of foggy with this fatigue, but I haven't actually blacked out or anything.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, I want to make sure we're watching for that, especially with the symptoms you're describing. Your family history—I'm looking back here—your grandmother on your mother's side, she had some issues with coronary artery disease, didn't she?
PATIENT: Yeah, she did. Had a heart attack when I was a kid, actually. She's been gone for years now. I think about that sometimes, wondering if that puts me at risk too, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's something we keep an eye on. Given your hyperlipidemia—that's the high cholesterol—and that family history, we want to be proactive. Let me pull up your recent labs here. Typing these up now... So your hemoglobin a1c came back at 6.8%, which is pretty solid.
PATIENT: Is that good? I'm never sure what these numbers mean.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's a good diabetes control number. But combined with the severe fatigue that's getting worse and this new vision issue, I want the doctor to evaluate you more carefully. I think we need to refer to endocrinology to make sure nothing's being missed on the metabolic side.
PATIENT: Do you think something serious is going on?
CARE_COORDINATOR: I think we need the specialists to take a closer look, especially since these symptoms are evolving. Are you comfortable with a refer to endocrinology? That can happen at your next visit.
PATIENT: Yeah, if you think that's what I need. I'd rather get it checked out.
NURSE: The doctor's ready for you now. Come on back.
CARE_COORDINATOR: One more thing before you go—we're also going to schedule a follow-up visit for you. I'll get that on the calendar. In the meantime, the doctor's going to talk with you about increasing your daily walking. That's something we really want you to work on over the next three months, okay?
PATIENT: Walking, I can do. My dog's been wanting more exercise anyway, so that works out.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. See you in a few. We'll get everything lined up.

CARE_COORDINATOR: ...so the dizziness started this morning, you said?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah. It's been pretty severe, honestly. I woke up and the room was just spinning. It's about the same as it was a couple hours ago, hasn't gotten worse or better really.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. And you've got the chest pain too—how's that progressing?
PATIENT: That one started three days ago. It's moderate pain, but actually it's getting better. I was worried at first, but yeah, each day it feels a bit less intense.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good, that's good. Let me just check your heart rate here. Got 68.
PATIENT: That normal?
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's solid. Look, I need to ask about your medication compliance. You're on the losartan still, 25 mg once daily—you taking that regularly?
PATIENT: Um, yeah, well... I've missed some doses, I'll be honest. It's not that I don't want to take it, it's just—life gets chaotic, you know? Some mornings I just forget.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We need to tighten that up, especially with the peripheral artery disease you've got and the atrial fibrillation. Missing doses isn't helping.
PATIENT: I know, I know. It's not on purpose. I should set a—what's the word—like a reminder on my phone or something.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's one option. Now, the hydrochlorothiazide—we're actually bringing that down. You've been taking it 12.5 mg once daily as prescribed, right?
PATIENT: Haven't missed a single one of those, every day like clockwork. Why the change?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Blood pressure control. It's been running a bit lower lately, so we're adjusting the dose down. You'll get a new prescription for that.
PATIENT: Lower's good, I guess. Better than the old days when it was through the roof.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right. So we're going to keep you on the losartan at 25 mg once daily the way it is—no change there. But you have to actually take it.
PATIENT: Yeah, I hear you. I'll do better.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And given what you've got going on—the peripheral artery disease and the atrial fibrillation—we need to monitor blood pressure at home. Can you do that?
PATIENT: I've got a cuff. I can do that, yeah.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. Start that right away, and we'll check in about it in 4 weeks. I'll make sure the nurse knows.
PATIENT: Okay. And, uh... should I be worried about the dizziness? Like, if it gets worse, what do I do?
CARE_COORDINATOR: If it becomes severe and you can't stand up safely, or if you develop chest pain that's worse than what you had, get to urgent care. The dizziness could be tied to the atrial fibrillation. Right now it's about the same, so that's holding, but keep an eye on it.
PATIENT: At this rate I might need to quit my job and just sit on the couch.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Not yet. Let's see how this goes. One other thing—you might think about cutting back on salt, especially with your blood pressure. I know it's not the most exciting conversation.
PATIENT: Next week? I don't know, maybe. I'll think about it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Fair enough. And we should probably schedule a follow-up visit in 4 weeks as well to see how things are tracking, but let's loop back on that later. Sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds fine. I appreciate it.

CARE_COORDINATOR: So I'm looking at your chart here, Claire, and it says you were discharged five days ago. You're having some swelling in your legs—can you tell me what that's been like?
PATIENT: Yeah, it's... it's pretty bad. Severe leg swelling, really, since my last visit.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Severe swelling since your last visit. And is it getting better or worse?
PATIENT: Worse. It just keeps getting worse.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. What about your sleep—how's that been?
PATIENT: Not great. Difficulty sleeping, you know, between the swelling and... and just not feeling right.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Not feeling right in what way? And we know you have obstructive sleep apnea—are you using your CPAP at night?
PATIENT: I am, I am using it. But the swelling... it's in my calves, and when I lie down it just gets worse, or so it feels like it...
CARE_COORDINATOR: Has your appetite changed at all?
PATIENT: Yeah, actually. Severe poor appetite for the past few days, but it's... it's been getting better now, I think.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Better is good. Let's talk about your medications. We had you on empagliflozin 25 mg once daily. Are you still taking that?
PATIENT: No, you told me to hold it for now. I haven't been taking it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right, that's correct. And the duloxetine—60 mg once daily—how are you managing with that?
PATIENT: I've... I've missed a few doses, if I'm being honest. I forget sometimes.
CARE_COORDINATOR: You've missed some. That's actually part of why we're bringing the dose down—we're trying to get better blood pressure control. We're reducing it, and then we're starting you on something new for sleep. It's called amitriptyline, 25 mg at bedtime. Have you started that yet?
PATIENT: Yeah, I have. Every single day at bedtime, I'm taking it as prescribed.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. That's really important. Now, can you tell me your weight for me today?
PATIENT: I weighed myself this morning. 204 pounds.
CARE_COORDINATOR: 204 pounds—okay. That's important to track, especially with the leg swelling. I want to make sure we're monitoring things closely. I'd like you to monitor blood pressure at home. Does that sound doable?
PATIENT: Yeah, I have a monitor. I can do that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Great. And we're going to order follow-up bloodwork to check a few things. We know you have a long history of anemia, and I want to see where you're at, given everything. Your old records show that, and it's still something we're managing.
PATIENT: Okay. That's... that's fine with me.
CARE_COORDINATOR: So just to wrap up: you're going to monitor blood pressure at home, we'll order follow-up bloodwork, you'll keep taking the amitriptyline every day, and the duloxetine dose is coming down. We need to touch base in about a week to see how that leg swelling is responding. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah. Yeah, that sounds good.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Alright. Call us if anything gets worse, especially with that swelling or if you're having any other issues.
PATIENT: Will do.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Hi there—is this still a good time to chat? I've got your latest labs in front of me and wanted to walk through a few things that came up.
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, now's fine. My wife's here too if you need to know anything.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: Hi, I'm listening. He's been... well, he's been different lately.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good to have you both. So Beckett, I want to start with something you mentioned at your last visit—you said you'd been noticing increased thirst. Can you tell me what that's been like?
PATIENT: Oh man, it's been severe, honestly. I'm going through like two, three bottles of water a day, maybe more. And I'm still just... parched all the time. I wake up at night thirsty.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That sounds really uncomfortable. And when did that start to feel noticeable to you?
PATIENT: I don't know, maybe three weeks ago? It just crept up on me. Or—I don't know, maybe it's been longer and I just didn't... I wasn't paying attention until about three weeks.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: It's been worse the last couple weeks especially. I noticed he was refilling his water glass constantly during dinner.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I appreciate you both flagging that. The other thing in our notes is that you woke up with numbness in the feet this morning, is that right?
PATIENT: Yeah, when I got out of bed, my feet were numb. Like moderate numbness—not terrible, but I could definitely feel it. And actually it's been getting better as the day goes on, so that's... that's good.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, so this morning you woke up with it and it's already improving. Any tingling, or just that numb sensation?
PATIENT: Just numb, mostly. A little pins and needles when I first stood up, but then it settled down.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Mm-hmm. And have you had any nausea to go along with either of these things—the thirst or the numbness?
PATIENT: No, I don't think—well, I mean, I haven't felt great, but no, not nausea. Not really.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Not really, or no nausea? I want to make sure I'm clear on that.
PATIENT: No. No nausea. I'd know if I was nauseous. I'm not.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright. Your hemoglobin a1c came back at 8.6 percent, which tells me your glucose control hasn't been where we want it. And your blood pressure today is running very high—I mean, we're seeing a very high blood pressure reading. I want to get you in with cardiology pretty urgently to make sure we're not missing something with your heart. This is urgent.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: How high are we talking about? Should we be worried?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's elevated enough that I don't want to wait. Your hypertension—the high blood pressure you've had for years—isn't controlled the way it should be right now. And I want to rule out heart failure with reduced ejection fraction because some of what you're describing, combined with these readings, has me concerned. I'm not convinced yet that's what's going on, but I think we need to look.
PATIENT: Heart failure? I—like, my heart doesn't... it's not failing, is it?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's what we're going to find out. Right now I'm saying I want to rule it out. Let's talk through your medications and make sure we have you on the right regimen. Are you still taking the lisinopril, the blood pressure pill?
PATIENT: Uh, no actually, I stopped taking that a couple months ago. The lisinopril 10 mg once daily—I haven't been taking it. My blood pressure felt okay without it and I just, I didn't refill it.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: Wait, you didn't tell me that. Why would you stop it?
PATIENT: I don't know, I just thought maybe I didn't need it anymore or—look, I'm sorry, I should've mentioned it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, so we're going to need to restart that and get it filled. What about your insulin aspart—you take 6 units with meals by injection?
PATIENT: Yeah, I'm taking that as prescribed. Every single day, 6 units with meals. I haven't missed any doses.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good, I'll get that refilled for you. And the semaglutide—are you still on that 0.25 mg once weekly?
PATIENT: I haven't been taking it. I know I should be, but I wasn't sure if it was helping and it felt like a lot of medications, so...
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright. We're going to restart the lisinopril, keep the insulin aspart going the way you are—which is excellent—and we should probably revisit the semaglutide. I also think it makes sense to refer you to endocrinology given your glucose numbers and the complexity of what we're looking at. Are you comfortable with that referral?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's... yeah, that makes sense. I want to get this sorted out.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And in the meantime, we'll be scheduling you with cardiology urgently. After you see them, we might float the idea of a follow-up visit next week just to touch base, depending on what cardiology finds. But let's get those urgent pieces moving first.
