text:
PHYSICIAN: So let's start by going over what's happened since you got home from the hospital. You've been back three days now, is that right?
PATIENT: Yes, three days. And I've been... well, I'm worried about the dizziness, frankly. It's been severe since my last visit, but at least it's getting better now. That's something.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, that's good to hear it's improving. When you say severe—how's that affecting your day-to-day right now?
PATIENT: I can't get around the house without holding onto something. My daughter's been here helping, but I'm afraid to go up the stairs alone. Though like I said, it was worse when I first came back.
PHYSICIAN: Right. And you also mentioned on the phone that you've been having a headache. Tell me about that.
PATIENT: Just a mild headache, nothing terrible. It's been there since Monday, and it hasn't gotten any worse or any better. Just sort of sitting there.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, so it's not changing. Let me pull up your discharge medications here and we'll make sure you're on track with everything. You left with quite a few, so let's go through them.
PATIENT: I have them all written down. I've been really careful about it.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Let's see—you're on allopurinol, 200 mg once daily. How's that going?
PATIENT: Every single day, like clockwork. I haven't missed a dose. Take it right after breakfast.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. We'll need to get that refilled for you—the nurse can arrange that. Now, you've also got hydralazine, 10 mg three times daily. That's three times a day. How are you managing with that one?
PATIENT: I'm taking that as prescribed. Morning, afternoon, and evening. The only thing is—I don't remember why I'm on it, exactly. Is it for the blood pressure?
PHYSICIAN: Yes, exactly. It's another blood pressure medication working alongside the allopurinol to help control your hypertension. We're going to keep you on the same dose for now. And then there's the colchicine, 0.6 mg once daily.
PATIENT: That one... I've been a little spotty with it, I'll be honest. I've missed a few doses. Some days I just forget.
PHYSICIAN: That happens, especially when you're managing multiple medications. Let's keep it the same for now, but it would be helpful if you could try to be more consistent with it. Now, I want to make sure we're keeping a close eye on your blood pressure at home. Do you have a monitor?
PATIENT: My daughter picked one up yesterday. We haven't really used it yet, though.
PHYSICIAN: Great. So here's what we'll do—we need you to monitor blood pressure at home every day, and we'll check in on those numbers in about four weeks. The nurse will make sure you know exactly how to use the cuff and what to write down. Does that sound manageable?
PATIENT: Yes, I can do that. My daughter will help.
PHYSICIAN: Excellent. And because of the medication adjustments we're considering, we'll want to adjust allopurinol dose based on what we see in your blood work. Let's plan to reassess that in four weeks as well, once the nurse has those home readings. We might need to change the dose, but we'll see how you respond first.
PATIENT: How will you know if it needs adjusting?
PHYSICIAN: We check your uric acid level and your kidney function through bloodwork. You also take this for your hyperlipidemia, to manage cholesterol and the other fatty stuff in your blood. All of that gets measured.
PATIENT: Oh, hyperlipidemia—is that the cholesterol thing?
PHYSICIAN: Yes, that's the medical word for when you have high levels of fats in your blood. In your case, we're treating it to keep your heart and arteries as healthy as possible.
PATIENT: That makes sense. So four weeks, then?
PHYSICIAN: Four weeks to monitor blood pressure at home, and we'll also order follow-up bloodwork around that same time—probably—to see how you're doing. I'll talk with the nurse about the timing on that. You okay with all of this?
PATIENT: Yes. I feel better knowing we have a plan. I was nervous coming in today.

NURSE: —so the blood pressure's actually been trending better on what we adjusted last month, which is good news. How's the pantoprazole working out for you?
PATIENT: Fine. I take it every single day, so.
NURSE: Great. And the heartburn itself—how bad is it typically?
PATIENT: Moderate. It's there most days, especially at night.
NURSE: Okay. We're actually going to bring that dose down a bit since your numbers have stabilised. We'll go with 40 mg once daily instead of what you've been on. That should still give you good coverage for the heartburn. Think that'll work?
PATIENT: Yeah, I guess. As long as it doesn't flare back up.
NURSE: We'll monitor it. Now, you've got some nausea going on too. Tell me about that.
PATIENT: It's mild. Started for the past few days. Nothing major.
NURSE: Is it getting worse, staying about the same?
PATIENT: About the same.
NURSE: Alright. And then you mentioned the dizziness on the form. When did that start?
PATIENT: Last week. But it's getting better now.
NURSE: How would you describe it—how moderate is it? Or is that not quite the right word?
PATIENT: No, it's moderate. Some days I just feel kind of... unsteady. Like the room's not really spinning but I'm off.
NURSE: Got it. And you're saying it's trending better since last week?
PATIENT: Yeah. Probably be gone by next week if I'm lucky.
NURSE: Do you have a fever at all?
PATIENT: No, nothing like that.
NURSE: Any blurred vision?
PATIENT: No.
NURSE: Okay. How's the migraine been? Is that still active for you?
PATIENT: Yeah, it comes and goes. Had one yesterday. They're not fun.
NURSE: I hear you. And the gout—is that flaring right now or is it controlled?
PATIENT: It's flaring. My left foot is absolutely thrilled about it. Really making my day, you know?
NURSE: Yeah, not ideal. So on a zero to ten scale, where would you put your overall pain today?
PATIENT: 2. It's manageable.
NURSE: Good. Now let's talk about your losartan. You're on 100 mg once daily for blood pressure. How's that been going—are you taking it consistently?
PATIENT: Um, mostly. I've missed a few doses here and there. I forget sometimes.
NURSE: Okay, I'll be honest—that's probably contributing to some of what we're seeing on the monitor. We're going to keep you at 100 mg once daily, but really try to get into a rhythm with it. Maybe set a phone reminder if that helps?
PATIENT: Yeah, I could do that.
NURSE: We'll also probably want to check in with you next week—see how things are settling. And if the numbers don't level out by then, we might need to order follow-up bloodwork to see if there's anything else going on. Does next week work for you?
PATIENT: Next week is fine.
NURSE: Good. And look, when you come back, we can talk about whether adjusting things like the losartan dose might make sense—just to see if we can smooth things out a bit more.
PATIENT: Okay.

PATIENT: Okay so I had a ten o'clock but then the office called and said they needed to bump me to ten-thirty, which is honestly fine, I've just been sitting in the waiting area scrolling through my phone. Anyway, yeah, so I'm here because of the wheezing, and I've been really tired. Like, exhausted. I can barely get through a shift at work without needing to sit down.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright, let's start with the wheezing. When did that start?
PATIENT: Oh, last week. It's mild, you know, it's not terrible, but it's there. Like when I breathe in I can hear it sometimes, especially at night.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And is it getting worse, staying about the same, or has it actually improved a bit since last week?
PATIENT: It's about the same. Hasn't really changed. Oh, and then yesterday I noticed my chest was tight. Like, mild chest tightness. It started yesterday and it's just... it's the same since then. I was wondering if maybe I'd been working out too hard or something, but I haven't really been exercising much because I'm so tired.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, chest tightness started yesterday. Got it. Let me ask you about your inhalers—the fluticasone-salmeterol that you're on. How's that going? Are you using it?
PATIENT: Yeah, so I'm supposed to be on it, 1 puffs twice daily, and I have a refill that I've been meaning to get. But I mean, honestly, I've missed some doses here and there. Some days I just forget, especially on weekends when my routine is different. My hairdresser, actually, she's been having all these problems—she had kidney stones last month and let me tell you, she was miserable. Anyway, I've got the refill situation sorted now though.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, so we'll make sure a refill is arranged for the fluticasone-salmeterol. That's important, especially if we're seeing some respiratory symptoms. Before we talk about your chest, I want to circle back on something. Earlier you mentioned some of this came on recently. Have you been sick at all? Any fever, cough, anything like that?
PATIENT: Well, I did have kind of a lingering cough a week or so ago, yeah. I thought it was just a cold, but it hung around. I was coughing up some stuff. My manager kept giving me these looks, you know? Very supportive but like, I could tell he was hoping I'd stop coughing in the office.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: A cough that's been productive—you're bringing up phlegm. Given the wheezing and the fatigue on top of that, I'm thinking about community-acquired pneumonia. Has anyone diagnosed you with that, or have you heard that term before?
PATIENT: No, no one's said that. I mean, I know what pneumonia is, but I didn't think it was that bad. Pneumonia sounds serious.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Community-acquired pneumonia can range from mild to severe. We'll want to check some things. Let me get your oxygen saturation real quick.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. Should I be worried?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Not yet. Let's see what we're working with. [places pulse ox on finger] And that's 97 percent, which is good. That's a healthy reading.
PATIENT: Okay, so that's... that's normal? Ninety-seven is good?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Yes, 97 is right where we want it. Now, let me ask about your medications more broadly. You mentioned you haven't been great about taking the inhaler. What about any antibiotics? Have you been on anything like that?
PATIENT: Oh, yeah, there was... I think it was amoxicillin? Someone gave me that a few weeks ago. But honestly, I haven't been taking it. I just haven't, so there's no point in me pretending I have. I wasn't sure if I really needed it or if I could just ride things out, you know?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Amoxicillin, 250 mg, three times daily—is that what you were prescribed?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds right. But like I said, I stopped taking it. Or actually, I never really started. I have the bottle but...
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, so we're not going to change anything with that one since you're not taking it anyway. We're reviewing it, and we'll leave it at that. Given what we're seeing though—the wheezing, the fatigue, the chest tightness, that lingering cough—I do want to address the community-acquired pneumonia concern. We should start you on appropriate treatment and get you recovering.
PATIENT: So what does that mean? Do I need to go to the hospital or something?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: No, not at this point. Your oxygen is fine. But we will want to follow up with you. I want to schedule a follow-up visit in 3 months to see how you're doing.
PATIENT: Three months? That seems like a long time.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We can adjust if needed, but let's see how you respond to treatment first. In the meantime, I'd also like you to increase daily walking. Nothing intense, just a regular routine. Even just fifteen or twenty minutes a day will help your lungs clear and help with the fatigue.
PATIENT: Okay, I can do that. I've been so tired I haven't been doing much, so it'll actually be nice to get moving. Yeah, I'll increase daily walking.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. So to recap: we're arranging a refill for your fluticasone-salmeterol, 1 puffs twice daily. You're going to be consistent with that. We're treating this as community-acquired pneumonia. And we're going to schedule a follow-up visit in 3 months, and in the meantime you're going to increase daily walking. Does that sound like a plan?
PATIENT: Yeah, that makes sense. I feel like I know what's going on now instead of just feeling crappy and not knowing why. I'll keep up with the inhaler this time.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's the right attitude. We'll get you back on track. Any other questions before you head out?
PATIENT: No, I think that's everything. Oh, well, actually—my sister has a dog, a golden retriever, and she's always asking me to take him for walks, so I can probably just do that and kill two birds with one stone. That'll help me increase daily walking and make her happy.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's perfect. Getting out and moving, spending time with the dog—that's exactly what you need right now. Take care, and we'll see you in 3 months.

CARE_COORDINATOR: The waiting room was actually pretty calm today, wasn't it? I mean, usually it's — anyway, so we've got you down here because of the swelling and some chest—
PATIENT: Yeah, the leg swelling showed up this morning, actually. Woke up and my left ankle was just... puffy. I didn't think much of it at first, figured maybe I'd slept funny or something, but it's moderate leg swelling, you know? Been there all day.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And is it changing at all as the day goes on? Getting worse, getting better, or pretty much staying the same?
PATIENT: About the same, I'd say. Hasn't gotten any worse. Haven't gotten any relief from it either.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. And the chest pain — when did that start for you?
PATIENT: Three days ago. But here's the thing, it's mild. It's not like I'm clutching my chest or anything. It's more like a tightness, and honestly, it's getting better already. Each day it's a little less there.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's good to hear it's improving. Tell me about what you were doing when you first noticed it.
PATIENT: I was at work, actually. I was sitting at my desk, and I felt this kind of... what's the word... not quite a pressure, but more like a sensation right behind my sternum. And my coworker Mike, he was complaining that day too, but his thing was completely different — he's got shingles, which is just awful for him. Anyway, when the tightness came on, I figured maybe I'd been hunched over too long.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Has anything else been going on? Any other symptoms?
PATIENT: Well, yesterday I got hit with severe dizziness. Like, I stood up from the couch and the room just tilted. It spooked me a little, to be honest. But by the end of the day it was less intense, and today it's even better.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: When you say it's getting better — do you still feel any dizziness right now, or is it pretty much resolved?
PATIENT: Still a little bit there if I turn my head fast, but it's definitely on its way out. Mostly getting better.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And how have you been sleeping through all this? Any trouble with that?
PATIENT: Actually, my sleep is not great. I mean, I have obstructive sleep apnea — been dealing with that for a while now. Some nights I'm gasping awake, some nights I'm just restless. It's been rough.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Are you on any treatment for that, or are you just managing it as it comes?
PATIENT: I was supposed to use the CPAP machine, but I haven't been great about it, if I'm honest. Hard to get into the habit.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I understand. Let's talk about your medications, because that's important here. You were just started on nebivolol — that's a heart medication, a beta-blocker. How are you getting on with that?
PATIENT: The nebivolol 10 mg, once daily — I'm taking it exactly as prescribed. Haven't missed a single day. It's the one I take in the morning with my breakfast.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's excellent. And the rosuvastatin — that's for cholesterol control. How about that one?
PATIENT: The rosuvastatin 10 mg, once daily... I've missed some doses, I'll admit. Some mornings I just forget, and then by evening it's too late to take it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We can work on that. Maybe setting a phone reminder would help? We can arrange a refill for you today and chat through some strategies.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. A reminder might actually help.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And then there's the spironolactone 25 mg, once daily — how are you managing with that one?
PATIENT: Honestly, I'm not sure how I've been taking that. I don't remember if I'm consistent with it or not, couldn't say for certain.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's okay. We'll keep you on it for now — no change there. But I do want to check your numbers. Your LDL cholesterol came back at 84 mg/dL, which is reasonable, but given the chest symptoms and the swelling, I want to keep an eye on things.
CARE_COORDINATOR: So here's what we're going to do. We'd like you to monitor blood pressure at home — we'll send you home with a log and a machine if you need one — and check in again in 4 weeks. That's something you're comfortable doing?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Now, one thing we might look at down the road is whether we need to adjust nebivolol dose — that's something we can revisit in 4 weeks depending on how you're doing and what your blood pressure readings show. We'll see where you're at.
PATIENT: Okay. And is there anything else I should be doing?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: One possibility is to cut back on salt — that can help with the swelling and blood pressure — but that's something to think about over the next week and we can discuss what feels realistic for you.

PHYSICIAN: Hi Terry, this is Dr. Ramirez from the office. Do you have a few minutes right now to go over your medications and what's been happening with you?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I've got time. Thanks for calling.
PHYSICIAN: Good. So your last visit notes mention fatigue. How's that been?
PATIENT: It's gotten worse, actually. It's moderate fatigue since my last visit, and I just—I feel like I'm running out of steam by mid-afternoon. Even when I've slept, which hasn't been much lately. And my psoriasis has been flaring up too, which isn't helping things.
PHYSICIAN: The sleep—tell me about that.
PATIENT: Severe difficulty sleeping, started three days ago. I'm just lying there, tossing around, and it's not really getting any better. I mean, it's about the same every night.
PHYSICIAN: Are you waking up at night or can't fall asleep?
PATIENT: Both, really. I fall asleep okay enough but then I'm up at two, three in the morning and can't get back to... you know. Back to—
PHYSICIAN: Right. And your legs—any swelling?
PATIENT: Actually, yes. Mild leg swelling this morning. It's getting worse as the day goes on, and I noticed it this morning when I put my shoes on.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. Let me pull up your list here. You're on metformin, 500 mg once daily?
PATIENT: That's right. I take it every single day, as prescribed. Haven't missed a dose.
PHYSICIAN: Good. We'll refill that. Escitalopram, 20 mg once daily—still on that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I think so. I mean, yes. I'm taking it as prescribed every day, but I—I guess I'm not sure if that's still... if you want me to keep going.
PHYSICIAN: We'll keep you on it for now. No change there. And carvedilol, 25 mg twice daily.
PATIENT: I've been taking that, but honestly, I've missed some doses. I forget sometimes with the twice-a-day thing, especially in the afternoon.
PHYSICIAN: That's—that's something we need to address, given your heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Missing doses can be risky.
PATIENT: I know, I know. I'm not trying to—it's just a lot of pills to keep track of.
PHYSICIAN: I hear you. We can talk about that more at your next visit. Let me grab your blood pressure. It's reading 118/72.
PATIENT: That's not bad, right?
PHYSICIAN: That's fine. Now, you mentioned worse fatigue, leg swelling today, and sleep issues. With your history—the heart failure—I want to get nephrology involved. We can schedule a follow-up visit and put in a refer to nephrology at that time. Does that work for you?
PATIENT: Yeah, that... that makes sense to me. I'm willing to do that.
PHYSICIAN: Also, your older sister—she has hyperlipidemia, yes?
PATIENT: She does, yeah. Had some heart trouble too, actually, so—
PHYSICIAN: Right. So that's family history to keep in mind. One more thing: we need you to cut back on salt. The swelling and fatigue can be related to fluid retention, and salt makes that worse.
PATIENT: Okay. I can do that. Less salt, got it.
PHYSICIAN: Good. So let's schedule a follow-up visit—aim for two weeks out—and we'll revisit the carvedilol timing then and get things set up with nephrology. Sound alright?
PATIENT: Sounds good. Thank you.

text:
PATIENT: Before we start, I need to ask—these new pills you sent me home with, the smaller ones, how long before they're supposed to kick in? Because I've still got that awful nausea.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good question. Let's talk through everything. So you're experiencing nausea—how long has that been going on?
PATIENT: Oh, it started right after I came home. I thought maybe it was just the ride home or something settling wrong, but it's still there. I've got gastroesophageal reflux disease, you know, so I thought maybe it was acting up again.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That makes sense given your gastroesophageal reflux disease history. And on top of that you've mentioned the nausea—has anything else been bothering you since discharge?
PATIENT: Well, I've had terrible muscle aches, actually. Severe muscle aches over the weekend. They're getting worse, not better.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Severe muscle aches over the weekend—got it. And they've been worsening since then? Anything else?
PATIENT: I'm tired too, but I don't know if that counts. Moderate fatigue, I'd say. Started since Monday.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Is it getting worse or staying about the same?
PATIENT: About the same, I think. Hasn't gotten worse anyway.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. I want to make sure—have you had any heart palpitations? Any skipping or racing?
PATIENT: Oh no, thank goodness, nothing like that. No palpitations at all. That would really scare me.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. That's a relief. Now, on a zero to ten scale, where zero is no pain and ten is the worst you could imagine, where would you rate the muscle aches?
PATIENT: I'd say 5. Right in the middle. They're there but I can move around.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Five, okay. Let me look at your med list. You're on the ibuprofen—how have you been taking that? Because the lab work came back and we may need to adjust ibuprofen dose based on those results.
PATIENT: I... honestly, I'm not sure. I think I've been taking it as needed when the aching gets bad, but I don't remember exactly how many times a day. I couldn't say for certain.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's all right. We're going to dial that in for you. We'll adjust ibuprofen dose at your next visit, okay? We want to get ahead of this with the labs showing what they showed.
PATIENT: Okay, fine. I just hope it doesn't get too expensive. My insurance is already flagging a bunch of things.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I understand. We'll keep an eye on that. Now, the omeprazole—the 20 mg once daily for your reflux. How are you managing with that?
PATIENT: Oh, I've been taking that as prescribed every single day. Haven't missed a dose.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Great. Actually, we're going to come down on that one a bit. The newest blood pressure readings suggest we can lower the dose, so that should help with some of the side effects. Still 20 mg once daily, but we're optimizing for blood pressure control now.
PATIENT: Wait—are you lowering it or keeping it the same? You said 20 mg once daily...
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good catch. Sorry, I misspoke—we are bringing the omeprazole dose down, but we're continuing the 20 mg once daily regimen itself. Timing-wise, the adjustment happens next visit. The key thing is your blood pressure readings have improved enough that we can reduce your overall exposure to this medication.
PATIENT: Okay, so... the same pill, same time, but less of it somehow?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right—we may split a dose or adjust the formulation, we'll sort that at your next visit. What matters is the direction of travel. And I need you to monitor blood pressure at home. That's something the physician wants to see happen every couple weeks—just jot down those readings. We'll review in 3 months.
PATIENT: Every couple weeks is... that seems like a lot, but I have one of those cuff things at home. I can do that.

PHYSICIAN: So last time we saw you, you'd just come back from that trip and your blood pressure was running a bit high, if I'm remembering correctly. You were on a couple of things for your atrial fibrillation at that point. How's that been settling?
PATIENT: Yeah, well, the trip was actually the month before that, but yes, things have been... you know, I've got a lot on my plate right now. My neighbour, the one down the hall, he's been dealing with kidney stones, absolute nightmare. We've been talking about it quite a bit—he's supposed to see urology next week, poor guy, can barely walk. But me, personally, I'm not having that issue, thank God.
PHYSICIAN: Right, yeah, that's rough for him. Let me focus in on you for a moment though. What's actually brought you in today?
PATIENT: It's the sleep. I've been having real trouble sleeping, and it's been for the past few days now. Not just waking up, I mean I'm lying there for hours. The quality is terrible. I'd say it's moderate difficulty sleeping, honestly—it's affecting how I function during the day.
PHYSICIAN: Moderate difficulty sleeping for the past few days—okay. Any sense of what might have triggered it? Stress? Changes in your routine?
PATIENT: I'm not entirely sure. My appetite's been poor too, which is unusual for me. I'm not eating the way I normally do. And then there's this other thing—I've got some numbness in the feet, started three days ago, and I've got to tell you, it's getting worse. The numbness is moderate, or maybe worse than that, I don't know.
PHYSICIAN: Moderate numbness in the feet since three days ago and it's progressing. That's worth looking at. Let me ask you about chest pain—have you had any of that?
PATIENT: Chest pain? No. I mean, I've been a bit anxious about all this, but no, I haven't had chest pain. Not at all.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Let's go through your medications and make sure we're on the same page. You're on duloxetine for mood—60 mg once daily. How have you been taking it?
PATIENT: The duloxetine... I'm not sure, actually. I think once daily, but I don't remember if I've been completely consistent with it. Most days I take it, but honestly I couldn't say with 100 per cent certainty.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, that's helpful to know. So there might be some variability there. We can refill it for you, but let's make sure you're taking 60 mg once daily going forward, ideally at the same time each day. That might help with the sleep too.
PATIENT: Yeah, that makes sense. The sleep thing is really getting to me. Insurance has been a bit of a nightmare with the copays lately, so I'm watching costs, but I need to get this sorted.
PHYSICIAN: I understand. Let me make a note about the refill. You're also on dapagliflozin, 10 mg once daily. Are you still taking that?
PATIENT: The dapagliflozin... I'm not sure if I'm even still on that one, to be honest. I don't remember how I've been taking it or if I'm doing it at all. There's so many pills.
PHYSICIAN: That's fair. We'll review that—10 mg once daily is the prescription. It's for your blood sugar, so it's important to be consistent, but we don't need to change anything today. Just want to make sure you're aware you should be taking it.
PATIENT: Right. I'll look at it when I get home. Sometimes I think I'm doing it, then I realize I'm not sure if it was today or yesterday.
PHYSICIAN: Understood. And your escitalopram—5 mg once daily. What's your sense with that one?
PATIENT: That one I'm definitely on top of. I haven't missed a single dose, every single day, as prescribed. That one's easier for me to remember.
PHYSICIAN: Good. That consistency is important. Alright, let me pull up your recent labs. Your hemoglobin a1c came back at 6.8 %, which is actually quite reasonable.
PATIENT: Is that good? I'm not great with the numbers, to be honest. I know a1c is the blood sugar thing.
PHYSICIAN: It's good, yes. It means your diabetes is well controlled. Your peak flow is 380 L/min, which is also solid for someone with your history.
PATIENT: Okay, so nothing alarming there. That's one thing, at least. I was worried about the numbness—I didn't want to hear that it was something serious.
PHYSICIAN: The numbness we need to take seriously though. Combined with the poor appetite and the sleep issues, and the fact that it's getting worse—I want to be thorough about that. Now, I know you've got your osteoarthritis as well, which can sometimes make sleep harder with the pain. Has that been worse?
PATIENT: The osteoarthritis is always there, you know? My knees have been creaky, my hips too. But I don't think it's suddenly worse. It's more just... everything at once, I suppose.
PHYSICIAN: Mm-hmm. So thinking about what we can do—one thing that might help is to think about your sodium intake. Next week, it might be worth trying to cut back on salt and see if that helps with how you're feeling generally.
PATIENT: Cut back on salt? I mean, I don't think I eat a ton of it, but I suppose I could try. How would that help with the sleep?
PHYSICIAN: It's less about sleep directly and more about overall fluid balance and blood pressure. You've got the atrial fibrillation to manage, and salt can affect that. But let's not make it a big project—just something to keep in mind next week.
PATIENT: Alright, I can do that. Speaking of which, did you want to refer me to nephrology or should I wait on that? I'm thinking about costs again, honestly—every specialist adds up.
PHYSICIAN: That's a fair concern. We might want to refer to nephrology next week, but let's float that for now and see where we stand. It's not urgent.
PATIENT: Okay. And what about the numbness? Do we need more testing for that?
PHYSICIAN: Yes, potentially. We could order follow-up bloodwork in 4 weeks to look into that further, just to see if there's an underlying cause. We can talk about it and see if that feels like the right move for you.
PATIENT: Four weeks? I was hoping to get something sooner, given that it's getting worse. But I guess bloodwork takes time. And yeah, like I said, gotta watch the costs of all this.
PHYSICIAN: I hear you. We can move on that if needed. For now, try to be consistent with the duloxetine at 60 mg once daily, and we'll get you a refill. Make sure you're taking the dapagliflozin, 10 mg once daily as well. And let's touch base in about a week or so.
PATIENT: Right. And I'll think about that salt thing. Do I need to do anything else right now?
PHYSICIAN: Just monitor how you're doing. If the numbness gets significantly worse or you start having other symptoms, don't wait—call the office. Otherwise, we'll check in soon.

spans.label: date
spans.text: in about a week or so

text:
NURSE: —and so we're going to keep the rivaroxaban at the same dose, yeah? You've been taking that exactly as prescribed, no issues?
PATIENT: Yeah, every single day. Haven't missed once. It's the one thing I actually remember to do without setting an alarm.
NURSE: Good. The deep vein thrombosis is still something we're monitoring closely with that medication, so consistency is really key. Now, how's the nausea been since you got home?
PATIENT: Oh, it's been pretty rough, honestly. Severe nausea, especially in the mornings. I can barely get through coffee without feeling like I'm going to...
NURSE: Okay. And you think that's connected to the gastroesophageal reflux disease, or is this something new?
PATIENT: I mean, it could be the reflux acting up again. But it feels different this time. More persistent, you know? I'm wondering if it's the medications.
NURSE: That's a really good observation. Let me ask you about the metoprolol tartrate—have you been taking that at the 100 mg twice daily like we prescribed?
PATIENT: Actually, no. I haven't been taking it. The side effects were just... they were making everything worse. I was getting these headaches and I felt like my heart was doing weird things, so I just stopped taking it about a week ago.
NURSE: How are you feeling since you stopped?
PATIENT: Better, actually. The headaches went away. But the nausea is still hanging around, unfortunately.
NURSE: Okay, so we do need to address the metoprolol—we can reduce that dose instead of having you off it entirely, because we need that cardiac support. We'll bring it down and see if that helps with the side effects. Does that make sense?
PATIENT: Yeah, that makes sense. Lower dose, hopefully fewer problems.
NURSE: Exactly. Now, on the aspirin—you're still doing 325 mg once daily, correct?
PATIENT: Yes, every morning with breakfast.
NURSE: We're actually going to increase that. You mentioned some side effects with it before?
PATIENT: I mean, it's been giving me a little stomach irritation, but honestly at this point I'm kind of used to it. Why the increase?
NURSE: Because of the deep vein thrombosis, we need better anticoagulation support overall. We're bumping it to a higher dose, but we'll pair it with something to protect your stomach. You'll need to take it exactly as prescribed with the new regimen.
PATIENT: Okay. So I'll still be taking it once daily, just... more of it?
NURSE: Right. We'll have the pharmacy send you the new bottle with clear instructions. You haven't missed any doses of the current aspirin, have you?
PATIENT: Not one. I take it like clockwork, even on the days I feel terrible.
NURSE: That's good. Now, I want to circle back to the other symptoms. You mentioned the incision pain over the weekend—how's that doing now?
PATIENT: Oh, the mild incision pain? Yeah, it's getting better. It was worse right at the start of the weekend, but it's... it's tapering off now.
NURSE: And the fatigue? You said that started, um—
PATIENT: Since Monday, yeah. I've had severe fatigue since Monday. But honestly, that's also improving. Some days I can actually stay up past four in the afternoon now, which is basically winning the lottery.
NURSE: I hear you. So both the pain and the fatigue are trending better, but the nausea's the main thing that's not cooperating yet?
PATIENT: Exactly. The nausea is the... the thing that's really getting in my way, if that makes sense.
NURSE: It does. Has anyone in your family had any GI issues like this, or—and I know this might seem like a random question—but has anyone had earlier memory or cognitive issues? I'm asking because sometimes there are patterns.
PATIENT: Well, my younger brother was diagnosed with Alzheimer disease a couple years ago, so I guess that's something to keep in mind down the line for me. But as far as GI stuff, not really that I know of.
NURSE: Okay, we'll keep an eye on things. Now, one more thing—how's your alcohol consumption been? Any changes since discharge?
PATIENT: I've been having a glass of wine or two most nights, if I'm honest. Helps me unwind after all this.
NURSE: I think we need to reduce alcohol, especially given the medications you're on and the reflux you're dealing with. Would you be open to cutting back?
PATIENT: I can try. It's not going to make me happy, but I get why it matters.
NURSE: We'll make this a focus at your next visit, and I'm going to order follow-up bloodwork to make sure everything's stable with your counts and your anticoagulation levels. Sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds fine. When will you get those results back?

PATIENT: Well, here I am again. Can't seem to stay away from this place.
NURSE: I see you're back for your post-discharge check-in. How are things going at home?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, some good days and some not so good. I've been having trouble sleeping, actually. Mild difficulty sleeping since Monday, but it's been getting a bit better, I think.
NURSE: That's helpful to know. Since Monday — so about a week now? And you said it's improving?
PATIENT: Yeah, it's not as bad as it was right after I came home. But there's something else bothering me more, if I'm being honest. The nausea. I've had moderate nausea since my last visit, and it's actually getting worse, not better.
NURSE: I'm sorry to hear that. Moderate nausea since your last visit and it's worsening — that's definitely something we need to address. Have you noticed anything that makes it worse or better? Certain times of day?
PATIENT: Mostly in the morning, and sometimes in the afternoon. I've been trying to eat smaller meals but it doesn't seem to help much.
NURSE: Okay. And have you experienced any shortness of breath?
PATIENT: Hmm... let me think. No, I don't think so. No shortness of breath.
NURSE: Good. Now, I do want to ask — this morning when you woke up, did you feel okay?
PATIENT: Actually, now that you mention it, I had mild dizziness this morning. Just a little lightheaded when I stood up too fast. And honestly, it's been getting worse as the day's gone on.
NURSE: The dizziness started this morning and it's worsening throughout the day. That's important. Let me pull up your medication list here. I want to go through what you're taking and make sure everything's still working for you.
PATIENT: Sure, go ahead.
NURSE: I see you have the warfarin on your list. That's for your deep vein thrombosis, which is long-standing. Are you taking that as prescribed?
PATIENT: Well, actually, I'm not taking it. I stopped taking the warfarin a few days ago. It was giving me side effects — just made me feel terrible, and I couldn't take it anymore.
NURSE: Which dose were you on?
PATIENT: The 5 mg once daily.
NURSE: Okay. So you've been off the warfarin due to side effects. That's important. Because we'll need to adjust the warfarin dose — maybe lower it or look at your symptoms more carefully. That's definitely part of our plan today. Now, what about the naproxen? I have you down for 500 mg twice daily.
PATIENT: Oh, that one I'm taking as prescribed. I haven't missed a single dose. Every single day, twice a day like clockwork.
NURSE: Good to hear. And the tramadol — 50 mg as needed for pain?
PATIENT: Yeah, I take that when I need it. Though honestly, I've missed a few doses here and there. Sometimes I forget to take it, and then I'm not sure if I should catch up or just skip it.
NURSE: That's okay. We can work with that. I'll arrange a refill for the tramadol and we'll get you back on track. By the way, how's your son doing? I remember you mentioning he was helping you get settled.
PATIENT: Oh, he's doing well. He comes by on Saturdays to check on me and bring groceries. Really helps with the heavy stuff. And my neighbor — actually my next-door neighbor has been dealing with sciatica, poor thing. Been quite painful for her.
NURSE: That's nice that your son helps out. Sorry to hear about your neighbor's sciatica, though. Now, I think we should order follow-up bloodwork to monitor how you're doing, especially with the warfarin situation. Does that sound reasonable?
PATIENT: Yes, that makes sense to me. I want to make sure everything's okay.
NURSE: Perfect. So we're going to order follow-up bloodwork. And as I mentioned, we need to adjust warfarin dose. I'm going to start you on a lower dose, and we'll see how you respond. Once we get your nausea and dizziness under control, we may be able to dial that back. You comfortable with that plan?
PATIENT: Yes, I feel better having a plan. Lower is probably better anyway, given how I was feeling.
NURSE: One more thing — I want you to monitor blood pressure at home. Our care coordinator will set that up with you at your next visit. In the meantime, write down any readings you take so we can look at them together. Make sense?
PATIENT: That makes sense. I have a blood pressure cuff at home, so I can do that.
NURSE: Excellent. Let's get you scheduled for a follow-up in about two weeks so we can see how the adjusted warfarin dose and the other changes are working. Does that timeline work for you?
PATIENT: Two weeks is fine. I'll write it down before I leave.

CARE_COORDINATOR: —so the weight's been an issue, and I know we talked about adjusting your semaglutide, but before we get there, George, your daughter wanted to know about the Monday thing. When you say the weight loss started Monday, are we still seeing it drop, or has it kind of plateaued?
PATIENT: It's about the same now. Moderate weight loss, I'd say. Not getting worse, not getting better. Been about a week.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: Dad, you told me you were scared it might be something serious. That's why I came today.
PATIENT: Well, yes, but the doctor'll sort it. More bothering me is I'm in the bathroom every twenty minutes. Frequent urination—it's driving me up the wall.
CARE_COORDINATOR: How long has that been happening?
PATIENT: Oh, couple weeks at least. And my increased thirst, my God. Severe, it is. I started about a month ago and it's getting worse.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Drinking a lot of water?
PATIENT: Can't keep up with it. I'm—what's the word—I'm like a sieve, nothing stays in me.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He's been refilling his water bottle constantly. I've never seen him like this.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Any swelling in your legs? Puffiness around your ankles?
PATIENT: No leg swelling, thank God. That's one thing I don't have to worry about, at least.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. Let me pull up your meds. You're on pravastatin 20 mg at bedtime for your cholesterol—that's your hyperlipidemia management. And we've been meaning to adjust that because of side effects you mentioned. We're going to go up the dose, so we need you to keep taking it exactly as prescribed. Haven't missed a day, right?
PATIENT: Every single day, before bed. I haven't missed it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. Now the semaglutide—you're supposed to be on 1 mg once weekly, but I'm hearing you've skipped some doses?
PATIENT: Yeah, I've missed a few. The injections were making me feel sick to my stomach, so I just... forgot to do it some weeks. But if it's helping, I'll try again.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We're actually bringing that down because of those side effects, so that should help. And the simvastatin, 20 mg at bedtime—how are you managing with that one?
PATIENT: Um, honestly I'm not sure how I'm taking it. I couldn't say if I've been doing it right or not.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We're going to keep that exactly as it is, so just maintain the 20 mg at bedtime. Let's talk about your atrial fibrillation. Any palpitations, dizzy spells?
PATIENT: Nothing really. Well, maybe a fainting episode a few weeks back, but it passed.
CARE_COORDINATOR: A fainting episode. When you say a few weeks—was it before or after the thirst started?
PATIENT: Around the same time, I think. I don't keep good track anymore.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's something we should get looked at more closely. You might want to swing through the emergency department and get checked out, just to be thorough with that.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: Is he okay? Should I be worried?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's routine, just want to make sure we're not missing anything. Now, I want to order follow-up bloodwork in 3 months, and I'm also going to refer to endocrinology in 3 months so they can look at what's driving the thirst and the urination. That's all something they'll want to investigate.
PATIENT: Endocrinology—that's the gland doctor?
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's right. They'll look at your glucose, your metabolism, figure out what's going on. You okay with all that?
PATIENT: Yeah, fine. I trust you lot.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: So we'll get the bloodwork and see the endocrinologist. Should I be watching for anything in the meantime?
CARE_COORDINATOR: If the thirst or the urination gets worse, or if there's another dizzy spell, that's when you'd want to reach out. Otherwise we'll see where the bloodwork takes us.

PATIENT: Yeah, so my main thing is I can't stop drinking water. Like, I'm going through bottles constantly. Started for the past few days, and it's just this mild increased thirst that won't quit. And my feet have been weird — there's this numbness in the feet, and it's been last week, but honestly it feels like it's getting better, so that's good.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, I'm hearing the thirst and the feet. Let me just make sure I have the timeline right. The increased thirst — you said the past few days, and it's mild. And the numbness, that came on last week but you're noticing it's improving?
PATIENT: Right, yeah. The thirst is definitely there every day though. And the feet thing — I mean, it's still there, the numbness in the feet is still pretty severe, don't get me wrong, but it's not as bad as it was when it started. I'm not going crazy.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I've noticed it too, the water thing. He's been refilling his cup all night. I was actually getting concerned because I thought maybe his blood sugar was going off track again.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's a really good observation. Those do go together — excessive thirst and numbness can both point to blood sugar control. I also want to rule out a few other things, including whether there's a transient ischemic attack we need to watch for, though I'm not convinced yet that's what we're dealing with. Have you had any episodes of dizziness, slurred speech, or weakness on one side of your body?
PATIENT: No, no. I mean, I feel a little tired sometimes, but nothing like that. No weakness or weird speech stuff. Just the feet and the thirst.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's reassuring. One more thing — over the weekend, did you notice you needed the bathroom more often than usual?
PATIENT: Oh man, yeah, actually. Over the weekend I was up and down constantly. It's moderate urination, I guess you could say. Not like an emergency every five minutes, but definitely more than normal.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. So we've got increased thirst, numbness in the feet, and moderate frequent urination over the weekend. Let's look at your fasting glucose from this morning — it's 118 mg/dL. That's a bit higher than we'd like.
PATIENT: Great. That's not great.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's not ideal, but it's something we can address. I want to run through your medications with you. First, the dulaglutide — the injection you take. How are you getting on with that?
PATIENT: That one I'm taking — I think the dose is 1.5 mg once weekly. I haven't missed a dose, I get it out of my fridge every Sunday and just do it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, good. Actually, I want to double-check the dose with you. Is it 1.5 mg?
PATIENT: Uh, let me think. I pulled up the bottle earlier today because I had a feeling you'd ask. It's actually 0.75 mg once weekly. Sorry, I had that mixed up. But yeah, as prescribed, every single time.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's perfect, thank you for checking. And we can go ahead and arrange a refill on that for you. Now, the sitagliptin — 100 mg once daily. Are you still taking that one?
PATIENT: No, actually I stopped taking that one. I don't know, it was making me feel a bit off, and I just... I haven't been taking it for a couple of weeks.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, I appreciate you being straight with me. We'll note that as discontinued. And then the linagliptin — 5 mg once daily. How's that going?
PATIENT: I've missed some doses, honestly. It's the one I'm supposed to take every day, but I'll admit I forget sometimes. I'm not great at keeping track of two tablets in the morning, you know?
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He's been better about it since I started putting them in the organizer, but he still skips the odd one when he's running late.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's actually really helpful information. Okay, so with the hypertension you have, combined with the blood sugar readings and your symptoms, I think we need to get you in with endocrinology — that's the specialist for diabetes and metabolism. I want to refer to endocrinology, and we should aim for about 3 months out. How does that sound?
PATIENT: I mean... three months is a while, but I guess if it's not super urgent? I don't love waiting, to be honest, but if that's what you think is best.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I think it's the right move for a comprehensive review. It'll give us time to stabilize things in the meantime and get you the detailed metabolic workup they can do. So yes, we'll refer to endocrinology in 3 months. And I want to schedule a follow-up visit with us in 4 weeks to see how you're doing, check in on those symptoms.
PATIENT: Four weeks, okay. At least that's sooner. And maybe by then my feet won't feel like I'm walking on bubble wrap anymore.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: The nurse can schedule a follow-up visit, right? I can help him get that on the calendar.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Absolutely, yes — the nurse will schedule a follow-up visit in 4 weeks. And we're going to keep an eye on that hypertension as well. Between now and then, if anything changes — if the numbness gets suddenly worse, or you have any neurological symptoms, you reach out. Otherwise, let's touch base in a month.

CARE_COORDINATOR: So I've got here that you're on three different blood pressure medications right now, and your last EKG showed atrial fibrillation. Let me just confirm—you're still having those palpitations?
PATIENT: Yeah, kind of. Not as much, but... yeah.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. And how long has that been going on?
PATIENT: Umm, it comes and goes. I don't know, a few weeks maybe?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Few weeks. Have you also noticed any shortness of breath?
PATIENT: Yeah, moderate shortness of breath, actually. That started a couple weeks ago. It's getting better, though.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good to hear it's improving. Any lightheadedness?
PATIENT: A little, yeah. Mild lightheadedness, but... about a month ago, that is. And it's getting better too.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's good. Any nausea?
PATIENT: No, not like last time when I had that flu. This is definitely not nausea. I feel pretty okay otherwise.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Alright. So let me pull up your vitals from today. Heart rate is 62.
PATIENT: That's... good?
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's good, yeah. And your LDL cholesterol came back at 72 mg/dL, which is where we want it. Now, I want to go through your medications with you. You're on atorvastatin right now?
PATIENT: Yeah, I think so.
CARE_COORDINATOR: You think so? How have you been taking that?
PATIENT: Um, honestly I'm not sure. I mean, I take it most days but I couldn't say exactly how... like, I don't remember if it's the right dose or when I'm supposed to take it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. Well, we're looking to increase your atorvastatin dose because of some side effects you reported last month. You mentioned muscle aches, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, that was rough. But I thought... wait, if I'm going up, won't that make it worse?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Fair question. Actually, sometimes a lower dose of a different formulation can actually help with that. We might do 10 mg once daily instead, but that's something to work through. Maybe adjust atorvastatin dose next week and we'll see how you feel?
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, I can try that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And you're also on nebivolol, which is a beta-blocker for your atrial fibrillation. That's 5 mg once daily, correct?
PATIENT: Yeah, I take it every single day. Haven't missed one.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. We're actually going to be lowering that because of some of the side effects you've been having—fatigue, right? That's partly from the obstructive sleep apnea too, which we should address. We're bringing it down.
PATIENT: Oh. Okay, that makes sense. The tiredness has been... yeah.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And then the losartan, 50 mg once daily. How are you managing with that one?
PATIENT: Um, I'm not taking it right now. I stopped taking it a couple weeks ago because my blood pressure was dropping too low at night.
CARE_COORDINATOR: You stopped taking it. That's important information. We should have discussed that first, but given your numbers today I think stopping it is probably fine. We're going to monitor blood pressure at home to make sure things stay stable, and I want you checking it regularly. Can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. How often?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Let's do it daily for the next 4 weeks, and then we'll reassess. The nurse will go over the specifics with you on your way out. Does that work?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's fine.

PHYSICIAN: So we had you down for 1:45 but the room's open now, so we're good. Let me pull up your chart real quick.
PATIENT: Oh, great. Yeah, I was early anyway.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Okay, so I'm looking at your med list from last time, but I want to walk through it with you because things shift. How's the sacubitril-valsartan been working for you—you're on 97 mg twice daily, right?
PATIENT: Um, yeah, I think so. I mean... I'm not sure, to be honest, exactly how I've been taking it. Every day, definitely, but whether I'm, uh, getting both doses in—couldn't say.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, so 97 mg—let me just confirm that, 97 mg twice daily—so ideally morning and evening. But you're uncertain about the actual pattern. That's actually helpful information. And the sertraline?
PATIENT: The sertraline, that one I know. I take it 50 mg once daily, every single day. Same time, right with my coffee.
PHYSICIAN: That's good consistency. So 50 mg once daily and you haven't missed—that's excellent. But I'm noticing something in the chart, and I want to check in about sleep. How's that been?
PATIENT: Well, that's actually... it's been rough. Really rough. I've got severe difficulty sleeping. For the past few days it's been—I don't know, getting worse actually.
PHYSICIAN: When you say severe, how many hours are we talking? Are you able to get to sleep, or is it more staying asleep?
PATIENT: Both, really. I'm lying there for maybe an hour before anything happens, and then I wake up at like three in the morning and I'm just... done. Can't get back.
PHYSICIAN: So fragmented. And this started for the past few days—did anything coincide with it? Any stressor, any medication changes?
PATIENT: Not that I can think of. Though, actually, now that you mention it, my appetite's in the toilet too. I'm just not hungry.
PHYSICIAN: Poor appetite alongside the sleep disruption. That's... okay, that's a pattern worth tracking. How long on the appetite thing?
PATIENT: Same window. Few days, maybe three or four.
PHYSICIAN: So coincident onset. It's been about a month ago that it started getting worse, and it's just not getting better, you know? I'm up at two, three in the morning just lying there.
PHYSICIAN: Moderate difficulty sleeping — that's been going on steadily since about a month ago, you're saying? Not getting better, not worse?
PATIENT: Yeah, about the same. Same every night, pretty much. And then there's this other thing, which is weird — my feet have been numb. Mild numbness in the feet, started, I dunno, for the past few days now.
PHYSICIAN: Getting worse or better since it started?
PATIENT: Actually, it's getting better. That part I'm less worried about.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, good. Any chest pain or anything like that?
PATIENT: No, no. Like, my chest feels fine.
PHYSICIAN: You're sure? Sometimes people aren't always—
PATIENT: No, I'm sure. No chest pain.
PHYSICIAN: All right. And how's your appetite been?
PATIENT: Poor appetite, honestly. I'm not eating like I used to. I'll sit down and just... I'm not hungry. Part of me wonders if that's the sleep thing, like, if you're not sleeping you just don't want food.
PHYSICIAN: That can definitely play into it. Let me ask about your medications. You're on amitriptyline for sleep — still taking that 50 mg at bedtime?
PATIENT: Yeah, I am, but I'll be honest — I've missed some doses. Especially when I travel, or just some nights I forget, you know? So I haven't been as consistent as I should be.
PHYSICIAN: That's useful to know. We can talk about that. For now, I think we'll keep the amitriptyline at 50 mg at bedtime the same. But let's focus on not skipping doses. And the spironolactone — 25 mg once daily — how's that going?
PATIENT: Uhh, I'm not sure, to be honest. I take it, but I don't remember if I'm always taking it right. Like, sometimes I think I take two at once, sometimes I space them out. I couldn't say for certain.
PHYSICIAN: I'll make a note that we need to clarify that with you. We'll get a refill arranged, and I want you to take it as 25 mg once daily — just once, every day. What about the insulin glargine? You're on 24 units once daily for that.
PATIENT: Yeah, the insulin... I'm not sure I'm still even using that one. I don't remember when I stopped, or if I did, or... I'm sorry, I don't remember.
PHYSICIAN: That's okay. We need to sort that out — whether you're still on it or not. But given the chronic kidney disease stage 3 that you have, we do need to keep a closer eye on a few things. Your weight was what when you came in?
PATIENT: 224 pounds.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. I want to order follow-up bloodwork — get your kidney function, your electrolytes, all of that checked. And I'm going to refer you to nephrology for the chronic kidney disease stage 3, to make sure we're managing it properly given the numbness you're experiencing and everything else. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds good. I just... I hope the insurance will cover it. It gets expensive, you know?
PHYSICIAN: It does, and we'll help navigate that. The care coordinator will set up the nephrology referral for you and they'll verify everything with your insurance before you go. That way there shouldn't be any surprises.
PATIENT: Okay, thank you. So when you said earlier about not skipping the amitriptyline — does that help with the appetite too, or just the sleep?
PHYSICIAN: It's primarily for sleep, but sometimes stabilizing your sleep actually does help your appetite come back. Might not be a direct thing, but it's worth being consistent and seeing. Give it a couple weeks and we'll check back in.
PATIENT: All right. I'll do that.

PATIENT: Here we go again. Back so soon, huh? I feel like I was just here.
NURSE: I know, it's only been a week since your discharge. Let's see how you're doing. What's been bothering you the most?
PATIENT: Honestly, I'm exhausted. Like, really tired all the time.
NURSE: How long has that been going on?
PATIENT: Three days ago it started. It's mild fatigue, I guess—not like I can't get out of bed or anything, but it's just... there.
NURSE: And is it getting any worse, staying about the same?
PATIENT: About the same, really. Nothing's changed on that front.
NURSE: Okay. Anything else?
PATIENT: My stomach's been killing me. Heartburn yesterday and it's just... wow.
NURSE: Severe heartburn?
PATIENT: Yeah, severe. But actually it is getting better, bit by bit. At least there's that.
NURSE: Good sign. And this started yesterday?
PATIENT: Yesterday, yeah.
NURSE: Let me get your blood pressure real quick.
PATIENT: Sure, go ahead.
NURSE: Okay... looks like 124/78 mmHg. That's good. And what's your weight been running?
PATIENT: 152 pounds. I've been pretty consistent there.
NURSE: Good. Let me pull up your medication list here. *types* So we need to talk about the omeprazole. How are you taking that?
PATIENT: Um, honestly I've missed a few doses here and there. I skipped it a couple times because I wasn't sure if it was helping or if it was making me feel weird.
NURSE: Side effects, you mean?
PATIENT: Yeah, something like that. I don't know, just felt off.
NURSE: Well, we're going to go ahead and increase it to 20 mg once daily. See if that helps better with the heartburn and gets you more consistent relief. We think the dose adjustment might actually help with those side effects too.
PATIENT: Okay, whatever you think is best.
NURSE: Now, the escitalopram at 5 mg once daily—how have you been with that one?
PATIENT: I mean, not sure, honestly. I don't remember if I've been taking it every day or every other day or what. I couldn't say for certain.
NURSE: Are you having any side effects from it?
PATIENT: Yeah, I get this weird feeling in my chest sometimes, and some dizziness. It's been frustrating.
NURSE: Given those side effects, we're actually going to bring that dose down. That should help. The chlorthalidone at 12.5 mg once daily, how are you with that?
PATIENT: That one I'm taking as prescribed. Every single day, haven't missed any doses.
NURSE: Good. We're going to keep that one exactly where it is. Now, I want to ask about your family history. Your grandfather, he had atrial fibrillation, is that right?
PATIENT: Yeah, he did. Had it for years before he passed away. My dad actually joked he inherited it from him but so far so good for me. Though my dad's been a pain about reminding me to exercise more because of it.
NURSE: That's something we want to keep an eye on, especially with you. Have you had any other symptoms—any chest discomfort, palpitations, shortness of breath?
PATIENT: No, nothing like that.
NURSE: Okay. One more thing—you mentioned you've had a headache too, is that right? I'm looking at the notes from your discharge.
PATIENT: Oh yeah, that. A moderate headache, on and off. Started a couple weeks ago.
NURSE: Is it getting better or worse?
PATIENT: It's getting worse, actually. I've just been dealing with it, figured it would go away on its own.
NURSE: We should look into that. Given your gout and your osteoarthritis, we want to make sure nothing's overlapping here. So here's what we're thinking for the plan. First, we need to reduce alcohol. I know, I know, but especially with the gout and your stomach issues, it's really important. Can you commit to that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can try. I'm not a big drinker anyway, so it shouldn't be too hard.
NURSE: Great. And we need to order follow-up bloodwork at your next visit. That'll help us see how you're responding to the medication changes and get a better picture overall.
PATIENT: Fine with me.
NURSE: And because of your family history with your grandfather's atrial fibrillation, we want to refer you to cardiology. We'll get that set up for you in 3 months, okay?
PATIENT: Sure, that makes sense.
NURSE: We'll have the care coordinator handle the reduction of alcohol reminder and the bloodwork order for your next visit. In the meantime, take your omeprazole at 20 mg once daily, make sure you're consistent with it, and take the escitalopram at the lower dose as we discussed.
PATIENT: Got it. When should I come back?
NURSE: We'll schedule that before you leave today. Two weeks if you can make it, but no more than a month.

NURSE: —so we've got the discharge note here, but I want to circle back on what's been happening since you came home.
PATIENT: Yeah, well. Things aren't great, honestly. The nausea started three days ago and it's just getting worse. I can barely keep food down at this point.
NURSE: Severe nausea for three days. Any idea what might've triggered it, or did it just come on?
PATIENT: No idea. It was fine one day and then—bam. Just hit me. Given my heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, I'm wondering if it's related to that, or maybe the medications...
NURSE: That's a valid concern. Let's go through your medications and make sure you're taking them as intended. You're on torsemide, 40 mg once daily—how's that been going?
PATIENT: Um, I'm not sure, to be honest. I think I've been taking it, but I couldn't say if I've missed any doses or mixed things up. The bottles all kind of blur together.
NURSE: That's common. We'll work on organizing that. You're also on naproxen, 250 mg twice daily. How's that one?
PATIENT: I don't remember. I mean, was I supposed to be taking that at home? I genuinely don't recall picking it up or... I'm not being very helpful here, am I?
NURSE: You're being helpful. For now, we're going to hold the naproxen. Given the nausea, NSAIDs might be making things worse anyway. What about your warfarin, 2.5 mg once daily?
PATIENT: That one I know I'm doing. I haven't missed a single day. Taking it exactly as prescribed. I'm very careful with that one because of the blood thinning and everything.
NURSE: Good to hear. Actually, we need to adjust that dose down based on your last lab results. Your INR came back a bit high, so we're lowering you on the warfarin.
PATIENT: Down? Okay. So less of it. Am I at risk or...? I don't want to have a stroke or anything.
NURSE: No, you're in a safe range. We just want to fine-tune it. I'm going to write you a new prescription. Now, let's talk about the incision pain you mentioned in the discharge checklist.
PATIENT: Yeah, so that started yesterday. Moderate, I'd say. Tender to the touch. It's not getting better but it's not worse either—just kind of sitting there, if you know what I mean.
NURSE: Have you noticed any redness, warmth, or discharge around the incision?
PATIENT: A little bit red maybe. Nothing that looks actively infected or anything. It's just sore. Reminds me why I hate being cut open—which, knock on wood, will be my last time, right?
NURSE: We'll keep monitoring it. Let me get your vitals—heart rate is 92, which is reasonable for you. Blood pressure is 138 over 88. So here's what I'm thinking about going forward. With your type 2 diabetes mellitus and the nausea, it might help to reduce alcohol. Are you drinking?
PATIENT: A little wine in the evening sometimes. I wouldn't call it heavy.
NURSE: Even moderate amounts can worsen nausea and mess with your blood sugar. In the next four weeks, I'd like to see you cut back or eliminate it if you can. Can you do that?
PATIENT: I can try. I suppose... yes, I can manage that. What else?
NURSE: One more thing—would you be open to monitoring blood pressure at home over the next four weeks? We could get you a cuff and a log, just to track trends.
PATIENT: I could do that, yeah. Maybe. I'd have to see if I have the space for another device, but... we'll see.
NURSE: Fair enough. And given the nausea that's not quite settling, someone mentioned possibly referring you to pulmonology next week to rule out anything respiratory contributing to this. Would you want to pursue that?
PATIENT: I... I'm not sure about that. Is it necessary? I mean, I guess if you think it would help, but... I'd rather not add more appointments right now if I don't have to.
NURSE: Understandable. Let's revisit it if the nausea doesn't settle in the next few days. For now, focus on the medication adjustments, reduce alcohol, and we'll check in with you in two weeks. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah. Sounds reasonable. Hope this clears up soon.
