text:
NURSE: Okay, so I'm looking at your chart here and it says you were in last month for a respiratory followup. And your oxygen saturation was 91 at that visit. How are things going with your breathing?
PATIENT: Well, honestly, I've been pretty okay, but then this morning I woke up with this severe cough and it came on just like that. This morning, just out of nowhere, and it's been awful, but I have to say it's getting better already, which is good.
NURSE: Okay, so the severe cough started this morning. And it's improving? That's a good sign. Any other symptoms going on in your chest or lungs?
PATIENT: Well, yes, there's that and also... I mean, I noticed some wheezing too, which I don't usually get. Or maybe I do and I just don't pay attention, I don't know. But yeah, there's definitely wheezing.
NURSE: Wheezing, got it. And then separately, how long have you had chest tightness?
PATIENT: Oh, the chest tightness, that's been going on for a bit. I'd say last week is when it really started to bother me. And it's pretty severe, honestly. It's the same as it was yesterday, kind of just... it's not getting better but it's not getting worse either, just staying the same.
NURSE: So severe chest tightness for about a week now, and it's remaining stable. I do want to ask—have you had any palpitations at all? Any flutter or racing feeling in your heart?
PATIENT: No, no, I don't think so. I mean, nothing that I've noticed.
NURSE: You're not completely sure? Let me ask again just to be clear—any palpitations?
PATIENT: Oh no, definitely not. No palpitations at all. I would know if my heart was doing something weird like that.
NURSE: Good. And fever? Any fever at all?
PATIENT: No fever, thank goodness. I'm glad it hasn't happened because I really don't need that on top of everything else right now.
NURSE: Alright. Let me go through your medications with you real quick. You're on azithromycin—that's the antibiotic—and we've been running that at 250 mg once daily. Are you taking that as prescribed?
PATIENT: Yes, I haven't missed a day. Every single day, 250 mg once daily like clockwork.
NURSE: Perfect. So actually, we're going to adjust azithromycin dose. The doctor wants to go up on that for better blood pressure control. I'll make sure that gets communicated to you before you leave.
PATIENT: Oh okay, so it's going up then. That's fine, I can do that.
NURSE: Great. Now, the dulaglutide—that's your injection you do once weekly at 1.5 mg—how have you been doing with that one?
PATIENT: Mm, well, I've been trying, but honestly I've missed a couple of doses here and there. I get busy and I forget, or maybe I skipped one because I wasn't feeling great. It's been a little hit-or-miss, I'll admit.
NURSE: I appreciate you being honest about that. Based on your recent lab results, we're actually going to bring that dose down anyway, so that'll be 1.5 mg still but we're adjusting the plan. That should help.
PATIENT: Oh, okay, so it's coming down. That might actually be easier for me to keep track of.
NURSE: We'll see. And then sitagliptin—you take 25 mg once daily of that for your blood sugar. How's that going for you?
PATIENT: Uh, honestly, I'm not sure. Like, I think I'm taking it, but I couldn't say for certain if it's every day or if I've been skipping it. I'm sorry, I don't remember exactly.
NURSE: No worries, we'll keep it exactly as-is for now and see how you do. What I do want to circle back to—your mom, she's got chronic kidney disease stage 3, right? Is that something she's dealing with?
PATIENT: Yeah, my mom was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease stage 3 a couple years ago. She's on medication for it and does blood work all the time, but she's doing okay with it, you know? It's managed.
NURSE: Okay, good to know. And just checking—nothing like that in your own kidney function as far as you know?
PATIENT: No, not that they've told me. My kidney numbers have been normal the last few times they checked.
NURSE: Alright. So I'm looking at everything—the cough onset this morning, the wheezing, the chest tightness, and your oxygen saturation being 91—I do want to rule out anemia, we'll get some labs on that. But more importantly, I think we need to refer to pulmonology just to make sure we're not missing anything with your lungs. Does that sound reasonable to you?
PATIENT: Yeah, I think that makes sense. I mean, this cough came out of nowhere and the tightness... yeah, I want to get it checked out properly.
NURSE: Good. So we'll adjust azithromycin dose like we talked about, and we're going to refer to pulmonology. I'll get those referrals sent off today. Any other questions before you go?
PATIENT: No, I think I'm good. Oh, wait—my brother-in-law has psoriasis and he's always complaining about it. I was just wondering if that's something that runs in families? I know it's probably not related to all this, just curious.
NURSE: Well, it can run in families, but it sounds like that's his thing to manage. Let's focus on getting your lungs sorted out, yeah?
PATIENT: Yeah, you're right. Thanks for seeing me.

CARE_COORDINATOR: —so the scale this morning showed you down about eight pounds from last time. That's what, a week and a half?
PATIENT: Yeah, I didn't think much of it until my daughter here mentioned it. I mean, over the weekend I just... I wasn't feeling great, you know, tired mostly.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I told Dad when I picked him up on Sunday—I said 'Dad, your pants are hanging different.' And when we weighed him at home, that's when we saw the moderate weight loss was real. So we wanted to get that flagged.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I appreciate you bringing it in. And the weight loss, has it been steady or has it stopped, picked back up—?
PATIENT: No, it's about the same. Hasn't changed really since over the weekend. Same clothes feel loose.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. And have you noticed anything else, Carson? Any changes in how much you're eating, or your energy level?
PATIENT: Well, I'm going to the bathroom more often. Not a ton, but... it's mild, you know, nothing crazy. Started right around Monday.
CARE_COORDINATOR: When you say more often—are we talking daytime, nighttime, both?
PATIENT: Both, but it's actually getting better already. Yesterday and today it's eased off quite a bit.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's good to hear it's trending in the right direction. Any burning or pain when you go?
PATIENT: No, nothing like that. And I have increased thirst—like, severe. It's been that way since my last visit, maybe even before. I wake up in the night just parched.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He's been drinking water constantly. Like, the pitcher's empty by noon most days.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's important information. Let me ask about the swelling in your legs—any puffiness, tightness in the ankles or calves?
PATIENT: No, I don't think so.
CARE_COORDINATOR: You don't think so, or no leg swelling?
PATIENT: No. No leg swelling. I would notice that—I remember when my friend had it, his whole foot would puff up by evening. Mine don't do that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. Now, let's talk about your medications. You're on lisinopril for the blood pressure—are you taking that as prescribed?
PATIENT: Every single day, no exceptions. I don't mess around with that one.
CARE_COORDINATOR: The dose we discussed upping to 40 mg once daily for better blood pressure control, and I want to make sure you got that message.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He called me about the new bottle. I helped him set it in the organizer.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. And the simvastatin—we're bringing that down to 10 mg at bedtime based on your lab results, especially since your LDL cholesterol came back at 72 mg/dL, which is really solid. How's that going?
PATIENT: I haven't missed a dose, all as prescribed. No side effects that I can tell. Though at my age, if I'm taking anything—(laughs)—I figure I'm doing better than not taking it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Fair point. Do you have any other concerns we haven't touched on yet?
PATIENT: The gout has been acting up a bit. My foot, my... the big toe joint. What's that called, when it flares?
CARE_COORDINATOR: When it gets red and swollen? That's the gout doing its thing. We'll keep that on the radar. You're also managing your hyperlipidemia well based on these numbers, so that's—
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: You know, my Uncle Rick—my dad's younger brother—he has chronic kidney disease stage 3, and we've always wondered if genetics had something to do with these things. Do you think that's part of what we should be watching for?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's smart that you're thinking about that. We'll monitor his kidney function closely. As for next steps, adjusting lisinopril dose could be something to revisit in 4 weeks depending on his blood pressure readings—we might go higher or hold, we'll see. And I'm wondering if a refer to cardiology and endocrinology might make sense next week, just to get another set of eyes on these symptoms—weight loss, the thirst, the frequent urination all together.
PATIENT: I mean, if you think that's worth doing. I'm open to it.

PATIENT: So I've been getting this chest pain. It comes and goes, but it's been worrying me. And I can't seem to catch my breath—not all the time, but enough that I notice it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Tell me more about the chest pain. What does it feel like when it happens?
PATIENT: It's kind of a heaviness, you know? Like something's sitting on my chest. And it radiates down my arm sometimes. I've had coronary artery disease for a few years now, so I keep thinking, is this it? Is something worse happening?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's a real concern to have. How long has the chest pain been going on?
PATIENT: A few weeks here and there, but the shortness of breath—that's the part that scares me. I've had severe shortness of breath for the past few days. I mean, it's been getting worse, I think. No wait, actually—it's getting better. I was worried yesterday, but today I can move around a little more without feeling like I'm suffocating.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So you said it was getting worse, but now it's actually getting better over these past few days?
PATIENT: Yeah, sorry, I misspoke. It's definitely getting better. Yesterday was the worst, and today I'm breathing easier.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's actually good to hear. Apart from the chest pain and the shortness of breath, have you noticed anything else going on with your heart?
PATIENT: Well, there's this fluttery feeling sometimes. Palpitations, I guess. Started last week, and honestly, they seem to be getting worse. Some days I barely notice it, other days I'm very aware of it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: How would you describe the intensity of those palpitations?
PATIENT: Moderate, I'd say. Not severe, but noticeable. Enough to make me stop and focus on it for a minute.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I want to talk about the medications you're taking. What's your current routine like?
PATIENT: Okay, so I'm on the nebivolol 10 mg once daily—I haven't missed a day with that one, I take it every single day as prescribed. But the pravastatin 40 mg at bedtime? I stopped taking it a couple months ago. Just felt like I wasn't tolerating it well.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You stopped taking the pravastatin. What was the issue you were having with it?
PATIENT: Muscle aches, joint pain. It was getting to me. Plus I read some things online and got paranoid about side effects. I know I probably should've talked to someone about it first, so, dark humour here—I basically decided to be my own doctor. Didn't work out great.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's understandable, and I'm glad you're being honest about it. We can address the pravastatin—we may not need to restart it or we can try a different approach. What about the hydralazine?
PATIENT: The hydralazine 50 mg three times daily? I haven't been taking that either. It gives me headaches. Like, really bad headaches. And I just... I stopped taking it a while back because I couldn't function with those headaches.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So you're not taking the hydralazine because of the headaches. That's important for us to know. Given your coronary artery disease and these symptoms, I think we need to get you in with cardiology—refer to cardiology so they can take a closer look at what's happening with your heart and make sure we're managing everything appropriately.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. I think I need that. I don't love the idea of more appointments, but I know I can't keep managing this on my own.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's the right call. While we get you set up with them, I want to make sure we get you back on appropriate blood pressure control with the hydralazine. I'll arrange a refill of the hydralazine 50 mg three times daily, and we can work with cardiology on whether we need to adjust the dose or try something different for the headaches. Does that make sense?
PATIENT: Okay, yeah. That sounds fair.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And we should cut back on salt. A lower sodium diet can help with both the blood pressure and the shortness of breath. Are you willing to work on that?
PATIENT: Cut back on salt? I mean... I like salt. But I get it. If it's going to help me not feel like I'm drowning every time I walk up the stairs, then yeah, I'll do it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Last thing—I want to order follow-up bloodwork so we can check your cholesterol, kidney function, and a few other markers. That'll give us baseline numbers before cardiology sees you.
PATIENT: Sure, that makes sense. When do you want that done?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We can do it today or tomorrow. The sooner the better. And regarding the pravastatin—we're going to stop that for now. Let's see what cardiology recommends once they've evaluated you. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, that works. Thank you. I feel like I'm actually going to get some answers now.

PHYSICIAN: Okay, so we've got you down for thirty minutes, and I've pulled your discharge summary from last week. Let's start with the sleep stuff—you mentioned that when you called.
PATIENT: Yeah, so I'm just—I've got difficulty sleeping. It's mild, I mean it's not keeping me up all night, but it started a couple weeks ago and it's actually getting worse now.
PHYSICIAN: A couple weeks ago. And worse as in—taking longer to fall asleep, or waking up in the middle?
PATIENT: Both, honestly. I fall asleep and then I'm up at two or three in the morning. Just can't get back down.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. And you mentioned numbness in the feet—you've got that too?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's—that's been worse. Severe, really. Started about a month ago, and like I said on the phone, it's getting worse.
PHYSICIAN: Both feet, or one more than the other?
PATIENT: Both. Bottom of the feet, like the soles. And the toes are kind of tingly. Makes it hard to walk sometimes.
PHYSICIAN: That's a concern with your type 2 diabetes mellitus. Your A1C from the lab is 8.6, which tells me the blood sugar's been running higher than we'd like. Your peak flow measurement also came back at 260 L/min, which is something we should monitor given your respiratory status.
PATIENT: Right. So the numbness—that's from the diabetes?
PHYSICIAN: It's compatible with that. We call it diabetic peripheral neuropathy. The high sugars damage the nerves in your feet. But before we go further, anything else that's been off?
PATIENT: Um, poor appetite, I'd say. Moderate, I'd say. That came on for the past few days. Otherwise I'm eating okay, it's just—I don't want much.
PHYSICIAN: Started when, you said?
PATIENT: Past few days. It's about the same, hasn't really gotten worse.
PHYSICIAN: Alright. Let me check on your meds. You're on sertraline now, new one—how's that been?
PATIENT: I've got the bottle, but honestly I'm not sure how I've been taking it. I think once a day, but I couldn't say for certain if I've been remembering it every morning.
PHYSICIAN: That's the sertraline 25 mg, once daily. And spironolactone—you're staying on that for your heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
PATIENT: Yeah, I've got the refill. Though I'll be honest, I've missed some doses. Life gets hectic.
PHYSICIAN: I understand. We need you to take that more consistently though—it's important for your heart. Now, the empagliflozin, 25 mg once daily. Where are we with that one?
PATIENT: I'm not taking that one right now. I stopped taking it a few weeks back because I wasn't sure if it was helping, and honestly the pills are a lot to keep track of.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, we're not making any changes to the empagliflozin for now—we'll just review it. But we do need to circle back on that. Speaking of which, my dog ate my lunch the other day, so I get the overwhelm.
PATIENT: Ha—yeah, well, this is probably less forgivable than a dog.
PHYSICIAN: So here's what I want to do. We're going to get you started on that sertraline—25 mg once daily—for mood and sleep. For the numbness and the blood sugar control, we need to see a specialist. I'm going to refer to nephrology—in 3 months—because I want someone to look at your kidney function given the diabetes and the heart failure. And at home, I need you to monitor blood pressure at home, and we'll check those numbers at your next visit.
PATIENT: Monitor blood pressure—like every day?
PHYSICIAN: Every day if you can. Or at least three times a week. You have a cuff at home?
PATIENT: I do, actually. Okay, I can do that.
PHYSICIAN: Good. So to recap: sertraline 25 mg once daily, you're starting that now—write it on a sticky note if that helps. Spironolactone 50 mg once daily, we're refilling that, and you've got to try harder not to skip doses. And the empagliflozin 25 mg once daily stays the same for now, but I need you back on it. We can talk through the side effects if that's what's making you hesitant.
PATIENT: Okay. And I'll monitor blood pressure at home. Got it.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. And the refer to nephrology in 3 months—I'll have the office call you once that appointment's scheduled. Any questions?
PATIENT: No, I think that covers it. Oh—my neighbor next door, he just had kidney stones, and he was in agony. So I'm glad we're doing this proactively.
PHYSICIAN: Yeah, kidney stones are brutal. We're not at that point with you, but good to stay on top of it. See you in a month.

text:
NURSE: Sorry I'm running about ten minutes behind—got stuck with the prior patient. Let's jump in. So you're coming in today with fatigue, is that right?
PATIENT: Yeah, and also heartburn. Like, really annoying heartburn. It started three days ago and it's just gotten worse every day.
NURSE: Moderate heartburn, okay. And how long have you had the fatigue?
PATIENT: Um, I'd say it's mild fatigue, but it's been going on for a few weeks now. And then I also noticed—oh, this is random—but I had a headache yesterday. It's mild, just a mild headache, and it's kind of still there but it's not getting worse or anything.
NURSE: Okay, so mild fatigue, the moderate heartburn that started three days ago, and a mild headache since yesterday. Do you have any shortness of breath?
PATIENT: No. Definitely not.
NURSE: Good. Let me check on your medications. You're on colchicine, 0.6 mg once daily—how's that going?
PATIENT: I've been taking it exactly as prescribed, every single day. Why, is something happening with that one?
NURSE: Actually, we're going to increase it. The plan is to bump up the dose for better blood pressure control. You should get the new prescription after we're done here. And then allopurinol—you're at 300 mg once daily. How are you managing that one?
PATIENT: Um, honestly, I've missed a few doses. Like, I forget sometimes. I know I'm supposed to take it every day but... yeah, it's happened a couple times.
NURSE: That's actually something we need to address. Your recent labs came back and we're going to bring that dose down. Hopefully the lower amount will be easier to remember. And the chlorthalidone, 12.5 mg once daily—are you taking that?
PATIENT: No, I'm not taking it. I stopped taking that one a while back.
NURSE: Okay. I'm going to keep it at the same dose for now, but we need to talk about why you stopped. That's important for your blood pressure.
PATIENT: I just... I don't know, I felt like I didn't need it or something. My blood pressure has been fine when I check it at home.
NURSE: Right, we'll circle back to that. But first, let me dig into the heartburn a bit more since that's acute. You mentioned it's moderate and it's been getting worse since three days ago. Did anything change in your diet, or are you under more stress?
PATIENT: Well, I was at this bowling tournament last weekend with my work league, and I was eating a lot of fried food, drinking beer, just... you know. And then on Monday morning I woke up with the heartburn and I've just had it ever since.
NURSE: That tracks. So going back to your fatigue and the headache—have you noticed any other patterns? Any night sweats, sleep issues?
PATIENT: I mean, I wake up a lot at night. And sometimes when I wake up I feel really groggy. My roommate actually says I snore sometimes, which... I don't know, I never really thought about it before.
NURSE: Hmm. That's something I want to rule out—we might be looking at obstructive sleep apnea. We're not there yet, I'm not convinced yet, but those are the kinds of things that would make sense with your fatigue and your headaches too. I'm going to order a sleep study for you.
PATIENT: Wait, so you think I have like, sleep apnea? That sounds serious.
NURSE: I want to rule it out. It's just one piece of the puzzle. But the fatigue, the waking up groggy, the snoring—those are clues. We'll get more information from the study. In the meantime, let's focus on what we know is going on—the gastroesophageal reflux disease. You should avoid trigger foods and we might start you on something to help.
PATIENT: Okay, so the heartburn thing is... gastroesophageal reflux disease. Got it.
NURSE: Right. And actually, I should mention—my friend Marcus on my bowling team, he just got diagnosed with gallstones. Had to have an ultrasound done. But that's not you, I'm just saying because you mentioned the tournament.
PATIENT: Oh man, is he okay?
NURSE: He'll be fine. But anyway, back to your plan here. We're going to order follow-up bloodwork in 4 weeks to check how your labs are trending with the allopurinol adjustment.
PATIENT: Okay, so more blood draws. Fun. Anything else?
NURSE: One more thing—you mentioned you were drinking beer at the tournament. I'd like you to reduce alcohol over the next 3 months. That'll help with the reflux, and it's better for your blood pressure too.
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. I mean, I don't drink that much anyway—it was just the tournament weekend.
NURSE: Great. So to recap: colchicine dose is going up, allopurinol dose is coming down, we're keeping chlorthalidone at 12.5 mg even though you haven't been taking it, you need to start taking it again, and we're reducing alcohol and ordering follow-up bloodwork in 4 weeks. Does that sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds good. And the sleep study?
NURSE: I'll have the office call you with an appointment. Any other questions before we wrap?
PATIENT: No, I think I've got it. Thank you.

PHYSICIAN: The traffic out there is just—anyway, come on in. How'd you manage in the waiting room?
PATIENT: Oh, it wasn't too bad. A little warm, but I brought my book. You know, the one about the gardens? My daughter gave it to me for Christmas, and I've been meaning to finish it because there's this whole section on roses and I kept getting distracted—but anyway, yes, it was fine. Not too crowded today, at least.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Well, we wanted to check in with you about four weeks post-discharge now. Let me start with the basics—are you still having that dizziness?
PATIENT: Some, yes. It started about a couple weeks ago, actually—or maybe closer to three weeks now, I lose track. It's been severe at times, especially when I stand up too fast. But I will say it's getting better. Some mornings I wake up and I barely feel it.
PHYSICIAN: That's good to hear it's improving. And the incision—how's that wound feeling?
PATIENT: The incision pain, yes. I'd say it's moderate. It's been going on about a month ago when I first came home, and it just... lingers. Some days I barely notice it, other days if I move wrong it catches me.
PHYSICIAN: Is it draining at all, any warmth around it, any redness?
PATIENT: No, no. It's just sore. I'm keeping it clean like you said. Though I have had cellulitis before, years ago on my leg, and I know what that looked like—nothing like that now, thank goodness.
PHYSICIAN: Good, we want to keep an eye on that given your history. Any nausea at all?
PATIENT: A bit here and there, but nothing bad. Maybe once a day, and it passes pretty quick.
PHYSICIAN: All right. Let's talk medications. You're on aspirin—325 mg once daily. How are you doing with that?
PATIENT: I haven't missed a day. Every single day, just like you told me. I keep it right by my coffee maker so I see it first thing.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. We'll go ahead and arrange a refill on that for you. And the apixaban, the 5 mg twice daily—how's that been?
PATIENT: Um... not sure, honestly. I mean, I think I'm taking it? I don't remember exactly. My pill organizer is a little... well, I couldn't say for certain whether I've been consistent with that one.
PHYSICIAN: That's okay. We'll keep you on the same dose—5 mg twice daily—and we can help you set up a better system for keeping track. Sometimes it helps to tie it to meals or use a phone reminder.
PATIENT: That might be good. I'm not always the best with remembering things twice a day.
PHYSICIAN: Let me check your fasting glucose real quick—you came in fasting today, right?
PATIENT: Yes, nothing since last night.
PHYSICIAN: Your fasting glucose is 124 mg/dL. That's reasonable. Your hyperlipidemia is something we want to keep managing well, especially with your history—you know, my understanding is your grandmother on my mother's side had a stroke, didn't she? Or no, sorry—
PATIENT: Oh, my grandmother—yes. On my mother's side. That was... well, that was years ago now, and she recovered some, but it left her with a lot of limitations. Scared us all half to death at the time.
PHYSICIAN: Right, so family history matters. We want to keep your cholesterol and blood pressure well-controlled to reduce your own risk. I'd like us to monitor blood pressure at home. That something you can do?
PATIENT: I can do that, yes. My daughter has a cuff I can use.
PHYSICIAN: Great. The nurse will walk you through how to do it properly. Let's plan to check in on that in 4 weeks. We'll also need to adjust aspirin dose—the nurse will go over the details when she comes in, but that's something we'll plan to revisit in 4 weeks as well.
PATIENT: Okay. That sounds... I feel better having a plan.
PHYSICIAN: Good. You're doing well. Keep an eye on that dizziness, and don't hesitate to call if the incision pain gets worse or if you notice anything unusual.
PATIENT: I will. Thank you.

NURSE: So you came in today for a post discharge check-in, right? After the procedure?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's right.
NURSE: And we're just following up on how you've been managing at home. Let's start with what's been bothering you the most.
PATIENT: I've been pretty nauseous. Like, moderate nausea. Started this morning, actually.
NURSE: This morning — okay. Is it getting better or worse as the day goes on?
PATIENT: It's getting better, I think. Not as bad as it was when I woke up.
NURSE: That's good to hear. What else?
PATIENT: I'm experiencing fatigue. Like, really tired.
NURSE: How long has that been going on?
PATIENT: Three days ago. Just mild, but it's been there the whole time. Though it's getting better too.
NURSE: And with your heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, we want to make sure we're catching everything. Have you noticed any leg swelling at all?
PATIENT: No, thank God. Nothing like that.
NURSE: How's the pain at your incision site?
PATIENT: That's actually the worst part. Severe incision pain, started yesterday. And it's getting worse, not better.
NURSE: Okay, we'll need to keep an eye on that. Let me ask about your medications. You're on tramadol as needed — have you been taking it?
PATIENT: I missed a couple of doses. I keep forgetting to take it when I should.
NURSE: That's understandable, but 50 mg as needed — try to grab it when the pain picks up. And your warfarin — do you know how you've been taking that?
PATIENT: Um, I... I'm not sure, honestly. I think I've been taking it but I couldn't say exactly when or if I missed
NURSE: It's been 5 mg once daily — that's what you should be on. But we're thinking about bumping it up. Partly for your blood pressure control.
PATIENT: Bumping it up? What does that mean, like more of the medication?
NURSE: Right, a higher dose. Your blood isn't thinning as much as we'd like it to be with the heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that you have going on.
PATIENT: Okay, I guess that makes sense.
NURSE: And your metoprolol succinate — the 25 mg once daily — we're actually going down on that based on your lab results. But I know you've been taking it exactly as prescribed, haven't you?
PATIENT: Yeah, every single day. I haven't missed a single dose of that one.
NURSE: Good. Now, with your migraine history and everything else going on, we might want to adjust warfarin dose next week and have cardiology take a look at how you're responding. Would that be something you'd want to consider?
PATIENT: I... I guess? What would that involve?
NURSE: Just some tweaks to get you on a better level. And we could order follow-up bloodwork next week to make sure everything's tracking right. Something to think about.
PATIENT: Yeah, okay.

text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So last time you were in, we talked about getting your diabetes better controlled, and I think we added something to help with your heart—your atrial fibrillation—isn't that right? How's that been going for you?
PATIENT: Yeah, well, that was a few months back. But actually, the reason I came in today is I've got this numbness in the feet. Severe numbness in the feet, to be honest. It started over the weekend and it's been there ever since.
NURSE: Let me get your blood pressure while we're getting started. Just relax your arm on the armrest there.
PATIENT: Sure thing. You know, my daughter was calling me about my meds the other day—she's always on my case about whether I'm taking them right. I've got so many bottles now.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's actually something we need to go through carefully today. Let's come back to that in a moment though. Tell me more about the numbness—has it been getting worse, or is it pretty much the same as when it started?
PATIENT: About the same, I'd say. No better, no worse. Just this tingling feeling all through both feet.
NURSE: Blood pressure is 158 over 92. I'll get his weight as well.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. And besides the feet, have you noticed anything else? Any trouble with your vision?
PATIENT: Well, actually, yeah. Since Monday I've had this mild blurred vision. Nothing terrible, but things aren't quite as sharp as they used to be.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Is that stable, or is it getting worse day by day?
PATIENT: No, it's about the same since Monday. I get it first thing in the morning mostly, and then it settles down a bit.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Have you had any chest pain?
PATIENT: Not like I did two years ago when I had that scare. Nothing like that at all. This is completely different—just the feet and the vision thing.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. And shortness of breath—how's that been?
PATIENT: I'm okay there. No problems breathing.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You're sure? Like when you walk up the stairs or do your usual activities?
PATIENT: Yeah, I'm sure. I mean, I get a little winded sometimes, but nothing I'd call shortness of breath. I'm fine.
NURSE: Weight's holding steady at 198 pounds.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright. Let's talk about your medications now, because that's really important for managing both your hypertension and your atrial fibrillation, as well as the diabetes. We started you on linagliptin at your last visit. How are you taking that?
PATIENT: The linagliptin? Um, I'm not sure, to be honest. I thought it was 10 mg, but then I looked at the bottle the other day and it says... no wait, it's 5 mg. Yeah, 5 mg once daily.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, so 5 mg once daily—that's the right dose. And are you remembering to take it?
PATIENT: Most days, yeah. I keep it by my coffee pot so I don't forget. Well, most days anyway. I couldn't say with complete certainty I've never missed it, but I really try.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's good. Now, the pioglitazone—that's the 30 mg once daily—how are you getting on with that one?
PATIENT: The pioglitazone, yeah. Honestly, I don't remember if I'm taking that one every day or not. Some days I think I do, other days... well, I'm not sure. My insurance keeps giving me a hard time about it too, keeps saying they might not cover the refill, so I've been rationing it a bit.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's important information. We'll make sure we get that refill arranged so you don't have to worry about running out. And then the dapagliflozin—the 5 mg once daily—how are you with that?
PATIENT: That one I take exactly as prescribed. Every single day, no exceptions. That one feels like it's helping, so I don't skip it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Perfect. Let me check your last labs real quick. Your LDL cholesterol came back at 72 mg/dL, which is actually pretty good for you. But I want to circle back to the numbness in your feet for a second. That's been severe and it started over the weekend, right?
PATIENT: Yes, exactly. Over the weekend it just started. And I'm wondering if maybe it's the diabetes or something, or if I'm taking something wrong. That's partly why I'm here.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We're going to figure that out. The good news is your LDL is controlled, and we need to focus on these symptoms and make sure we're on top of your medications. I think we should adjust linagliptin dose and monitor things closely. But we also need you to monitor your blood pressure at home—can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. My son gave me a cuff, actually. I've got it sitting somewhere in the kitchen.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. So here's what we're going to do. We'll adjust linagliptin dose, and I want you to monitor blood pressure at home. We'll see you back in 3 months and reassess everything—the numbness, your vision, your blood pressure readings, all of it. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds fine. I'll try to get the readings written down or something.

CARE_COORDINATOR: —so the pharmacy flagged that your pantoprazole prescription's coming due, and before we just renew it, I want to circle back on how the reflux's been treating you.
PATIENT: Oh, the heartburn. Yeah, it's actually better than it was. I mean, it's still there, moderate heartburn, but it's not waking me up at night like it was.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's good to hear. And when did this start for you, just to get a timeline?
PATIENT: A couple weeks ago, maybe a little longer. But like I said, it's getting better, so whatever I'm doing is helping.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right, that tracks with the discharge notes. The reason I'm asking is we might want to adjust pantoprazole dose at some point next week—I'm thinking out loud here—but let's back up and make sure we've got your full picture first. Are you still on the naproxen?
PATIENT: Yeah, I am. I'm taking it, the 250 mg twice daily like you said. Well, I think I am. Honestly, I'm not sure exactly how I've been taking it—some days I remember both times, some days I think I might've missed one? I couldn't say for certain.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, that's useful to know. So we can't necessarily credit all the improvement to the pantoprazole alone. Are you having any other symptoms since you got home? Anything besides the heartburn?
PATIENT: There's this dizziness. Not terrible, just mild, you know? But it's been about a month ago when it started, and if anything it's getting worse. I keep thinking it'll pass on its own.
CARE_COORDINATOR: When you say it's getting worse—are we talking more frequent, or more intense, or both?
PATIENT: More like... both? Most days it happens at least once. I'll stand up from my desk and the room just tilts for a second. It's annoying. And then the last few days I've had this moderate nausea on top of it, which is just fantastic. Really helps with the work day.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, so nausea for the past few days. And that's also worsening?
PATIENT: Yeah, it is. Started mild and it's been ramping up. Yesterday I barely ate lunch.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's concerning, especially with everything else. Let's talk about your other medications then. How's the losartan going?
PATIENT: The 100 mg once daily? Um, I've been taking it, but—I'll be honest, I've missed a few doses. Probably more than a few. Some mornings I just forget, or I'm traveling for work and my routine gets scrambled.
CARE_COORDINATOR: How many days a week would you say you're actually taking it?
PATIENT: Maybe five out of seven? Could be four some weeks. I know it's not great.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Well, we pulled your labs after discharge and they came back a bit off, which is part of why I wanted to talk to you today. What I'm thinking is we might actually bring the losartan down from 100 mg once daily, given what we're seeing. But we're also probably going to want to do some follow-up bloodwork next week to see how you're responding. Does that make sense?
PATIENT: So—wait, you're lowering it? I thought missing doses would mean my blood pressure was higher, not lower.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's a fair question. The lab results are telling us something different than what we'd expect, which is exactly why we need to track it. We'll order follow-up bloodwork to see what's actually happening. Is next week okay for that?
PATIENT: Yeah, next week is fine. But I'm confused about the pantoprazole. You said something about adjusting it?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right—so here's where I'm at. Your heartburn is better, which is great. But the dizziness and nausea are new, and they're trending the wrong way. The pantoprazole at 20 mg once daily might need to come up, especially if we're trying to manage your blood pressure control as well. We could adjust pantoprazole dose next week once we see the labs and get a clearer picture.
PATIENT: But wouldn't a higher dose of heartburn medicine help with the nausea?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Maybe, or we might find the nausea is tied to something else—medication timing, food, the blood pressure changes we're working through. That's part of why I don't want to commit to that change right now. Let's let the labs guide us. You're taking the pantoprazole exactly as prescribed, right? Haven't missed any?
PATIENT: No, I haven't missed any. I take that one every single day like clockwork. After my coffee, before breakfast.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's really good. That consistency is helping. Okay, and just to get a complete picture—what do you weigh right now?
PATIENT: 164 pounds. I checked this morning.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. Now, given the dizziness, the nausea that's getting worse, and your lab results, I do think we need to get you in front of nephrology—that's the kidney specialist. With your history of hyperlipidemia and especially with gastroesophageal reflux disease, and now these new symptoms, we want to make sure your kidneys are handling everything okay. Can you work with that?
PATIENT: Another specialist? Do I need to... I mean, is something wrong with my kidneys?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Nothing necessarily wrong. It's precautionary given what we're seeing. The labs suggest we should get their take. I can have the clinic get you on the list, and you'll hear about an appointment in the next week or so. Are you okay with us doing that referral to nephrology?
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. If you think it's necessary, then yeah. I'll go see them.

spans.text: in the next week or so

text:
PATIENT: I've been really dizzy the last week, and I'm kind of worried it's going to get worse. Like, I'll stand up and the room just tilts for a second.
PHYSICIAN: Mild dizziness starting last week. Does it happen every time you stand, or is it random?
PATIENT: It's pretty random, honestly. But it's been happening a lot. And I also have this nausea that won't go away.
PHYSICIAN: How long has the nausea been going on?
PATIENT: Same time, so the last week as well. It's not super bad, but it's there. Plus my muscles are aching.
PHYSICIAN: Muscle aches too. When did those start?
PATIENT: Yesterday. Just mild muscle aches, nothing terrible. And they're about the same as they were yesterday, not getting worse or anything.
PHYSICIAN: All right. Any blurred vision, or are your eyes okay?
PATIENT: Not really, not that I've noticed. My vision's fine.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Let me check your blood pressure.
PATIENT: Okay.
PHYSICIAN: It's reading 162/96. That's elevated. I'm seeing your peak flow is 260 L/min. Let me ask about your medications—you're on hydrochlorothiazide, 25 mg, once daily, correct?
PATIENT: Yeah, I think so. I'm not sure exactly how I've been taking it, to be honest. Some days maybe I miss it?
PHYSICIAN: You don't remember if you're taking it consistently. We're going to keep you on the hydrochlorothiazide, 25 mg, once daily exactly as you have it, but I want you to be more deliberate about it. And the valsartan, 40 mg, once daily—how are you with that one?
PATIENT: That one I take as prescribed. Haven't missed it.
PHYSICIAN: Good. We'll get a refill arranged for you. Now, the ibuprofen, 600 mg, as needed—are you still taking that?
PATIENT: No, I stopped taking it a while back. Just didn't need it anymore.
PHYSICIAN: Understood. I want to rule out chronic kidney disease stage 3 here, given your blood pressure and the symptoms you're describing. Your kidney function's been fine historically, but I'm not convinced yet that we've got a complete picture, so we need to look closer.
PATIENT: Wait, kidney disease? Like, is that serious? I mean—I don't really know much about that.
PHYSICIAN: It's something we're investigating, nothing confirmed. But the elevated pressure and the dizziness together warrant checking it out. Also, I know you had community-acquired pneumonia a few months back that cleared up, but given your peak flow today, I want to refer to pulmonology just to rule out anything lingering.
PATIENT: My lungs are fine now though, like, I'm not coughing or anything. Why do I need to see another doctor for that?
PHYSICIAN: It's just caution. The peak flow is lower than I'd expect, so let them take a look. And I also want to refer to cardiology because of that blood pressure, especially at your age.
PATIENT: Cardiology? For my blood pressure? I guess... I mean, that seems like a lot, but okay. I'm not going to argue with you.
PHYSICIAN: All right. So we're going to order follow-up bloodwork to check your kidney function and electrolytes, and we'll get that arranged before you leave. Your care coordinator will schedule the refer to cardiology at your next visit.
PATIENT: So I have to come back, then?
PHYSICIAN: Yes, we need to see how you respond to being more consistent with the hydrochlorothiazide, and we need those bloodwork results. Three weeks from now, give or take.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, I can do that. And what about the refer to pulmonology—when do I see them?
PHYSICIAN: Coordinator will call you with availability. Usually within a month if we can swing it. In the meantime, if the dizziness gets significantly worse or you have chest pain, shortness of breath, don't wait—go to urgent care or the ER, yeah?
PATIENT: Yeah, will do. Hopefully it's all just my blood pressure and I'm not actually falling apart.
PHYSICIAN: You're not falling apart. We're just being thorough.

NURSE: So looking at your last labs from three weeks ago, your potassium was running a little low again. And the BP readings you logged, those have been creeping up at the end there.
PATIENT: Mm-hmm, yeah, I've noticed my pressure's been higher. I've been meaning to... well, I don't know, it's just been a lot.
NURSE: I hear you. Before we get into that though, I need to ask—how's the fatigue been? You mentioned at your last visit it was pretty...
PATIENT: Severe. It's still severe, honestly. Started a couple weeks ago and it's just not getting any better. I wake up and I'm already exhausted, and then I can't even make it through the day without... I don't know, just wiping out.
NURSE: Okay. Same level since it started, or is it worse?
PATIENT: About the same, really. Not worse, but not better either.
NURSE: And appetite—how's that?
PATIENT: Yeah, poor appetite, I guess you'd say. I mean, I'm just not that hungry. It started about a month ago, like I'd open the fridge and nothing appealed to me. My husband's been trying to get me to eat more but...
NURSE: Sleep's probably not helping things either, I'm guessing?
PATIENT: No, I've got difficulty sleeping too. I'll fall asleep fine but then I'm up at three in the morning and just lying there. It's maddening.
NURSE: Yeah, that cycle makes everything worse. So let me check where we are with your meds. You're on metoprolol tartrate, 50 mg twice daily—how's that going?
PATIENT: It's fine, I mean... I take it most of the time. I've missed some doses here and there, to be honest, but mostly I get them in.
NURSE: Okay, we'll keep you on that same regimen for now. Your potassium chloride—you're currently at 10 mEq once daily. We need to bump that up based on those labs.
PATIENT: Okay, how much are we talking?
NURSE: The doctor's going to increase it. We want to get that level back to normal to help with blood pressure control. You've been taking it as prescribed, right?
PATIENT: Oh yeah, I haven't missed a single one. Every single day, like clockwork.
NURSE: Great. And then the torsemide—that's 40 mg once daily right now—we're actually going to bring that down based on your recent labs.
PATIENT: Bring it down? Why, is something wrong with the... or, I mean, is my deep vein thrombosis... does that affect the...
NURSE: No, no, your deep vein thrombosis is stable right now. This is just about optimizing based on what the labs showed. You're taking it exactly as prescribed?
PATIENT: Yes, I haven't missed any of those either. Every day, as prescribed.
NURSE: Excellent. Let me grab a peak flow reading. Go ahead and blow into this... Okay, you're at 300 L/min, that's good.
PATIENT: That's... is that normal? I don't really know what that number means.
NURSE: It's solid. Now, given everything you're dealing with—the fatigue, the appetite, the sleep trouble, plus the low potassium—I think the doctor's going to want a nephrology referral just to make sure there's nothing else going on with your kidneys.
PATIENT: Nephrology? Like a kidney doctor?
NURSE: Yes. And we'll want to look at your thyroid numbers too, given your hypothyroidism—that can definitely contribute to fatigue. But with the blood pressure situation and your potassium, it's good to have them take a look.

PATIENT: —and the line was just backed up to the front desk, must've been twenty people, and I thought I'd be here for—
PHYSICIAN: Yeah, Tuesdays can be rough. So let's dig into what's been going on. I see here you mentioned numbness in the feet?
PATIENT: Oh yes, that's—well, it started last week, and it's pretty severe, you know. Like when you sleep on your leg wrong and it wakes up all pins and needles, except mine don't go away. Stays right there in both feet.
PHYSICIAN: Both feet, okay. And has it been getting worse, or is it about the same since last week?
PATIENT: About the same, I'd say. Not getting better, but not any worse either. Just sits there, bothers me when I'm trying to walk around the house.
PHYSICIAN: Mm-hmm. And then your daughter mentioned fatigue on the phone the other day—how's that been?
PATIENT: Oh, that came on over the weekend. I woke up Saturday and just felt like I hadn't slept at all, you know? But actually, now that you ask, it's getting better. By yesterday I was feeling a bit more like myself. Still moderate fatigue, but the worst is over I think.
PHYSICIAN: That's good to hear it's trending up. Any other aches or pains?
PATIENT: Well, my knees—I've had osteoarthritis for years now, and sometimes I get mild muscle aches in my shoulders and neck. Nothing terrible. The osteoarthritis is probably the main thing that slows me down day to day.
PHYSICIAN: Let's talk through your medications, make sure everything's still working for you. You're on canagliflozin—
PATIENT: Yes, 100 mg once daily. I take that every single day, never missed it. I know how important that one is.
PHYSICIAN: Good. And we can refill that for you today. What about your pantoprazole?
PATIENT: Um, that one—I'll be honest with you, I've skipped some doses. Some mornings I just forget, and then by afternoon I figure, well, I've already gone that long without it. How important is that one?
PHYSICIAN: It helps protect your stomach lining, so it's good to stay consistent with it. Let's just keep you on the same—pantoprazole 20 mg once daily—and maybe setting a phone alarm might help you remember.
PATIENT: Okay, I can try that. My grandson is always telling me to use the phone for reminders anyway.
PHYSICIAN: Now, the insulin aspart—the fast-acting insulin you use with your meals. 4 units with meals, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, that one. Though honestly, I'm not sure I've been doing it exactly... I mean, I couldn't say for certain I'm getting the timing right with meals every time. Sometimes I eat a snack and wonder if I should've done the injection first, or if I'm remembering to do it at lunch when I'm rushing around.
PHYSICIAN: I hear you—the timing can be tricky. Your fasting glucose this morning was 124 mg/dL, which tells me we might want to think about bumping up your insulin aspart dose to help bring that down. We can adjust insulin aspart dose when you come back in next week, and in the meantime we could have you check some readings if you have a meter at home.
PATIENT: I've got one somewhere. My daughter was helping me use it a few months back.
PHYSICIAN: That would be helpful. Now, I'm curious—any family history of high blood pressure or heart problems?
PATIENT: My grandmother on my mother's side, she had hypertension. Had to take pills for years. I remember my mother saying it was a problem in their family, so I've always been a little worried about that.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. That's good to know about your family history. Given that and your blood pressure trending a bit higher on our end, it might be worth checking it at home more regularly—just to get a sense of what it looks like day to day. Something we could revisit next week after you've got a few days of readings.
PATIENT: I don't have a blood pressure cuff.
PHYSICIAN: You can pick one up pretty affordably at a pharmacy, or if you wanted we could lend you one from the clinic. But that's something to think about—might help us get a clearer picture.
PATIENT: Mm, maybe. I'll think about it. So what about these symptoms, the feet and the tiredness? Is there something wrong?
PHYSICIAN: The fatigue improving over a few days is a good sign. The numbness—we want to keep an eye on that. Your hypothyroidism is well controlled on your current medication, but sometimes numbness like this can have a few different causes. Let's see how it's doing in a week or so.
PATIENT: Okay. And I can still take my walks?
PHYSICIAN: If it's not hurting, yeah—gentle activity is good. We'll circle back after next week. Any questions for me before we wrap up?
PATIENT: No, I think you've covered everything. I'll get that phone alarm set up.
PHYSICIAN: Great. And we'll have you back next week to check in on those blood sugar readings and how you're feeling overall.

PATIENT: Yeah, so the numbness in the feet has been, um, pretty severe for the past few days. That's mainly what I wanted to talk about today.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, I'm glad you brought that up. Can you walk me through what that feels like? Is it both feet, or just one side?
PATIENT: Both feet. It's like pins and needles, but duller than that. And honestly, it's been getting better since it started, so maybe it's not as bad as I'm making it sound.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's helpful to know it's improving. How long exactly have you had this symptom?
PATIENT: For the past few days, yeah. I'm not sure what triggered it.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He hasn't mentioned anything else bothering him, but I did notice he's been drinking a lot more water lately. Like, constantly.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's a great observation. Have you noticed that too, or is this the first you're hearing it?
PATIENT: No, yeah, she's right. I've had this moderate increased thirst since last week, and I'm going to the bathroom way more than usual. Like, multiple times a night.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Multiple times at night—so the frequent urination is disrupting your sleep?
PATIENT: Pretty much. I'm tired all the time now because of it. At this point I'm just joking that my kidneys are trying to get a side gig as a water fountain.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: It's not funny. We're worried.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Let's talk about your medications. Are you taking your insulin glargine the way we discussed?
PATIENT: Yeah, I take the insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime every single day. I haven't missed a dose of that one.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. That's consistent. And your metformin?
PATIENT: Um, okay, so with the metformin I'm... I mean, I've missed a few doses. It's the twice daily thing that's hard for me. Some days I just forget.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I've been trying to remind him, but he has to set his own alarm or—
PATIENT: I know, I know. It's on me.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Well, your recent labs show your blood sugar control has drifted, which is why we need to make a change. I'm going to increase your metformin to 1000 mg twice daily. The higher dose will help bring things back in line, but you'll also need to commit to taking it consistently.
PATIENT: Okay. Is the higher dose going to make me feel sick or anything?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Some people get mild stomach upset initially, but it usually settles. Take it with food if your stomach bothers you. Now, given your type 2 diabetes mellitus and your chronic kidney disease stage 3, these symptoms and that drifting control are concerning. How's your blood pressure been?
PATIENT: I haven't checked it at home in a while. My mom's cousin actually had a stroke last year from hypertension—caught him off guard—so I know I should probably watch it more carefully.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I'm going to check it now.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He really should be more on top of this. He works construction and he's always rushing around. Not eating right half the time.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, I've got a reading here that concerns me. This is a very high blood pressure reading. I want you to go to the emergency department right now and let them take a full set of vitals and run some labs. This isn't something we monitor from here as an outpatient right now.
PATIENT: Oh, wow. Okay. Yeah, I can go right now.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. Once you're cleared there and we have those results, we're going to schedule a follow-up visit to make sure everything is stable, and at that visit we can also talk about ways to increase daily walking into your routine—that'll help with the blood sugar and blood pressure both.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I'll drive him.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Thank you. And we're going to order follow-up bloodwork in 3 months once we see how you're doing on the new metformin dose. Sound alright?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds alright. Let's go.

NURSE: Okay, so I'm looking here at your last echocardiogram from March—that confirmed the heart failure with reduced ejection fraction—and your ejection fraction was at 32 percent. Has anything felt different since then?
PATIENT: Um, well, yeah, I'd say I've got fatigue. I'd call it moderate fatigue, actually. It started yesterday, to be honest.
NURSE: Yesterday. And how's that progressing—is it getting better, or worse, or about the same right now?
PATIENT: Getting better, thankfully. I mean, I'm still tired, but I'm managing.
NURSE: That's good to hear. What about your sleep—have you been sleeping all right?
PATIENT: Not really, no. I'd say I have difficulty sleeping. It's mild, but it's been going on for a couple weeks ago, and honestly, it's getting worse.
NURSE: A couple weeks ago. And you're noticing it's worsening. Are you having trouble falling asleep, or is it more staying asleep?
PATIENT: Both, kind of. I'll lie there for an hour, sometimes two, and then I wake up at like three in the morning and can't—
NURSE: That sounds really frustrating. And have you noticed any night sweats at all, or—
PATIENT: Oh, the thermostat's been driving me crazy, actually, but no, I'm not—I mean, no night sweats. Not dealing with that.
NURSE: Okay, good. Now, I want to check in on something else. Your mother—she was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease stage 3, right?
PATIENT: Yes, years ago. She's been managing it pretty well, but it's always in the back of my mind, you know?
NURSE: I understand. We're keeping an eye on your kidney function because of that family history. Now, let me ask you about your appetite. How's that been?
PATIENT: Terrible, honestly. I'd say it's severe poor appetite. It came on about a month ago and it hasn't really changed since—still just not interested in food.
NURSE: About a month ago, and it's staying pretty consistent. Are you managing to eat enough, or—
PATIENT: I'm trying. I'll force down something at lunch, maybe a little dinner. But, I don't know, nothing sounds good.
NURSE: That must be challenging with everything else you're managing. Let me run through your medications with you. You're on torsemide 20 mg once daily—well, actually, we've been bringing that down for blood pressure control. Are you taking it as we discussed?
PATIENT: Um, I'm not sure, to be honest. I mean, I think so, but I don't remember exactly how many days—I couldn't say for certain.
NURSE: Okay, that's helpful to know. So we'll dial in the actual dose together before you leave. And warfarin—2.5 mg once daily. How's that going?
PATIENT: I haven't missed a single day. I take it as prescribed, every day, same time.
NURSE: Excellent. That's really important with the warfarin. Now, when I ask about pain, I'm wondering if—
PATIENT: Oh, I'd say it's an 8.
NURSE: An 8 on the scale. Where's that coming from?
PATIENT: Mostly my back, right side. It's been bothering me.
NURSE: We should definitely address that. One thing I want to bring up—and I know it might be sensitive—but we'd like you to reduce alcohol. Think that's something you—
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. I'm not drinking a lot anyway, but I'll cut back.
NURSE: Great. So we're on the same page about reducing alcohol over the next three months. And we want to schedule a follow-up visit in three months as well, so we can see how you're doing then. Does that work for you?
PATIENT: Yes, absolutely. Three months sounds fine.
NURSE: Perfect. And finally, I need you to monitor blood pressure at home over the next four weeks—we'll give you the log before you go. Can you do that for me?
PATIENT: Of course. I have a cuff at home, so that shouldn't be a problem.

text:
PHYSICIAN: Yeah, the waiting room was absolutely—oh, anyway. So let's get into what's been happening. I see on the chart here you mentioned a headache and some dizziness. When did the headache start?
PATIENT: Since my last visit, actually. It's been pretty severe, to be honest. But—and I know this might sound weird—it's actually getting better now.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, that's encouraging. And you'd say it's severe, but improving. Where does it sit on a scale of zero to ten for you right now?
PATIENT: Maybe a 4 today. Some days it was worse, but like I said, it's trending down.
PHYSICIAN: Right. And the dizziness—that's a different thing?
PATIENT: Yeah, that came on this morning. It's moderate, not debilitating or anything, but it's there. And that seems to be getting better too, actually.
PHYSICIAN: Moderate dizziness since this morning. Have you had episodes like this before, or is this something new?
PATIENT: I mean, I have migraine history, so headaches with some dizziness kind of go hand in hand for me. But I'm wondering if there's something else going on this time.
PHYSICIAN: That's worth asking about. We know you have a long-standing migraine pattern. But let me ask—any other symptoms? Nausea, sensitivity to light, anything in your stomach?
PATIENT: Actually, now that you mention it, I've had mild heartburn for three days ago. Wait, no—three days ago. That started it off, I think.
PHYSICIAN: Mild heartburn, onset three days ago. That timing lines up with when your headache started, then?
PATIENT: Yes, pretty much. I was wondering if the two were connected or if I'm just dealing with two separate things.
PHYSICIAN: It's definitely worth considering together. You have gastroesophageal reflux disease, as you know, and sometimes flare-ups can trigger or worsen headaches. Let me check where you're at with your weight and your medications. What's your weight today?
PATIENT: 224 pounds.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. And let's run through your meds. You're on lisinopril 40 mg once daily, correct?
PATIENT: Yes, I haven't missed a day. I take it every single day as prescribed.
PHYSICIAN: Good. We'll get that refilled for you. Now, the sertraline—100 mg once daily. How's that going?
PATIENT: Um, actually, I'm not taking that anymore. I stopped taking it a few months back because it didn't feel like it was helping the way I thought it would.
PHYSICIAN: I see. And you haven't experienced any problems stopping it on your own, or should we talk about that?
PATIENT: No, I feel fine. I mean, I know it's not ideal to just stop, but I wanted to see if I could manage without it.
PHYSICIAN: Alright, we'll note that and keep an eye on things. And the gabapentin—300 mg at bedtime. How are you managing with that one?
PATIENT: Honestly? I've missed some doses. I'll forget to take it, or I'll go to bed before I remember. I know I should be better about it.
PHYSICIAN: It happens. The timing at bedtime can be tricky. So here's what I'm thinking. We should monitor blood pressure at home—get a sense of the readings day to day. And I want to look at adjusting your lisinopril dose, which our care coordinator will handle at your next visit. Does that sound reasonable?
PATIENT: Yeah, I mean... I'm not totally sure why we need to change it, but if you think it'll help, then sure.
PHYSICIAN: It's part of getting us better control overall, especially with how you're feeling right now. And we'll definitely want you to monitor blood pressure at home—just a quick check once a day, morning's usually best. You have a cuff?
PATIENT: Yeah, I've got one at home.

PHYSICIAN: Hi, is this still a good time? I've got your chart up from your discharge summary and wanted to touch base about how things are going at home.
PATIENT: Yes, I've got a few minutes. Though I have to say I'm not entirely sure why I needed to come in — or, well, you're calling, but I thought I was doing okay.
PHYSICIAN: Fair point. We had you in last time for community-acquired pneumonia, and the idea today is just to make sure everything's settling down properly. How's the cough?
PATIENT: Oh, the cough is mostly gone. Still get a tickle in the throat if I, you know, exert myself, but nothing like it was.
PHYSICIAN: That's good to hear. I want to touch on a couple of other things though. You mentioned on the intake form — and I'm reading this now — that you've been having dizziness and that you've had poor appetite. Tell me about that.
PATIENT: The dizziness is what's really bothering me, honestly. It comes on when I stand up too fast, or sometimes just, I don't know, in the middle of the day. And the appetite thing, yes, it's been moderate since my last visit. Not terrible, but I'm not... I'm not eating as much as I usually do.
PHYSICIAN: Is the dizziness new, or has this been something you've had for a while?
PATIENT: Well, it's kind of — I mean, it's not completely new but it does seem worse since... I've been out of the hospital. I had a spell last Tuesday where it was pretty bad and I actually held onto the kitchen counter because I thought I might pass out, which scared me a bit.
PHYSICIAN: That's exactly the sort of thing I need to know about. Any blurred vision with it? Trouble speaking? Any weakness on one side?
PATIENT: No weakness that I noticed. Blurred vision, not really. I mean, my eyes don't feel quite right but I figured it was just, you know... normal stuff.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. I want to rule out a transient ischemic attack — basically a TIA, or what some people call a mini-stroke. I'm not convinced yet that's what this is, but given your history of hypertension and that episode on Tuesday, I'd like to get some more information to make sure we're not missing anything. [sound of typing] Let me pull up your most recent blood pressure reading from your last visit.
PATIENT: A stroke? That seems... I mean, I feel fine now. Are you saying I might have had a stroke?
PHYSICIAN: I'm saying I want to be thorough. A TIA is a warning sign more than anything, and we screen for it because if we catch risk factors early, we can do something about them. It doesn't mean you definitely had one. But let's go through your medications because that's where we can make some adjustments if we need to.
PATIENT: All right, fair enough. I'd rather be safe than sorry on that front.
PHYSICIAN: Good. So you're on aspirin 325 mg once daily — are you taking that regularly?
PATIENT: To be honest, I haven't been taking it. I know I probably should, but I kept forgetting and then I just... stopped taking it a few weeks ago. I meant to call about that.
PHYSICIAN: We can definitely get you a refill and I'd like you to restart it. It's important for someone with your blood pressure and the history we're looking at. And rivaroxaban — the 20 mg once daily — how's that going?
PATIENT: That one I'm taking as prescribed. I haven't missed a dose, it's just the aspirin I let slip. I take the rivaroxaban every single day, no problem with that.
PHYSICIAN: That's really helpful to know. All right, let's get your oxygen saturation quick. [pause] Okay, you're at 94%, which is good — that's right where we want you after the pneumonia. Your lungs are clearing well.
PATIENT: That's good at least. I was worried the pneumonia might have done some lasting damage or something.
PHYSICIAN: Not so far. The reason I want to dig into this dizziness, though, is to make sure we're not dealing with something that needs urgent attention. And honestly, with the appetite issue staying about the same — you said moderate since your last visit — I'm wondering if these things are connected. Are you getting enough water?
PATIENT: I guess I could drink more. I've been focused on just eating when I can, and I... well, actually now that you mention it, I haven't been as thirsty as I usually am, which is weird.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. Here's what I want to do. We're going to order follow-up bloodwork in 3 months to check a few things — your metabolic panel, lipids, and we'll take a closer look at your blood pressure control. I also want you to increase daily walking. Nothing crazy, but just a bit more movement than you're doing now, if you can tolerate it. Will that work for you?
PATIENT: Three months? I mean, I was expecting... I thought maybe we'd do something sooner given the dizziness thing.
PHYSICIAN: I understand the concern. We can absolutely follow up sooner if things get worse — if you have another bad spell or the dizziness is happening every day, I want you to call or come in right away. But barring that, three months gives us a good window to see if getting the aspirin back on board, staying hydrated, and getting a little more movement helps settle things down. And about increasing daily walking — even just a 10 or 15 minute walk most days. Does that seem doable?
PATIENT: I can do that, yes. Though I might start slow since I'm, you know, still recovering from the pneumonia and all.
PHYSICIAN: Absolutely. Start slow, listen to your body. And let me refill that aspirin prescription for you right now. You should get that filled today if you can.
PATIENT: Okay, I will. And the bloodwork in three months — is there anything I need to do to prepare for that? Any... I don't know, fasting or anything?
PHYSICIAN: We'll send you the details closer to the date, but yeah, it's typically fasting labs so you'll want to avoid eating the morning of. We'll text you with the appointment. One more thing — if that dizziness gets worse, or if you ever feel like something's really wrong, don't wait. Okay?
PATIENT: Got it. I'll call if anything feels urgent.

PATIENT: So before we get started, I wanted to ask you — I've been having some trouble with my legs, they're kind of puffy, and I'm wondering if that's something to do with the heart thing, or if it's just... I don't know, salt intake or whatever?
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's a really good question, and I'm glad you brought that up right away. Let me ask you a few things about that swelling. How long has it been going on?
PATIENT: For the past few days, really. Maybe four or five days now. And it's getting worse, if I'm honest. By the end of the day it's... it's pretty noticeable.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, and would you say it's mild, or is it more pronounced?
PATIENT: I'd say moderate swelling, yeah. I mean, my ankles don't look like my ankles anymore — could be the gout, I guess — and the rings I wear... well, I don't wear rings on my feet, but you know what I mean.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I understand. And that ties in with your heart failure with reduced ejection fraction — we want to keep a close eye on fluid buildup. Have you noticed any night sweats at all?
PATIENT: No, no night sweats, thankfully. I mean, nothing like that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Now, you also mentioned to the nurse that you've been experiencing poor appetite and it hasn't been what it usually is?
PATIENT: Yeah, that started last week, actually. It's been pretty mild, nothing crazy. I'm still eating, just... not as much as normal. It's kind of plateaued, to be honest — it's about the same as when it started.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And when you do eat, nothing is upsetting your stomach or making you feel worse?
PATIENT: No, no. I think maybe it's just stress or maybe I'm still recovering from... well, like over the weekend, my sleep has been really rough.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Tell me about that.
PATIENT: It's severe, honestly. Over the weekend, I just couldn't get any rest. I had difficulty sleeping — like, I'd fall asleep and then wake up at two in the morning and I'm just... done. And it's still not much better. About the same as when it started. It's killing me at work.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That sounds really frustrating. Now let's go through your medications and make sure we've got everything sorted out. You're on levothyroxine — what dose are you taking?
PATIENT: That's the thyroid one, right? I've been taking it as prescribed, every single day. I think it was 75 mcg, but I thought you mentioned something about changing it?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We are, yes. Based on your lab results, we're going to increase it. But I'm glad to hear you haven't missed any doses. Keep taking it once daily, but the dose is going up — your TSH came back a bit high.
PATIENT: Okay, got it. So higher dose to bring that down?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Exactly. Now, you're also on escitalopram for mood — I believe that's been 10 mg once daily?
PATIENT: I... well, I haven't been taking that one, actually. I stopped taking it a few weeks ago because I was worried it was affecting my blood pressure, and honestly, the cost was... it was a lot before my insurance switched, so I just kind of... didn't refill it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I appreciate you being honest about that. That's actually something we were going to adjust anyway — we want to bring the dose down from 10 mg once daily for the sake of your blood pressure control. So it sounds like the timing works out.
PATIENT: Really? So I'm not going to get in trouble for not taking it?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Not at all. We're going to lower it anyway, so let's just say you're ahead of the curve. And then your third medication is empagliflozin — 25 mg, once daily. How are you doing with that one?
PATIENT: That one I haven't missed — 25 mg once daily, just as prescribed. I know it's for the heart as well as the... what do you call it, the kidney thing?
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's right. And we're going to keep you on exactly what you're on — that's working well for you. Now, I do want to mention that we're concerned about your kidneys, actually. Your uncle had atrial fibrillation, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, he did. That was pretty scary when he had his... you know, his heart episodes with that. Why, do you think that runs in families or something?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It can, sometimes. But what I want to focus on is getting you referred to nephrology — kidney specialist — because of your reduced ejection fraction and some other factors. We'd like to get you in within 4 weeks.
PATIENT: Nephrology, so a kidney doctor. And that's the nurse who's setting that up?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Yes, the nurse will refer to nephrology, and she'll follow up with you to make sure that's scheduled. We also want you to monitor blood pressure at home — we'll get you a cuff if you don't have one — and check in every 4 weeks.
PATIENT: I can do that. I've got a cuff at home actually.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. And finally, we're going to order follow-up bloodwork in 3 months to check how the thyroid is responding to the dose increase, and to see how your kidney function is doing.
PATIENT: In 3 months, so like... October? That works for me. So to recap — higher thyroid medicine, stop the antidepressant but apparently that's what you wanted anyway, keep the empagliflozin, see the kidney doctor in a month, check my blood pressure, and bloodwork in three months?
CARE_COORDINATOR: You've got it exactly. And do call if that leg swelling gets any worse before your next appointment, or if the sleep doesn't improve. We want to make sure we're catching things early.
