text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So if I'm remembering right from last time, you were having some trouble with your blood sugar control, and we talked about adjusting things. How's that been going since we saw you?
PATIENT: Well, it's been... I don't know. Some days I feel okay, other days I'm just exhausted. And I've noticed I'm thirsty all the time. Like, I'm drinking water constantly.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Increased thirst—is that a mild thing you barely notice, or is it really bothering you?
PATIENT: It's mild, I guess. I mean, it's there, but it's not keeping me up at night or anything. Just annoying when I'm out.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And tell me more about the exhaustion piece. When did that start, and is it pretty constant?
PATIENT: That's been going on for months now, maybe longer. Some days I don't have the energy to leave the house. My daughter says it's the depression again.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You have major depressive disorder, and it sounds like it might be showing up again. Are you still on anything for that, or...?
PATIENT: I stopped taking those pills a while back. Felt like they weren't doing anything. And the side effects were rough.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Got it. We can circle back to that. But I also wanted to ask—you mentioned in your intake form that you've had numbness in the feet? Walk me through that.
PATIENT: Yeah, that started a couple weeks ago. Both feet, like a tingling, burning kind of thing. It's pretty severe, honestly. Just not going away.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: A couple weeks ago. And it's the same since then—not getting worse, not better?
PATIENT: About the same. Maybe a little worse in the mornings when I first wake up.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Hmm. And your vision—I see here you flagged blurred vision as well. Tell me about that.
PATIENT: That came on about a month ago. It's moderate, not terrible. I can still read and watch TV and all that. Things are just a little fuzzy around the edges sometimes.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And since a month ago, it's stayed about the same? Not worsening?
PATIENT: Yeah, stable. It's frustrating but... I'm used to things being a little off, you know?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I hear that. Let me just check on your weight for me. What are you at now?
PATIENT: 240 pounds. I know, I know. It's been creeping up.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: 240—okay. And your blood pressure today is running quite high. We got a very high blood pressure reading, and I want to be direct with you: that's a concern. We need to get you over to urgent care to have that checked right away. This isn't something we can wait on.
PATIENT: Oh. Wow. I... I didn't realize. I thought it was just, you know, white coat syndrome or whatever.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's possible, but we're not going to chance it. Your hypertension is real, and this reading is elevated enough that urgent care is the right place for you today.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I can call them right now and let them know you're coming. Do you have your insurance card handy? And can you head over there within the next hour or so?
PATIENT: Yeah, I have my card. I can go right now if you want. Should I bring anything?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Just your ID and insurance. Let me make that call.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Before you go, let me just confirm your medications. You're on atorvastatin 10 mg once daily, right? And you're taking it as prescribed?
PATIENT: Every single day, yeah. Haven't missed a dose.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. We'll arrange a refill on that. And the semaglutide—0.5 mg once weekly by injection. You're still taking that one as prescribed as well?
PATIENT: Yeah, I'm doing that every week, no problem.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And the dulaglutide? The 0.75 mg once weekly?
PATIENT: Oh, I'm not taking that one anymore. I stopped taking it a few months back—it was making me feel too sick.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Understood. So after you get back from urgent care, we should probably think about whether we want to adjust atorvastatin dose—we can circle back on that next week. And you might want to schedule a follow-up visit with us next week too, just to go over everything they tell you at urgent care and figure out where we go from here. Could be worth getting an endocrinology referral as well, given everything that's going on. But let's get your blood pressure sorted first, yeah?

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So Rigoberto, I see here your legs started swelling up yesterday. Tell me what that's been like.
PATIENT: Yeah, it came on pretty sudden. Both ankles, really severe leg swelling. I woke up and they were just... puffy. But it's actually getting better since this morning, so I'm not sure if I even needed to come in.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, I hear you — that's good that it's improving. But we still need to figure out what caused it. Have you had any shortness of breath with the swelling, or just the puffiness?
PATIENT: Not really shortness of breath. Though I will say I've been dizzy. Like, moderate dizziness that started a couple weeks ago, and honestly it's getting worse. I just thought it was stress or something.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: When you say it's getting worse, do you notice it's worse at certain times of day, or is it pretty constant?
PATIENT: It's like... it comes and goes, but yeah, if I stand up too fast, it really hits me. And there's something else — I've got chest pain. Severe chest pain, actually. Started about a month ago and it's getting worse too.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's important information. Where do you feel the chest pain, and is it constant or does it come and go?
PATIENT: It's like right here, across my chest, kinda pressure-like. Not all the time, but when I exert myself, climb stairs, that kind of thing. It's been sitting in the back of my mind for weeks now.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Right. And with your history of atrial fibrillation, plus the leg swelling and this chest pain pattern, I want to rule out heart failure with reduced ejection fraction — that's when the heart isn't pumping blood as efficiently as it should. That would explain the swelling and some of the chest discomfort.
PATIENT: Hold on — heart failure? I mean, I know I have hypertension and I had that arrhythmia years ago, but heart failure sounds pretty serious. Are you sure it's not something simpler?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I understand your concern. I'm not convinced yet it's definitely heart failure — that's why I said we want to rule it out. But the constellation of your symptoms right now is concerning enough that we need to work it up properly. Let me check where you're at on your medications. Are you still taking atenolol?
PATIENT: Yeah, 100 mg once daily. I haven't missed a day — I take it exactly as prescribed every single day.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. And the dabigatran for your atrial fibrillation?
PATIENT: Um, actually, I stopped taking that a while back. I'm not taking it anymore.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: When did you stop, and did someone advise you to, or did you decide on your own?
PATIENT: It was... I don't know, maybe six months? My old doctor said my afib was stable and didn't seem as urgent, and the medication made me feel weird, so I just kind of—
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, we're going to have a cardiology conversation about that, because with your history, we need to be thoughtful about anticoagulation. For now, let's keep you on the dabigatran 110 mg twice daily at least until cardiology reviews your whole picture.
PATIENT: But I just said I'm not taking it. I don't want to jump back on a medication that made me feel worse without understanding why.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I hear that, and I get it — but stopping anticoagulation without a plan when you have atrial fibrillation in your history is risky. Let me be clear: the dabigatran 110 mg twice daily — that's what we need. We can explore your concerns with the side effects, but I want that restarted, and we'll sort it out with the cardiologist. What about your clopidogrel, the 75 mg?
PATIENT: Yeah, that one I'm taking. 75 mg once daily, as prescribed. Never skipped it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: All right. And your cholesterol — your LDL came back at 88 mg/dL, which is actually where we want it. That's good control there.
PATIENT: Okay, so that's... something. I guess I'm managing something well, at least.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It is. Now, with the chest pain getting worse and the dizziness worsening over two weeks, I want to refer you to cardiology to get a full evaluation — probably an echo, maybe some other imaging. We need to figure out what's going on before this progresses further.
PATIENT: How soon are we talking? And... I don't know, do I need to be admitted or something?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Not necessarily admitted right now, but cardiology needs to see you soon. That'll be at the next visit window. In the meantime, I'm going to have our care coordinator adjust your atenolol dose — given your blood pressure response and these symptoms, we may need to optimize that. We also want you to monitor blood pressure at home; the coordinator will set you up with a home cuff and teach you how to log it.
PATIENT: So you're adjusting the blood pressure medicine, making sure I'm on the... the blood thinner again, and checking my pressure at home. Is there anything I should be watching for? Like, when do I call?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: If your chest pain gets significantly worse, if you have severe shortness of breath, or if you feel like you're going to pass out, don't wait — go to the ER. Also, I mentioned your lawn guy has colon cancer, right? That came up because someone in his family had it recently, and he was worried. Not you, but just so you know the context — that's why he's been a bit off lately.
PATIENT: Oh man, yeah, I did hear about that. Poor guy. I hope he's doing okay. But so to be clear, my situation is different — this is about my heart, not anything else?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Right, this is entirely your cardiovascular picture. We're working up your symptoms and making sure we're not missing anything with your heart function. The care coordinator will call you with those appointments and to set up the home blood pressure plan. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, I guess so. I'm still not fully convinced something's seriously wrong, but I'll do the refill on the atenolol and restart the dabigatran, and I'll go see the cardiologist.

text:
CARE_COORDINATOR: So I'm looking at your chart here, and I see you've had atrial fibrillation since 2019. Is that right? It's been pretty stable from what we can tell.
PATIENT: Yeah, that's been going on for a few years now. Some days are better than others, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: I bet. And I also see you have chronic kidney disease stage 3 documented. Have you been feeling okay otherwise, or is there something specific that brought you in today?
PATIENT: Well, the main thing is I've been dealing with some dizziness since Monday. It's been pretty severe, honestly. Makes it hard to get out of bed some mornings.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Severe dizziness since Monday—that's concerning. Is it getting worse or better as the days go by?
PATIENT: Actually it's getting better. I mean, it was worse the first couple days. Now it's more manageable.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, that's good. And have you been experiencing any cough, or is that—
PATIENT: No, no cough. I was actually thinking about that yesterday, and no, nothing like that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right. What about palpitations? Any fluttering or racing sensation in your chest?
PATIENT: Yeah, I've had some moderate palpitations since my last visit. That's been bothering me more than the dizziness, if I'm honest.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Since your last visit—so that's been going on for what, a couple weeks now? And is it getting better, worse, or about the same?
PATIENT: It's actually getting worse. I notice it more when I'm lying down or first thing in the morning.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Mm-hmm. Any lightheadedness along with the palpitations, or is that separate?
PATIENT: Yeah, some lightheadedness too, especially when the palpitations really kick up.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Alright. Let me just take your blood pressure here.
PATIENT: Sure, go ahead.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, I'm getting 128/82 mmHg. That's actually not too bad given everything. Now, let's talk about your medications. You've been on metoprolol succinate?
PATIENT: Right, yeah. I'm on that for the atrial fibrillation. Though I've got to be honest, I've missed some doses here and there.
CARE_COORDINATOR: How often would you say you're missing doses? Every week, or less than that?
PATIENT: Maybe once or twice a week. Life gets busy, you know? Sometimes I forget.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I understand. Well, based on your lab results—your kidney function especially—we're going to bump the metoprolol succinate up. We want you on 50 mg once daily. That means once you take your next dose, stay at that level. Can you do that?
PATIENT: Up from what, 25? Yeah, I can try to be more careful about it. 50 mg once daily.
CARE_COORDINATOR: And the other thing—you've been on hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, right? The diuretic?
PATIENT: Oh yeah, but honestly I haven't been taking that one. I stopped taking it about a month ago because I was getting these weird side effects.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, so you're not taking it at all. Well, your blood pressure control has actually improved—
PATIENT: Really? Even without—
CARE_COORDINATOR: —has improved, so we're going to keep going with that approach. But we do want to cut back on salt. Your sodium intake could be a factor in the palpitations too. Can you commit to cutting back on salt in your diet?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. Cut back on salt. I mean, I like my salty snacks, but if it'll help with this stuff, I'm willing to try.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I think you'll see improvement. Now, the aspirin—the 81 mg once daily—how are you doing with that one?
PATIENT: Oh, I'm taking that as prescribed. I haven't missed a single dose on that one. Every day.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Great. Keep it exactly as is. And I want to refer you to cardiology at your next visit. Someone needs to really look at your rhythm, especially with the palpitations getting worse. We'll set that up. Does that sound alright?
PATIENT: Yeah, that makes sense. I've been worried about the palpitations getting worse, so having a cardiologist look at it is good.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Exactly. So we're also going to schedule a follow-up visit with me in about four weeks—
PATIENT: Sounds good. Four weeks, I can—
CARE_COORDINATOR: —to check on how you're doing with the new dose and to make sure the dizziness hasn't come back. Actually, before you go, let me just step out and grab your referral paperwork. One second.
PATIENT: Sure, take your time.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So I have you down for a followup at 2:30 on the fifteenth—does that still work, or do we need to shuffle that around before we dive in?
PATIENT: The fifteenth should be fine. My daughter was going to drive me that day anyway, so it all lines up.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Great. Let me just get a temperature while we're at it, and then I want to hear what's been happening since we last saw you. I'm looking at your chart and it looks like your last visit was about three weeks ago?
PATIENT: Yeah, something like that. So what's happened is, I got sick—I mean, I think I got some kind of infection, maybe bronchitis or something, and my doctor put me on antibiotics. I was really knocked down for a bit there, just completely exhausted. That was maybe two weeks ago? And I've been trying to bounce back but I'm just...
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, okay. And the fatigue—is that what's bothering you most right now?
PATIENT: I mean, yeah, the severe fatigue has been for the past few days worse than before, but actually it's getting better. Like day by day I can feel it lifting a little. But it was really bad right after I got sick.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright. And when you say you got an infection—did anyone call it community-acquired pneumonia, or was it just treated as a general respiratory thing?
PATIENT: Oh yes, actually—the urgent care said it was community-acquired pneumonia. That's the term they used. I was so tired I kind of forgot to ask a ton of questions, but yeah, that's what they said.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Got it. So you're on antibiotics for that. And I'm also noticing you've had some shortness of breath?
PATIENT: Yeah, mild shortness of breath starting last week. And honestly, it's getting worse, not better like the tiredness. I notice it more when I'm moving around the house or going up the stairs.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: When you say it started last week, was that around the same time as the pneumonia diagnosis, or a few days after?
PATIENT: A few days after, I think. So the infection hit hard, and then a couple days in, I noticed I was huffing and puffing just walking to the kitchen.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. Let me just—sorry, hang on one second.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright, I've got your temperature here. It's 100.2 degrees Fahrenheit. That's still a bit elevated, so the infection's probably still working its way through. You're on antibiotics now though, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, I finished them three days ago. Or wait, maybe four? I want to say three or four days ago.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, that's worth noting. Now let me ask you this—any leg swelling at all? Any puffiness in your legs or ankles?
PATIENT: No. No leg swelling.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Night sweats?
PATIENT: Not really, not that I've noticed.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. So let's talk about your medications. You have the albuterol inhaler—the blue one, probably?
PATIENT: Yes, that one. I have it, but I have to be honest—I've missed some doses because I keep forgetting to carry it with me, especially when I'm out running errands.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: How often would you say you're taking it?
PATIENT: Maybe half the time I'm supposed to, if that. I'm not great with the inhaler thing in general, if I'm being real.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Well, let's get you a refill and maybe we talk about strategies to make it easier to remember. The dose is 2 puffs as needed, so we'll get you restocked there. Now, you were on montelukast—10 mg at bedtime—are you still taking that one?
PATIENT: No, I haven't been taking it. I stopped taking it I guess about a month ago because I wasn't sure if it was helping and I felt like I had too many pills.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's fair feedback. We can just review that for now and not make any changes. And the tiotropium, the maintenance inhaler you do once daily—
PATIENT: Yeah, I'm not taking that either. I stopped taking it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: The 18 mcg once daily one?
PATIENT: That's the one.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, we'll review that too without making a change today. But I do want to circle back to your blood pressure. How's that been?
PATIENT: I have that hypertension thing, right? The doctor mentioned it before. I haven't been checking it very much, so I'm not sure.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You're on medication for it, and the hypertension is something we definitely want to keep tabs on, especially with everything else going on. I'd like you to monitor blood pressure at home. Can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. I have one of those cuffs somewhere.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Great. Check it a few times a week and jot down the numbers, and we can look at them when you come back in. Now, given that you've got this community-acquired pneumonia still resolving and the shortness of breath that's persisting, I think we need to refer to pulmonology.
PATIENT: A lung specialist? Is that serious?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's a good precaution. We want to make sure your lungs are clearing properly and that we're managing everything optimally. Our care coordinator will set that up for you at the next visit.
PATIENT: Okay, I'm fine with that.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And we'll schedule a follow-up visit here before then. I'd like to see you back in a couple of weeks to check on how you're doing. Does that sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, that works.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Hi, is this still a good time for you to talk through some of your symptoms over the phone?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, go ahead. I've got a few minutes.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Great. So I've got your recent visit notes here, and I wanted to circle back on the chest pain you mentioned. You said it started about a month ago?
PATIENT: That's right. It's been... well, it hasn't really let up. Actually, it's been getting worse, if I'm honest.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I'm sorry to hear that. When you say worse—can you describe what that feels like? Is it sharper, or more constant?
PATIENT: It's mild, mostly, but it's just... there. Some days it feels like a heaviness, you know? And it comes and goes, but yeah, the frequency is picking up.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. And along with that, have you been noticing anything else—any shortness of breath, especially when you're exerting yourself?
PATIENT: Actually, yes. The shortness of breath has been... I mean, it's not like I can't breathe, but climbing stairs or walking up a hill, I'm getting winded quicker than I used to.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's important. And fever? Any fevers at all?
PATIENT: No. No fever.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: All right. I want to loop back on your coronary artery disease, because given what you're describing—the chest pain, the shortness of breath—we need to make sure we're optimizing your management. Let me pull up your medication list here. So you're on rosuvastatin, 10 mg, once daily. How's that been going?
PATIENT: Um, mostly good. I mean, I've... I've missed some doses here and there. Not every day, but some weeks I forget.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's really common. Would it help to get a refill with a better reminder system—maybe a pill organizer or an alarm on your phone?
PATIENT: Yeah, actually, that might help. I should probably... I mean, I know I should be taking it every day.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We can definitely arrange a refill. Now, you're also on losartan, 25 mg, once daily. How have you been with that one?
PATIENT: Uh, I'm not sure, honestly. I mean, I think I'm taking it... I don't remember if I've been totally consistent. Couldn't say with certainty.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's okay. We'll keep you at the same dose for now and just review it. The losartan is doing important work managing blood pressure—which, you know, runs in your family, right? Your grandmother on your dad's side had hypertension, didn't she?
PATIENT: Yeah, she did, actually. Got it early too, I think. I don't want to end up the same way.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Understood. And then there's your metoprolol tartrate, 100 mg, twice daily. You're taking that as prescribed?
PATIENT: Yeah, I haven't missed any of those. I take it every single day, morning and night. That one I stay on top of.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Excellent. Let me just... [typing] ...pull up your recent labs and vitals here. Your heart rate was running at 104 when we checked it last. That's a little elevated for where we'd like to see you, especially given your coronary artery disease and these new symptoms.
PATIENT: Is that... should I be worried? I mean, 104—is that bad?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's something we want to address, yeah. Looking at your lab results overall, I'm thinking we might need to adjust metoprolol tartrate dose to help bring that down and improve your symptoms. That's something the clinic can work through with you next week, actually—
PATIENT: Next week? Like, what would that look like? Would you—
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We'd likely increase it, possibly. But let's plan on you coming in so we can make sure it's the right move. In the meantime, what I do want to do is schedule a follow-up visit so we can get a full assessment.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, I can do that.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And I also think we should refer to cardiology. Given your chest pain, the shortness of breath, and your coronary artery disease, I'd like you to see a cardiologist to make sure we're not missing anything.
PATIENT: Cardiology? I mean... okay, if you think that's necessary, I'll do it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I do. And we'll get that ball rolling today. So we've got the rosuvastatin refill going through, we're reviewing your losartan regimen, and we'll sort out the metoprolol question at your visit next week. Does that sound like a plan?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds... that sounds alright. Thanks for walking me through this.

PATIENT: Before we get going, I wanted to ask you—is the tiotropium supposed to make my mouth so dry, or am I just... I don't know, is that normal?
NURSE: That's a good question. The tiotropium can definitely cause some dryness, yeah. We'll come back to that in just a moment because we need to talk about your dosing anyway. But first, walk me through what's been going on since last month.
PATIENT: Well, the night sweats started this morning, or... no wait, actually it was a few nights ago but they've been mild, really mild, and they're actually getting better now. But the cough, that's the real problem. That came on three days ago and it's severe, I mean it's getting worse, not better.
NURSE: Okay, so the night sweats this morning, mild, and improving. But the cough three days ago—severe and getting worse. Let me make sure I have that right.
PATIENT: Yes, that's it exactly. And I also have this... it's like a tightness, you know, in my chest? Started yesterday. It's not terrible, it's moderate, I'd say, and it's kind of just staying the same.
NURSE: Moderate chest tightness since yesterday, stable. Got it. And with your asthma, are you having trouble catching your breath with any of this?
PATIENT: The asthma's been... it's been okay mostly. The tightness is more annoying than anything else. Though I haven't been taking the tiotropium like I should—I've missed a few doses here and there, honestly.
NURSE: You've missed some doses. Do you remember what happened there? Was it hard to remember, or something else going on?
PATIENT: My blood pressure, actually. My doctor said—I mean, the previous visit, they said it was running a little high and that one of my medicines might be making it worse. So I've been kind of cutting back on my own, but I probably shouldn't have done that without—
NURSE: Right, okay. Your blood pressure control is important, so we're going to adjust your tiotropium dose—that's the 18 mcg one—to bring that down. That's something the care coordinator will handle at your next visit. But in the meantime, we want to be thoughtful about that, okay?
PATIENT: Okay, yeah. That makes sense.
NURSE: Let me just check your oxygen saturation real quick. I'm getting 93%—that's fine. And your peak flow is 340 L/min.
PATIENT: Is that... is that good? I don't really know what those numbers mean.
NURSE: For where you are, that's stable. Not the highest we'd want to see, but it tells us your breathing is holding. Now, the amoxicillin—how have you been taking that? Three times daily, 250 mg?
PATIENT: Um, I'm not sure, actually. I mean, I take it, but don't remember if I've been hitting all three times every day, or just... I couldn't say for certain.
NURSE: Okay, so you're not quite sure about your pattern with it. Let's keep it the same for now—amoxicillin 250 mg three times daily—and we'll dial in the timing better. What about the prednisone?
PATIENT: Oh, that one I'm doing right. Prednisone 20 mg once daily, every single day. I haven't missed it. I know my hypertension needs me to be consistent, and I know that one matters too, so...
NURSE: That's really important. So you're taking the prednisone 20 mg once daily as prescribed and you haven't missed any?
PATIENT: Right, not a single one.
NURSE: Good. We'll arrange a refill for that before you leave. Now, your symptoms—the cough getting worse, the night sweats even if they're mild, and honestly, with that chest tightness—I want to rule out anemia. I'm not convinced yet that that's what we're looking at, but I want to make sure. So we're going to order follow-up bloodwork at your next visit, okay?
PATIENT: Anemia? Really? I mean, I guess I could be... I do feel a bit tired, but I'm ninety-one, so—
NURSE: Fair point. But we need to check, especially with everything else going on. The care coordinator will set that up. Does that sound all right?
PATIENT: Yeah, sure. My insurance usually covers that stuff anyway, so no big worry there.
NURSE: Great. So here's what we're doing: we're going to adjust tiotropium dose to help with your blood pressure control, we're ordering follow-up bloodwork, and one more thing—have you been moving around much? Walking?
PATIENT: A little bit. I get around the house, you know, and I'll go to the... to the store or... I don't walk as much as I probably should.
NURSE: I want to increase daily walking. Nothing crazy, but getting out a little more each day will help your breathing and your stamina. Can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I think so. I can try to get out in the mornings. My knees aren't great, but I can manage.
NURSE: That sounds good. So to recap: we're increasing daily walking, the care coordinator is handling the adjust tiotropium dose at your next visit, and we're ordering follow-up bloodwork then too. You're going to keep the amoxicillin 250 mg three times daily exactly as is, keep the prednisone going as prescribed, and we'll refill that for you. Does that all make sense?
PATIENT: Yeah, I think so. Just to make sure—the walking is okay even with the cough getting worse?
NURSE: Good question. Start slow, and if the cough gets really bad, you can take it easier that day. But gentle movement should be fine. All right?
PATIENT: Okay, I can do that.

PHYSICIAN: So you're about two weeks out from discharge now. Let's start with the basics — how's the incision healing up?
PATIENT: It's... okay, I guess. There's still some moderate incision pain, but it started over the weekend, and it's been about the same since then. Not getting worse, anyway.
PHYSICIAN: That moderate pain's been stable — good. Are you able to move around comfortably, or is it limiting what you're doing?
PATIENT: I can walk, you know, short distances. I'm doing that most days. It's just when I reach or twist that it really bothers me.
PHYSICIAN: Understandable. And apart from the incision, how's your energy been? You feeling like yourself?
PATIENT: Not really. I've got mild fatigue, honestly. It started since Monday, but it's actually getting better than it was.
PHYSICIAN: That's encouraging. And what about your appetite — I noticed that's something we flagged on the discharge summary.
PATIENT: Yeah, that's been the worst part. I just... I don't feel hungry. Even things I normally love, I'll look at them and think, 'I can't.' I'm managing a little bit at lunch, but dinner is, uh, it's a struggle.
PHYSICIAN: Poor appetite is frustrating, especially when you're trying to recover. Any particular foods that seem worse than others, or is it pretty much everything?
PATIENT: Everything, really. Nothing tastes right. And I'm worried about it, because I know I need to eat to get stronger.
PHYSICIAN: That makes complete sense. Now, you finished a course of antibiotics in the hospital for community-acquired pneumonia. How are you feeling in your chest — any shortness of breath, any chest discomfort?
PATIENT: No, I mean... I can breathe fine. No sharp pains or anything like that.
PHYSICIAN: Good. I want to rule out pulmonary embolism given the context of your recent hospitalization, so I want to ask — any swelling in your legs, any calf pain, or heaviness in your legs at all?

NURSE: Mm-hmm. And your breathing—has that been okay? No issues there?
PATIENT: No, not at all. My breathing's been fine. No shortness of breath.
NURSE: Good to know. Let me pull up your current medications and we can go through those. You've got the heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that we've been managing, and we want to make sure everything's working well for you. You're on torsemide, 10 mg once daily—how have you been taking that?
PATIENT: Um, I think I'm taking it right. I mean, I'm not sure I've been completely consistent, to be honest. Most days I take it in the morning, but I couldn't say I've never missed one.
NURSE: That's really helpful to know. Consistency matters with the torsemide. Let's plan to keep it at 10 mg once daily, same as you've been doing, and we can work on making it part of your routine. You're also on rivaroxaban, 20 mg once daily. How's that been for you?
PATIENT: I've been taking that one exactly as prescribed. Haven't missed a single dose. I'm pretty careful with that one because I know what it's for.
NURSE: That's excellent. Well, I want to rule out deep vein thrombosis given some of what you're describing, so we're going to hold the rivaroxaban for now while we do some work-up, okay? Just for a bit.
PATIENT: Oh. Okay. How long is 'for a bit'?
NURSE: We'll see what the testing shows. Could be just a precaution. And then you've got naproxen, 250 mg twice daily for your osteoarthritis. How's that managing your pain?
PATIENT: It's doing alright. Keeps things under control. I haven't missed a dose on that either. I take it as prescribed, every single day.
NURSE: Perfect. We're going to keep that exactly where it is—250 mg twice daily. No changes there. Now, your osteoarthritis has been tough on you, and given some of the symptoms you're dealing with, I want to suggest increasing your daily walking. Start easy, maybe 15, 20 minutes a day, and build from there. What do you think?
PATIENT: Walking? I mean... I'm not super keen on it with the dizziness and the nausea. Won't that make things worse?
NURSE: That's a fair question. But gentle movement can actually help with both nausea and circulation. We'd start slow, and you'd listen to your body. By the time we check in with you in 3 months, I think you might be surprised. Does that seem okay?
PATIENT: I guess... I mean, I trust you, so okay. I'll give it a shot. Maybe start this week?
NURSE: That sounds good. And we're going to order follow-up bloodwork in 3 months as well so we can see how your numbers are looking, especially given the nausea and what we're checking for with the deep vein thrombosis concern. That'll give us a clear picture.
PATIENT: Three months, right. Oh—wait, was that when I saw you last? Back in... June?
NURSE: That would've been back in March, actually. Spring time.
PATIENT: Oh gosh, has it really been that long? I thought it was more recent.
NURSE: Time flies. But listen, if you develop severe shortness of breath, or if the nausea gets to the point where you can't keep anything down, I want you to go straight to the emergency department. Don't wait, okay?
PATIENT: Okay. To the emergency department. Got it. I really hope that doesn't happen, but I hear you.

text:
PATIENT: So my muscle aches have gotten worse, honestly. They're moderate and they've been going on since my last visit, and I'm starting to wonder if the medication I'm on isn't working anymore.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, let's talk through that. When you say they've gotten worse — we're talking about the aches themselves, or the frequency?
PATIENT: Both, really. Some days are worse than others. And then on top of everything, I woke up this morning with a mild headache that also seems to be getting worse.
PHYSICIAN: This morning, so relatively recent onset. And separate from the muscle aches, or are they connected?
PATIENT: I think separate, but I'm not sure anymore. There's also this dizziness that started three days ago — and it's not like a spinning thing, it's more like I'm heavy or something. It's severe enough that I had to hold onto the railing going down the stairs yesterday.
PHYSICIAN: Has the dizziness been stable, or is it changing at all?
PATIENT: No, it's about the same. Not getting better, but not worse either, which is... I don't know, kind of a relief? At least it plateaued.
PHYSICIAN: Fair enough. Let me check your blood pressure real quick. Okay, so we're looking at 118/72 — that's actually solid. I want to review what you're on and see if we can sort out what's driving this.
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I'm interested in that too. I've been pretty good with the medications, mostly. Well, except — you know, I do forget the lisinopril sometimes, I'll skip a dose here or there.
PHYSICIAN: The 40 mg once daily?
PATIENT: Right, that one. But I haven't missed the losartan, I take that 100 mg once daily like I'm supposed to. And the valsartan — 40 mg once daily — I take that exactly as prescribed, every single day without fail.
PHYSICIAN: So valsartan is solid, losartan you're compliant with, and lisinopril is where you're slipping. We should review your losartan status first — are you still feeling like you need to be on it, or has that become part of the background?
PATIENT: Honestly, I'm not even sure anymore. It's been on the list so long I just keep taking it. I figured you'd tell me if it wasn't needed.
PHYSICIAN: No change needed there for now — we'll keep monitoring that. But with the lisinopril, the fact that you're missing doses might be part of the picture here, especially with the symptoms you're describing. And I do want to discuss your hypothyroidism status, because that can definitely cause these kinds of aches.
PATIENT: Wait, I thought my hypothyroidism was stable? Aren't my levels okay?
PHYSICIAN: That's what we need to look at in your labs, which brings me to something — I'm going to arrange a refill on the valsartan while we're at it, and we should order follow-up bloodwork to check your thyroid numbers and everything else. We can do that at your next visit when our care coordinator pulls the labs.
PATIENT: So you want more blood tests. I hate needles, by the way — my brother is a phlebotomist, ironically, and he's tried to get me to just get over it for years. Not happening.
PHYSICIAN: I hear you. But the numbers will tell us if something's shifted with your thyroid, or if maybe the dizziness is something else entirely. Speaking of which — this friend of yours, does he have migraines or anything like that?
PATIENT: What? No, I mean — my guy at the gym, he has migraine all the time, complains about it constantly, but I don't know why that's relevant.
PHYSICIAN: No reason, just crossing wires. I'm focused on your stuff. One thing I want to address — have you been drinking more lately? Because dehydration and alcohol can both make the muscle aches worse, and they interact with blood pressure meds.
PATIENT: I mean, it's winter, so probably not? But okay, maybe a bit more than usual on weekends. Why, do you think I should reduce alcohol?
PHYSICIAN: I do, actually. Let's reduce alcohol and see if that helps with the headaches and the aches overall. It's worth trying before we change anything medication-wise.
PATIENT: Alright, I can do that. I wasn't planning on becoming a monk or anything, but... yeah, I'll cut back.
PHYSICIAN: Good. And I want to schedule a follow-up visit so we can review those labs and see how you're doing with everything we've discussed. Can you do that before you leave today?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's fine. Do I need to do anything else in the meantime?
PHYSICIAN: Mostly what we said — cut back on the alcohol, try not to skip the lisinopril doses, and come back for that follow-up. We'll have answers then.
PATIENT: Okay. I can work with that.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So we had you down for three weeks from now, but I'm wondering if we should nudge that earlier or later depending on how things have been. Let me pull up your chart here—okay, last time was what, six months ago?
PATIENT: That sounds about right. Yeah, I think it was around then. Time just flies, you know? One day you're coming in and then suddenly a whole season has passed. My daughter was still working at that coffee place downtown and now she's moved on to something else entirely.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I hear you. Well, let's focus on how your breathing's been. Any changes since my last visit?
PATIENT: Um, yeah, actually. I mean, the shortness of breath is there, but it's mild, you know? Like I can still do things. But it's been since my last visit that I've noticed it more, or maybe I just pay attention to it more now. Hard to say.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And is it getting better, or worse, or just kind of stable?
PATIENT: It's getting better, actually. I was worried at first but it's definitely improving.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's good to hear. Now, this morning—did anything happen that was different?
PATIENT: Well, this morning I woke up and I could hear myself wheezing. Like really noticeable. It was moderate wheezing, and it started this morning, just when I got out of bed.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Have you had any allergies acting up, or did you notice what might have triggered it?
PATIENT: I honestly don't know. I did have the window open last night because it was nice out, so maybe that. Or just a bad morning. It hasn't happened before this morning, not like that.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Let's talk about your chronic obstructive pulmonary disease—your COPD—because that's obviously part of the picture here. How are you managing that day to day? Are you using your inhalers?
PATIENT: Yeah, I have my albuterol. That's the blue one, right? As needed. I'm supposed to use it as needed and I do, but I'm... I've missed some doses, I guess. Sometimes I just forget to reach for it or I don't think I need it in the moment.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's pretty common, honestly. We're going to keep your albuterol at 1 puffs as needed, same as before. But I want to circle back to that. Now, on the prednisone—10 mg once daily—how have you been taking that?
PATIENT: Oh, the prednisone. Um, I'm not sure, to be honest. I take it, I think, but I don't remember if it's every morning or—I couldn't say if I've been missing any. I just kind of grab it when I see it there.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, we'll get you a refill and maybe we can talk about putting it somewhere more visible, or setting a phone reminder. That would help. Now, the other thing—I want to check in about the montelukast. You were taking that at bedtime, 10 mg at bedtime.
PATIENT: Right, yeah. I'm not taking that anymore. I stopped taking it a few months back. I just felt like I didn't need it and it was another thing to remember at night.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: All right, so we're not—

[There is a knock at the door and someone pokes their head in asking about a lab result.]

Just a second—we're in the middle of something. You can send that to my inbox.

Sorry. So we're confirming that you haven't been taking the montelukast. That's fine, we can leave that off for now. I do want to come back to the sleep, though. How's that been? Any snoring, or waking up gasping for air?
PATIENT: Oh, yes, actually. My husband mentioned the snoring. And a couple times I've woken up and felt like I couldn't breathe. I thought maybe it was just because I was sleeping weird on my neck.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That sounds like it could be the obstructive sleep apnea acting up—the OSA. We talked about that before. Have you been using your CPAP?
PATIENT: No, I haven't really. I have it, but it's uncomfortable and I kept taking it off in the middle of the night.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I understand it's not fun at first. Let's set up a follow-up visit in 3 months and we can address that then, too. We should schedule a follow-up visit to see how you're doing with everything—the breathing, the wheezing, how the medications are working if we get you back on track. Three months sound all right?
PATIENT: Yeah, three months is fine. That works for me.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Great. And one more thing—I'd like you to increase daily walking. Nothing crazy, just a gentle pace, maybe fifteen or twenty minutes if you can manage it. By the time you come back in 3 months we can see if that's made a difference with your shortness of breath. Does that sound doable?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. I actually like walking, so that's good.

CARE_COORDINATOR: I'm really sorry we're running about fifteen minutes behind today. One of the nurses called in sick and we're playing catch-up. But let's get straight into it—I've got your chart here and I want to talk through how things have been since you left the hospital.
PATIENT: No problem at all. Yeah, it's been okay, but honestly I've had some muscle aches that won't quit, and my legs—my left leg especially—has just swollen up something awful.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, so muscle aches and leg swelling. When did the swelling start?
PATIENT: Last week. It came on pretty sudden. The muscle aches have been going on a bit longer, but that leg swelling—it's been severe, you know? Though I will say it's getting better the last couple of days.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's good to hear it's improving. Have you noticed anything else—any chest pain, shortness of breath?
PATIENT: No, no chest pain.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right. And shortness of breath—you haven't had any of that?
PATIENT: No, I haven't. None of that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. Now let's go through your medications. You're on duloxetine—that's 60 mg once daily. How are you doing with that one?
PATIENT: Yeah, I take that as prescribed. Every single day, haven't missed once.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. And we're going to keep you on that at the same dose. You're also on sertraline 50 mg once daily, but we're actually holding that for now—does that make sense?
PATIENT: Holding it? What does that mean exactly?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good question. It just means we're pausing it for now—you're not taking it at the moment while we see how you do. We can restart it later if we need to. But before you were admitted, how were you taking it?
PATIENT: I was taking it as prescribed, every single day, no issues.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Excellent. Now, the furosemide—the water pill—we're going to bring that down. You were on 20 mg twice daily, and we're adjusting that. The reason is we want to help with your blood pressure control. Have you been taking it exactly as we had it?
PATIENT: Well, mostly. To be honest I've missed a few doses here and there. Some days I just forget, you know, with everything going on.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's understandable. The dose change we're making should actually help with that—fewer times a day to remember. We've got you on a lower regimen now, and we'll go over exactly what that looks like before you leave.
PATIENT: Okay, that sounds better.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Let me pull up your recent labs here. Your hemoglobin a1c came back at 8.6 percent, which tells us how your type 2 diabetes mellitus has been controlled over the past few months. That's something we want to work on together.
PATIENT: Is that good or bad?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's a little higher than we'd like—the target is usually below 7—so we're going to look at your diet and possibly adjust your diabetes medications at the next visit. But it's not a crisis. You also have chronic kidney disease stage 3, and we're monitoring that closely because it can affect how your body handles medications and fluids.
PATIENT: Stage 3... is that bad?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's moderate. Your kidneys are working at about 30 to 60 percent of normal function, which is why we're keeping an eye on things. That's actually where we need to refer to nephrology—that's a kidney specialist. They can help us make sure we're managing this the right way.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, if that's what I need.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. So we're going to refer to nephrology in 4 weeks, and I'll make sure that appointment gets scheduled. We'll also schedule a follow-up visit with me in 3 months to see how you're doing with all of this—the swelling, the muscle aches, and how your diabetes is managing. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yes, that sounds good. Three months from now?
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's right. We'll send you a reminder, and if anything comes up before then—if that leg swelling gets worse again or you develop any new symptoms—you call us right away. Any questions before we wrap up?
PATIENT: No, I think I've got it. Thanks for walking me through everything.

PATIENT: The thing is, the parking lot was flooded this morning, I had to circle around twice, and the guy at the desk said—
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Yeah, we heard about that. Let's get you back here, though. I'm Dr. Patel. So Aldo, I see here you've been flagged by your primary for some fatigue—not just tired, but severe fatigue—since Monday. Is that right?
PATIENT: That's right. Out of nowhere, Monday morning I just felt like I was dragging. And then on top of it I've been drinking water like I'm living in Arizona or something. Increased thirst, can't really explain it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. And the thirst—when did that start, or was it also since Monday?
PATIENT: No, that's been maybe the last week or so. But the fatigue is what got to me. I couldn't even get through my morning coffee yesterday.
NURSE: Let me grab your vitals while the doctor talks to you. Blood pressure first.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And I also see a note that you've had some mild weight loss about a month ago. Have you noticed that continuing, or has it leveled off?
PATIENT: It's getting better now. I mean, I lost a couple of pounds back then, but I don't think I'm losing any more. At least, my clothes fit the same as they did two weeks ago.
NURSE: Doctor, I'm reading a very high blood pressure reading. One-seventy over one-oh-five.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, let me recheck that. Can you just sit still for another minute?
PATIENT: That doesn't sound good. I mean, it's been fine at home. My machine at home has been normal, mostly in the one-thirties.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I'm confirming the same thing. That's a very high blood pressure reading, and with your fatigue and your thirst on top of that, I want to make sure we're not missing anything here. I'm going to have my colleague check you out in a few minutes—the on-call cardiometabolic clinician.
PATIENT: You think something's wrong with my heart? I don't have chest pain or anything.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Not necessarily your heart right now, but I want to rule out a transient ischemic attack—a TIA—when you tell me your fatigue hit so suddenly. We also need to make sure you don't have a deep vein thrombosis that could be contributing to these symptoms. We need to work that up. Your mother had a stroke, if I'm reading this right?
PATIENT: Yeah, she had a stroke, oh, fifteen years ago maybe. But I'm not having any numbness or anything. My face looks the same to me.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good to hear. But the combination is worth checking. Now, let's talk about your medications, because I also see your blood sugars have been climbing. Your fasting glucose came back at 156 mg/dL, your LDL cholesterol is 148 mg/dL, and I want to check on whether you're experiencing any symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease as well.
PATIENT: My sugar's up? I thought I had that under control with the pills.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's something we need to address. So you have type 2 diabetes mellitus, and I see you're on three medications right now. Let me walk through them. You're on linagliptin 5 mg once daily—are you taking that?
PATIENT: I actually haven't been taking that one for the past week or so. I ran out and didn't refill it. Didn't think it was making much difference anyway.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, well, that might be part of your problem right there. But we're going to adjust linagliptin dose anyway when you see the nurse, so let's not restart it today. Next, canagliflozin 100 mg once daily—how have you been with that one?
PATIENT: Um, I'm not sure, honestly. I don't remember if I've been taking it every day or if I've been skipping it sometimes. I couldn't say for certain.
NURSE: Let me get a refill arranged for that one. We'll make sure you have it for the next month.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. And the atorvastatin 10 mg once daily—tell me about that.
PATIENT: That one I haven't missed. I take it every single day. That one I remember to do as prescribed, no problem.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Great. That one's working well, and we're not going to change it. But here's what I want to happen. I'm not convinced yet that we can explain everything with just the diabetes control and the blood pressure spike today.
PATIENT: So what are you saying? You think I need to come back in or something?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You're going to see my colleague in just a moment. And also, I do want to order follow-up bloodwork—is next week okay for that?
PATIENT: Next week? I guess so, but I'm still not totally convinced I need all these extra visits. Seems like a lot.
NURSE: We're going to adjust linagliptin dose in 4 weeks after we see how you do. But first we need that bloodwork and the evaluation with the on-call clinician today. Do you have any questions before we step out?
PATIENT: No, I—I guess not. I mean, my mother's stroke was a long time ago, and I feel like I'm okay except for the tiredness. But fine. Let's do it. When should I eat breakfast?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Wait until after the bloodwork, actually. They're going to need you fasting. My colleague will be here in a minute.

NURSE: So we've got you down for a post-discharge follow-up today—you're about a week out from the hospital, right? Just want to make sure everything's settling down okay and we're not missing anything.
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds right. It's been... well, it's been a bit rough, honestly. I was expecting to bounce back faster than this.
NURSE: Okay, tell me what's been rough. What's been the biggest thing on your mind?
PATIENT: The sleep, mainly. I mean, I know I had heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and they told me to expect some adjustments, but—I'm just not sleeping. And it's getting worse, you know? For the past few days it's been severe, like I'll lie there for hours and just... nothing. My daughter's been checking in on me because I'm a wreck during the day.
NURSE: Severe difficulty sleeping for the past few days and it's worsening—got it. That's definitely worth paying attention to. Anything else bothering you?
PATIENT: Yeah, there's some nausea. But it's mild, I think. Started last week, and it's just been sitting there, not really getting better or worse. It's annoying more than anything.
NURSE: Mild nausea since last week. And how's the incision? Any pain or concerns with that?
PATIENT: Oh, there's definitely incision pain. It's tender when I move, and some of it's sharp if I reach too far. But I've been trying not to overdo it.
NURSE: That's wise. Let's check your oxygen saturation while we're here.
PATIENT: Sure thing.
NURSE: Okay, I'm getting a reading of 93.
PATIENT: Is that... is that okay?
NURSE: It's acceptable, though we'd like to see it a bit higher. But combined with the difficulty sleeping, we need to think about what's contributing to that. Now, your legs—any swelling at all? Any puffiness?
PATIENT: Not like before. I mean, I had some pretty bad leg swelling after the first procedure, where my ankles got huge, but this time around I'm not seeing anything like that. They're normal-looking to me.
NURSE: Good, that's actually reassuring. And with your hyperlipidemia, have you been able to keep up with diet stuff, or has that been on the back burner with everything going on?
PATIENT: Honestly, it's been hard to think about. But I'm trying. My neighbor brought over a casserole last week—bless her heart, she meant well—and I had to throw it in the freezer because I wasn't sure what was in it.
NURSE: People do mean well. Let's talk through your meds. How are you doing with the ibuprofen?
PATIENT: Um, well, I've been taking it as needed for the incision and everything, but I'll be honest—I've missed a few doses here and there. Some days I just forget by the time I actually need it, and then the pain's already ramped up. But I know we're supposed to be increasing it based on the lab results, right? So I'm trying to be more consistent.
NURSE: Right, so we do want to bump up the ibuprofen to 600 mg as needed. The lab results came back and that's what we're recommending. The key is—try not to skip doses, because if you let the pain build, it's harder to get ahead of it. Set a reminder on your phone if that helps.
PATIENT: Okay, 600 mg as needed. Yeah, I can do that.
NURSE: And the clopidogrel—the blood pressure's been running a little lower than we'd like, so we're actually going to reduce that dose to 75 mg once daily instead of what you were on. How are you doing taking it?
PATIENT: Oh, that one I haven't missed. As prescribed, every single day—I've got it in my morning routine, so I haven't skipped a dose yet.
NURSE: That's perfect. And the acetaminophen 325 mg as needed—keep doing exactly what you're doing there. Are you taking that as prescribed?
PATIENT: Yeah, as prescribed. I'll take one if the pain gets worse, but mostly the ibuprofen is doing the job now.
NURSE: Good. So we need to order follow-up bloodwork to check how you're responding to these adjustments and make sure your heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is stable. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, absolutely. That's fine.
NURSE: I do want to mention—if you ever notice severe shortness of breath, or if things suddenly feel off, you'd want to head to the emergency department rather than wait. You don't need to schedule anything for that, just recognize it if it happens.
PATIENT: Okay, got it. So emergency department if the breathing gets really bad.
NURSE: Exactly. Now, as you start feeling a bit better over the next week, getting a little more movement in—even just a walk around the house or outside if the weather's nice—that can help with the sleep and the overall recovery. Something to think about as you're ready for it.
PATIENT: I mean, I've been sitting around a lot. Maybe I could schedule a follow-up visit for next week just to see how that's working out? See if the walking and everything is helping?
NURSE: That's something you could definitely look into. I'll make sure the bloodwork gets ordered today, and we'll have those results in a few days.
