text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Hi Pedro, it's Sarah from the cardiology clinic. Is this an okay time to talk?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I can talk. What's going on?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So I have your chart here in front of me, and I see you called about your blood pressure medication. But before we get into that, I want to understand what's been happening with you lately. You mentioned some symptoms on the voicemail?
PATIENT: Right, well, I've been having this... I mean, it started yesterday, and I'm feeling short of breath. Like, moderate shortness of breath, and it's actually getting worse, not better.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, that's important. Tell me more about when that started—you said yesterday? And what does it feel like when you notice it?
PATIENT: Yeah, yesterday morning. It's like... I can't catch my breath when I'm walking, or even just going up stairs. And it kind of sits in my chest, you know?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Uh-huh. And has anything else been bothering you? Any chest pain, any swelling anywhere?
PATIENT: Actually, now that you mention it, my legs have been... they look a bit puffy. I noticed it a couple weeks ago, like mild leg swelling, but it's pretty much the same. Hasn't gotten worse or anything.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Mild swelling in both legs, you'd say, and that's been ongoing for a couple weeks ago without really changing. Let me pull up your blood pressure log here—
PATIENT: Mm-hmm.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I'm seeing your most recent reading is 158/96 mmHg. That's running a bit high. Can we talk about your amlodipine? You're supposed to be on 10 mg once daily, correct?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's... okay, I'll be honest with you. I've missed some doses. I sometimes forget to take it, especially when I'm busy at work.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's really helpful you're telling me that. How often do you think you're missing doses? Are we talking once a week, a few times a week?
PATIENT: Maybe... maybe a couple of times a week? I know I should... I mean, I'm just not good at remembering.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. And you have that long-standing hypertension, right? This has been something you've been managing for a while now?
PATIENT: Yeah, they diagnosed me with hypertension years ago. My dad had it too, so...
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Right, that makes sense. Now, what about your carvedilol? The 12.5 mg twice daily—how are you doing with that one?
PATIENT: That one I take as prescribed. I haven't missed a dose on that—I take it every single day, morning and night.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. And your dabigatran, the 75 mg twice daily, how's that going?
PATIENT: Same thing, I'm taking that as prescribed too.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Great. So given what you're telling me—the moderate shortness of breath that started yesterday and is getting worse, the leg swelling, and your blood pressure running high—I'm going to want to refer you to cardiology. I think we need to get a full workup, make sure we're not missing anything.
PATIENT: Cardiology? Do you think it's... I mean, is it serious?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I want to be careful and thorough, that's all. These symptoms together warrant a specialist's eyes. And we'll absolutely schedule a follow-up visit with me as well so we can recheck your blood pressure and work on that amlodipine refill to make sure you're staying consistent with it.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, that makes sense. I'll do the cardiology thing.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Perfect. And one more thing—I also want to talk about your psoriasis, since you've got that going on. But really, in the meantime, cutting back on salt is going to be important, especially with your hypertension and what we're seeing with your legs. When you come in for that follow-up visit, we'll have the care coordinator talk through some practical ways to cut back on salt. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can try that. I probably do use too much.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: You're not alone in that. So we've got a plan: refer to cardiology, schedule a follow-up visit with me, arrange that amlodipine refill, and the coordinator will talk salt at your next appointment. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, sounds good. Thanks.

PATIENT: So I've been drinking water like crazy, and I mean constantly. My mouth just feels permanently dry, and I keep going to the bathroom, which is… I don't know, it's getting old. But that's not even the worst part.
PATIENT: My feet have been numb. Like, the bottoms of my feet, they're just kind of tingly and dead feeling. Started about a month ago, but I think it's actually getting better now, so maybe it's nothing.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Walk me through what you mean by numb. When you say it's mild now, have you noticed any pattern to when it happens, or is it constant?
PATIENT: It's there when I wake up, mostly. And if I sit for too long it gets worse. But yeah, mild seems right. Most of the time I can ignore it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And the increased thirst—have you had any weight loss, any change in how you're feeling energy-wise, any fatigue that might suggest anemia, or any other symptoms along with that?
PATIENT: Honestly, my energy's been okay. No weight loss that I can tell. I'm just constantly parched. It's like my body forgot how to retain water or something. My sister jokes that I've got a bladder the size of a pea now.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Any visual changes at all? Sometimes that can go hand in hand with what you're describing.
PATIENT: Oh, yeah, actually. My vision's been blurry. Severe, really. It started about a month ago—no, wait, for the past few days it got worse. But it's getting better already, so I wasn't sure it was worth mentioning.
CARE_COORDINATOR: How quickly did that happen, the vision change? Did it come on all at once or gradual?
PATIENT: The past few days it was just suddenly there when I woke up. But like I said, it's already improving, so.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Any chest pain or anything in your chest that you've noticed?
PATIENT: No. Nothing like that.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. Let's talk about your medications. Where are we at with the simvastatin—the cholesterol one you take at bedtime?
PATIENT: 20 mg at bedtime, yeah. I've been taking it as prescribed every single day, no skipped doses or anything.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. We'll get that refilled for you, but I'm thinking we should adjust simvastatin dose as part of your care plan today. I'd like to see how you do on a slightly higher dose over the next four weeks.
PATIENT: Higher? Is that because of the blurred vision or the numbness or—I mean, is something going on that I should be worried about?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: These symptoms—the thirst, the blurred vision, the numbness—they're pointing us in a direction where we want to be more aggressive with your cardiometabolic management overall. The statin helps with that. It's preventive. We'll monitor closely at your next visit.
PATIENT: Okay, okay. I can do that.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: What about the semaglutide? The injection you do once weekly?
PATIENT: Yeah, the 0.25 mg. I've been doing that as prescribed every single week. No missed doses there.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Are you still using it actively, or has that tailed off?
PATIENT: Um, I mean, I have my pens, and I'm doing them. But honestly, I'm not even sure if my insurance is still covering it or if it's actually active. I just… I do what I have in front of me, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We can look into that verification piece. We'll make sure we know what's going on with that prescription before your next visit. No change to how you're taking it for now.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And the linagliptin, 5 mg once daily—how's that one going?
PATIENT: That one I've, uh, I've definitely missed some doses on that. I keep forgetting to take it in the morning. Some days I remember, some days I don't.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That happens to a lot of people. Would it help if we set something up—a reminder on your phone, maybe a pill organizer? Something to make it easier to catch?
PATIENT: Yeah, honestly that might help. The pill organizer thing—my dad uses one of those and he never forgets now, so I figured I was too young for it, but clearly I'm not.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We're going to schedule a follow-up visit with us in 4 weeks. That'll give us time to see how you're doing on the adjusted dose, and we can check in on those symptoms and run some labs if needed.
PATIENT: So in 4 weeks. Okay. And you guys will call me or send me a message about it?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We'll send you an appointment reminder and have you get checked in at the desk. If you don't hear from us in the next few days, just give us a call and we'll get you locked in.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Before you go, I want you to keep an eye on that vision and the numbness in the feet over the next week or two. If they get worse instead of better, if you have any severe vision changes that don't improve, or if you notice anything else new, you call us or come in sooner. Fair?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. Thanks.

PHYSICIAN: We've got you down for medication reconciliation today—should take about thirty minutes. Before we dive in, I wanted to check: are you still at the same address we have on file, or has that changed?
PATIENT: No, same place. Been there for... what is it, Mariko? Seven years now? She says eight, but I think it's seven. Either way, hasn't moved.
PHYSICIAN: All right, good. So let me start with what's brought you in today. You mentioned to the front desk that you've been having some numbness and you're feeling pretty tired?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's the thing. The numbness in the feet—it's mild, really—started, oh, a couple weeks ago. But it's, um, it's not getting any better. Actually it's getting worse, to be honest.
PHYSICIAN: Getting worse. Okay. And when you say mild right now, how many days a week would you say you're noticing it?
PATIENT: Pretty much every day now. And then the fatigue—that's been going on about a month ago. I mean, about a month. That one's, well... it's severe. Some mornings I can barely get out of bed, and I'll do maybe one or two things and I just hit a wall.
PHYSICIAN: Is that fatigue getting worse as time goes on, or is it staying about the same?
PATIENT: It's getting worse. Well, no—actually, it's the same. It comes and goes but it's pretty much where it was a month ago. Not really changing much, honestly.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, so about the same—not really changing. That helps. Have you had any fever with this, or any night sweats?
PATIENT: No fever. Definitely not. I'd know if I had a fever.
PHYSICIAN: Fair enough. Let me get your weight while we're at it. Can you step on the scale?
PATIENT: Sure. I think I'm still around 212 pounds, actually. Been stable there for a bit.
PHYSICIAN: All right, 212 pounds—that matches what we had. And let me get a blood pressure real quick here... okay, so we're at 128/82 mmHg.
PATIENT: That's not too bad, is it?
PHYSICIAN: That's actually pretty reasonable. So let's talk about what might be going on. You have type 2 diabetes mellitus, and you've also got anemia in your chart. Do those diagnoses—do those feel accurate to you?
PATIENT: The diabetes, yeah, that's been there for years. The anemia, I'm not—I mean, I guess my iron is low or something? I never really understood what that meant for me. But my blood doctor—well, my old colleague actually, not a doctor, my colleague Tom, he had something called plantar fasciitis and he couldn't walk for weeks. I was fine though, my feet were never that bad.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, those are different things entirely. The anemia is a blood count issue, not a foot problem. But I'm glad we're on the same page about the diabetes. Now, let's go through your medications. I want to make sure we're taking exactly what we think we are. Are you still on sacubitril-valsartan?
PATIENT: Uh... I'm not taking that one. I stopped taking it a few months ago. Too many pills, and I wasn't sure it was doing anything anyway.
PHYSICIAN: Right. We need to get you back on it, though—it's important for your heart and your blood pressure control. It's 49 mg twice daily. Let me write you a refill. What about spironolactone?
PATIENT: The one that's—what, for the blood pressure too?
PHYSICIAN: It helps with that, yes. 12.5 mg once daily. Are you taking that?
PATIENT: I haven't been taking that one either. I stopped after a couple weeks because it made me feel dizzy.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, we'll leave that off the active list for now. And then there's your insulin. You're on insulin glargine, 24 units once daily—how are you doing with that one?
PATIENT: That one I'm actually taking, yeah. I do it every single day, haven't missed it. I know that one matters for my blood sugar.
PHYSICIAN: Good. That's what I like to hear. You're taking it exactly as prescribed?
PATIENT: Yes, sir. Every morning.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. So we've got the insulin glargine solid, we're going to restart you on the sacubitril-valsartan—I'm getting that filled right now—and we'll hold the spironolactone.
PATIENT: Is the numbness in my feet going to go away if I take that sacubitril thing?
PHYSICIAN: The numbness might be related to your anemia and your diabetes, actually. That's something we need to—
PATIENT: [pause]—
PHYSICIAN: —look into more carefully. There's a knock on the door—
PATIENT: Come in if you need to.
PHYSICIAN: —okay, never mind, probably just the staff. Anyway, given what you're experiencing, I think we should probably float the idea of doing some follow-up bloodwork next week, if that's something you'd be willing to consider. And it might also be helpful if you could start to monitor blood pressure at home over the next week, just to get a baseline sense of how it's tracking for you. Does that feel doable?
PATIENT: I can try. I don't have one of those cuff things, but I could pick one up.
PHYSICIAN: That would be great. And we'll get you those prescriptions in order before you leave today.

NURSE: I'm so sorry I'm running a bit late this afternoon—thank you for being patient with us. Let me just pull up your chart here. So you're in for a respiratory followup today. How are you doing?
PATIENT: Oh, I'm all right, dear. A little tired, but you know, at ninety-one, that's not exactly news.
NURSE: I hear that. Well, let's talk about what's been going on. I see you've mentioned some chest tightness. Can you tell me about that?
PATIENT: Yes, it's been happening for the past few days. Nothing terrible, mind you—just mild chest tightness, really. Comes and goes.
NURSE: And have you noticed anything else along with it? Any sweating, particularly at night?
PATIENT: Oh yes, actually. I've been having night sweats. Wakes me up sometimes. I'll have to change my nightgown, it's quite damp.
NURSE: Mm, that's worth keeping an eye on. And your breathing—how's that been?
PATIENT: A bit off, if I'm honest. I get moderate shortness of breath, especially when I'm moving around. Started three days ago, actually, and it's... well, it's about the same as it was then. Not getting worse, but not better either.
NURSE: So three days ago was when that began, and it's been fairly steady since then. Okay. Let me ask you about your asthma. Have you been doing okay managing that?
PATIENT: My asthma's been with me for so long now, I barely think about it most days. I use my albuterol as needed—usually 1 puffs—and I haven't missed a single dose when I need it, so I'm taking it exactly as prescribed.
NURSE: Good, good. And the fluticasone-salmeterol—the inhaler you use twice daily—how's that going?
PATIENT: Well, I'll be honest, I've missed a few doses here and there. I sometimes forget in the morning, or I'll skip it if I'm not feeling as tight-chested. It was causing me some side effects anyway, so I haven't been as careful about it.
NURSE: What kind of side effects were you noticing?
PATIENT: Oh, my mouth gets a bit sore, and sometimes my throat feels raw. Makes me not want to use it, I suppose.
NURSE: That's something we can actually address. We might be able to bring your dose down, which could help with that. Now, I also see you were just started on montelukast. That's a newer one for you, right?
PATIENT: Yes, it's quite new. To tell you the truth, I'm not sure exactly how I've been taking it. Is it the one I take at bedtime? I couldn't say for certain.
NURSE: It is—montelukast 10 mg at bedtime. It's meant to help reduce inflammation in your airways, sort of a preventative medicine. Let me just look up the timing of when that was prescribed for you. [types] Okay, so you just got that recently. Have you noticed any change since starting it?
PATIENT: Not particularly, but then it hasn't been very long, has it? What does it do exactly? The inflammation part—is that what's causing my tightness?
NURSE: Inflammation is basically swelling inside your airways, which makes them narrower and harder to breathe through. That's often what causes the tightness and shortness of breath you're experiencing. Montelukast helps calm that down over time, but you're right—it takes a bit to work. I do want to mention, though, that your sister had some health issues I want to be mindful of.
PATIENT: Oh? Which sister are you talking about?
NURSE: Your older sister—I see she had colon cancer, is that right?
PATIENT: Yes, that was some years ago now. Fortunately, she's doing well. But yes, she did have colon cancer.
NURSE: Well, I'm glad she's doing well. That's good to know for your own health history. Now, given everything you're telling me—the chest tightness, the shortness of breath, the night sweats, and the fact that your symptoms are hanging on—I think we should refer to pulmonology. They're the lung specialists and they can give you a more comprehensive workup. Does that sound all right to you?
PATIENT: Yes, I think that's a good idea. I'd like to get to the bottom of this.
NURSE: Great. And we're also going to adjust fluticasone-salmeterol dose downward from 1 puffs given those side effects you mentioned. We'll lower it and see if your symptoms improve and the irritation settles. We'll have the pulmonology team weigh in on your overall management too.
PATIENT: That sounds fair to me. Thank you.

PATIENT: —and then the sky was just so grey this morning, I thought maybe it would actually rain for once, but it didn't, it just—
PHYSICIAN: Yeah, we could definitely use it. So, I'm glad we have time to catch up today. Your chart shows you're dealing with a couple of things right now. Let's start with what's been bothering you most.
PATIENT: Well, I've had this headache, and it's been pretty severe. It came on a couple weeks ago and it's actually getting better, so that's good. But I'm also noticing muscle aches, you know, mild ones, just in my shoulders and neck mostly.
PHYSICIAN: When did those muscle aches start?
PATIENT: Yesterday, I think. Or maybe the day before. It was definitely yesterday though.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, so yesterday. And they've been about the same since then—no worse, no better?
PATIENT: Yeah, they're pretty consistent. Just sitting there, kind of nagging at me. Not getting any better but not worse either.
PHYSICIAN: Have you noticed any dizziness along with this?
PATIENT: Actually, yes, a little bit. Not terrible, but when I stand up too fast, I feel a bit lightheaded.
PHYSICIAN: Got it. And your vision—has that been clear, or have you had any blurred vision?
PATIENT: No, my vision's been fine. It's not like three months ago when I had that episode where everything was really fuzzy and I couldn't see properly. Nothing like that now.
PHYSICIAN: Good to know. Let's take your blood pressure and see where things stand. Let me just get that reading for you.
PATIENT: Sure. Um, one thing—my cousin, she's been dealing with hypertension for years now. I've been a bit worried, you know, whether that's something I should be concerned about too.
PHYSICIAN: It's smart that you're thinking about family history. Let me get that reading. Okay, I'm getting 132/84 mmHg. That's not bad today.
PATIENT: Okay, so that's normal-ish?
PHYSICIAN: It's in a reasonable range, especially given that you have the chronic kidney disease stage 3 and the hyperlipidemia we've been managing. Speaking of which, let's talk about your medications. You're on hydralazine—how have you been taking that?
PATIENT: Um, the hydralazine, I'm not sure if I'm being honest. I think I'm taking it most days, but I don't remember if it's supposed to be every time, or... I couldn't say exactly.
PHYSICIAN: So you're not totally sure about the schedule. That's actually really important because it's 25 mg three times daily that I need you on. It's not something you can skip—it needs to be consistent for it to work properly.
PATIENT: Oh, okay. Three times daily. That's more than I thought I was doing. I think I've just been taking it... whenever. Can I get a refill and maybe some sort of reminder system or something?
PHYSICIAN: Absolutely, I can arrange that refill for you today. And a pill organizer might really help you stay on track. Now, your levothyroxine—how's that going?
PATIENT: That one I've got down. I'm taking it 100 mcg once daily, every single day. Haven't missed it.
PHYSICIAN: That's excellent. You're doing exactly what you should be doing there, so we're not changing anything with that one. We'll just keep it as it is.
PATIENT: Good. I'm glad at least that one's working.
PHYSICIAN: So here's what I want us to think about. You've got mild muscle aches and a severe headache that is fortunately getting better. The dizziness when you stand—that could be related to how you're taking your blood pressure medication. And with your chronic kidney disease and your hyperlipidemia, I want to make sure we're keeping a closer eye on things. I'd like to reduce alcohol, if you're drinking at all. I know it's not always easy, but it can really help with blood pressure and kidney function.
PATIENT: I mean... I have a glass of wine now and then. More than that on weekends maybe. I was worried you'd say that, but I guess I can try to cut back.
PHYSICIAN: I appreciate you being open to it. Let's make that one of the things we work on at your next visit. We should also order follow-up bloodwork to see how your kidney function and cholesterol are looking. And I'd like to schedule a follow-up visit so we can reassess everything.
PATIENT: When would that be, do you think?
PHYSICIAN: Why don't we aim for about six weeks from now? The care coordinator will help coordinate that along with the bloodwork. They'll reach out to you with the dates.
PATIENT: Okay, that works. And I'll try to remember the hydralazine three times daily going forward.

PATIENT: Here I am again. Third time this month—you guys must be getting tired of seeing my face.
NURSE: Not at all. We're glad you came back in. I want to go over those lab results from last week and talk about how you've been feeling. You mentioned fatigue when you scheduled the appointment—is that still your main concern?
PATIENT: Yeah, it's the fatigue that's really getting to me. I can barely make it through the afternoon without wanting to nap. I've been dragging for weeks now.
NURSE: Okay, and nothing's really changed in terms of your routine or stress at home?
PATIENT: No, not really. Work's the same as always. Though my lawn guy—you know, the man who cuts my lawn—he had a stroke last month, so I've been doing it myself, which is exhausting, but I don't think that's the main thing.
NURSE: That must have been stressful for him. But let's focus on you for now. I'm looking at your results, and your cholesterol levels are still elevated. We're managing your hyperlipidemia, but I want to make sure we're on top of it. Are you still taking your medications regularly?
PATIENT: Well, that's where it gets a little fuzzy, to be honest. With the 40 mg pantoprazole, I'm not sure how I've been taking it—I know it's supposed to be once daily, but I think I've been skipping it some days. And we're holding it now anyway, right?
NURSE: Right, we're holding the pantoprazole for now. But I want to understand the losartan better. You're on 100 mg once daily, correct? How have you been with that one?
PATIENT: I don't remember, honestly. I mean, I take it most mornings, but I couldn't say if it's every single day. Some weeks are better than others.
NURSE: That inconsistency could be contributing to some of what you're feeling. The losartan's been giving you those side effects we talked about, hasn't it?
PATIENT: Yes, the dizziness. It comes and goes. Sometimes I feel lightheaded in the mornings.
NURSE: That's part of why we're looking at bringing the dose down. We might adjust losartan dose to see if that helps with the dizziness and potentially with your overall energy. Does that sound reasonable to you?
PATIENT: Yeah, that makes sense. Anything to feel a bit more like myself.
NURSE: Good. Now, you also reported some heartburn when you came in last time. How's that been?
PATIENT: It's moderate heartburn, and it started about a month ago. It's pretty much the same, you know? Not getting worse, but not better either.
NURSE: About a month ago—that tracks with when you stopped taking the pantoprazole. The moderate heartburn you're describing, is it affecting your sleep or your ability to eat?
PATIENT: Not too bad during the day. It's worse at night, especially if I have wine with dinner.
NURSE: That's something we should talk about then. How much are you drinking on a typical week?
PATIENT: Maybe four or five glasses over the week. Nothing crazy, but I do like my wine.
NURSE: I hear you. That's not excessive, but given the heartburn and some of the fatigue, we might want to reduce alcohol a bit. Does that feel doable?
PATIENT: I can try. Maybe cut back to two or three a week?
NURSE: That would be a good start, and I think you'll probably notice a difference in how you feel. Now, your glucose levels came back a bit high on your fasting test—nothing alarming yet, but I want to rule out type 2 diabetes mellitus. I'm not convinced we need to jump to a diagnosis, but I'd like to see you come back in six weeks for a repeat test.
PATIENT: So you're saying I might have diabetes?
NURSE: I'm saying we need to keep an eye on it. One elevated result doesn't make a diagnosis, but with your hyperlipidemia and the fatigue you're experiencing, it's worth monitoring closely. Does that make sense?
PATIENT: Yeah, I get it. Better to catch it early if something's there.
NURSE: Exactly. And one more thing—on the pain scale of zero to ten, you rated your fatigue as a 7 when you checked in. Is that still where you're at?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds about right. Some days it's a bit better, but mostly it's hovering around there.

PATIENT: I'm so sorry, I meant to call you back last week about those labs but it completely slipped my mind. You know how it is—I've had so much on my plate.
NURSE: Oh, don't worry about that at all, Laura. These things happen. I'm glad you're here now. So how have things been going since you left the hospital?
PATIENT: Honestly, it's been rough. I've been dealing with some pretty severe fatigue since yesterday, and I'm not sleeping well at all. Like, I can barely get through the day.
NURSE: I hear you. Let's talk about that. You mentioned the severe fatigue started yesterday—is that when you first noticed it, or was there something before that?
PATIENT: No, yesterday is really when it hit me. Before that I was managing okay, but now I just feel completely wiped out. And the sleep thing—that's been going on for about a month ago now, and it's getting worse instead of better.
NURSE: A month, got it. So the difficulty sleeping has been severe and it's been worsening. And the fatigue is new as of yesterday but still quite intense. Are you noticing any changes in your appetite?
PATIENT: Actually, yes. I've been dealing with poor appetite for a couple weeks ago, and it's not extreme, just mild, but it seems to be getting worse. I'm just not interested in eating like I used to be.
NURSE: Okay. Let me check your vitals real quick. Your heart rate is 112, which is a bit elevated. Given your history with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, that's something we'll want to keep an eye on.
PATIENT: Yeah, I know that's high for me. I've been feeling the palpitations too, kind of fluttery.
NURSE: We'll definitely address that. Let me ask about your medications. How are you getting on with everything you're taking?
PATIENT: Well, the naproxen—I've been taking that 250 mg twice daily exactly as prescribed, haven't missed a single dose. But honestly, it's been giving me a stomach ache, so we talked about bringing that down, remember?
NURSE: Right, yes, we did discuss that because of the side effects. We'll go ahead and reduce that. And the metoprolol tartrate, 25 mg twice daily—how's that been?
PATIENT: Oh, um... I have to be honest, I've missed some doses. Work's been crazy and I just forget sometimes. Not every day, but yeah, I've skipped it a few times.
NURSE: I appreciate you being straight with me. The thing is, with your heart failure, it's really important to keep that consistent. We're going to keep the metoprolol tartrate at 25 mg twice daily, but let's see if we can find a way to make it easier to remember—maybe a pill organizer or an alarm on your phone?
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. A pill organizer might help. I can try that.
NURSE: Good. Now, I know you mentioned your aunt had some heart issues. Do you remember what exactly she was diagnosed with?
PATIENT: She had coronary artery disease. Spent a lot of time dealing with that before she passed. I think about that sometimes, you know, that it runs in the family.
NURSE: It's wise to be aware of that family history. It's one reason we want to keep a close watch on your own heart health. Now, one thing I want to talk about is reducing alcohol. I know you enjoy a drink now and then—
PATIENT: I mean, it's not like I'm drinking a ton, but... I guess I could cut back. I'm not sure how much difference it'll make, but if you think it'll help...
NURSE: I do think it'll help, especially combined with everything else. We can reduce alcohol over the next three months and see how you're feeling.
PATIENT: Alright, I'll give it a shot. So what else are we doing?
NURSE: We're going to order follow-up bloodwork in four weeks to check how your levels are looking with the medication changes and the lifestyle adjustments. And I want to schedule a follow-up visit with the physician in three months so we can see how you're progressing overall.
PATIENT: Three months sounds good to me. And you said the labs in four weeks, not six?
NURSE: Four weeks, yes. We want to check in a bit sooner given what we're seeing today. Does that work for you?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's fine. I'll make sure I don't forget this time.
NURSE: Great. So just to recap: we're reducing the naproxen to help with those side effects, keeping the metoprolol tartrate the same at 25 mg twice daily, reducing alcohol, and we'll get that bloodwork done in four weeks. Then the physician will see you again in three months. You feel okay about all that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I do. I'm feeling a bit better already just talking it through. Hopefully things'll improve.

text:
PHYSICIAN: So I'm looking at your chart here and it says your shingles cleared up last year, but I want to make sure that's accurate—you haven't had any recurrence or lingering pain from that, correct?
PATIENT: No, that's right. I mean, it was rough when I had it, but that's all behind me now. That was, what, eighteen months ago? More than a year. I'm good on that front.
PHYSICIAN: Good. And what's brought you in today, or I suppose what's been concerning you enough to schedule this visit?
PATIENT: Well, I've just been exhausted. Like, really worn out. And it's not the usual tiredness—it's been moderate fatigue for the past few days now, and I'm starting to wonder if something's not right.
PHYSICIAN: Moderate fatigue for the past few days. Okay. Help me understand what that feels like for you. Does it hit you all day long, or is it worse at certain times?
PATIENT: It's pretty much all day. I wake up tired, and by mid-afternoon I just want to collapse. I've got things I need to do, but it's hard to get motivated.
PHYSICIAN: Has anything changed recently—work stress, sleep, diet, or anything like that?
PATIENT: Sleep's been terrible, actually. I can't sleep through the night anymore. And I'm not eating much—I've got moderate poor appetite, started about three days ago and it's getting worse. Yesterday I barely touched lunch.
PHYSICIAN: The poor appetite came on at the same time as the fatigue?
PATIENT: Pretty much, yeah. And the sleep thing—difficulty sleeping—that's been... I don't know, a few weeks now? But this week it's gotten way worse.
PHYSICIAN: I want to circle back to something. You mentioned motivation being hard. Have you noticed your mood shifting at all—feeling down, hopeless, losing interest in things you normally enjoy?
PATIENT: Um. Yeah, I guess. Some days are definitely darker than others. I'm still going through the motions, but... I don't know. It feels like everything takes twice the energy it should.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's a reasonable question. Our care coordinator will work with your insurance to verify coverage when they call to schedule. Speaking of which, I also want to schedule a follow-up visit with me here at the next visit—we'll want to touch base in a few days after pulmonology sees you and gets back to us. Does that work?
PATIENT: A few days? That seems fast. But if it's pneumonia, I guess we shouldn't wait around. Okay, yes. I mean, is there anything I should be doing now? Anything that will help?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: For now, rest, stay hydrated, and please keep taking your medications as best you can. We may start you on an antibiotic once pulmonology confirms the diagnosis—they might see things on imaging that help us be more certain. And try to get what sleep you can even with the night sweats. Our care coordinator will call you tomorrow with those referral details and to schedule that follow-up visit.
PATIENT: Okay. And just to confirm—you think this is community-acquired pneumonia?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Based on your symptoms and the exam findings, that's my working diagnosis, yes. But we need the specialists to confirm and help guide treatment. Any questions for me?
PATIENT: No, I think I understand. Thank you. I appreciate you taking this seriously.

PATIENT: My feet have been acting up something fierce. There's this numbness in the feet, you know, mild at first but it's been there for the past few days now, not really getting worse or better, just sitting there like a visitor who won't leave.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Tell me more about that—when you say numbness, are you getting tingling too, or is it more of a dead feeling?
PATIENT: It's more like—I can feel things are there, but it's like my feet are wearing thick socks that aren't there, if that makes sense. And honestly, I've also been absolutely knackered. The severe fatigue started last week and it's only just beginning to get better, thank God.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He's been sleeping eleven, twelve hours some nights. I had to practically drag him out of bed yesterday morning to take his insulin. Which reminds me—we need to talk about whether he's actually keeping up with all his medications because I'm not always sure.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's a really important point to address. Let's start there—Cian, walk me through what you're actually taking day to day. Your insulin aspart, for instance—how are you managing that?
PATIENT: The insulin aspart—I'm doing 4 units with meals. Every single day, no missing it. Well, actually, no, I'm sorry, it's not 4 units, it's 10 units with meals. I've been taking it as prescribed, don't worry.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay, good—so 10 units with meals, that's the right dose. And you're not having any trouble with the injections themselves? Pain at the site or anything like that?
PATIENT: No, that's fine. The needle's small enough. My brother, he's terrified of needles—even watches the ceiling during blood draws—but I've gotten used to it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And the dulaglutide, the 3 mg once weekly injection—how's that going?
PATIENT: Ah, well, I'm not taking that one anymore. I stopped taking it a while back.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: You never told me you weren't taking it. When did this happen?
PATIENT: A few months now. It was upsetting my stomach, and I just... didn't feel like I needed it anymore. Probably foolish, but there you are.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We'll review that, but I want to circle back to what's happening with your sitagliptin—the 50 mg once daily tablet. How consistently are you taking that?
PATIENT: I've missed a few doses, I'll be honest with you. Some days I just forget. The pill bottle sits there and I look right past it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: When you skip doses, is it more a matter of forgetting, or are there days you actively choose not to take it?
PATIENT: Mostly forgetting. Sometimes it's the afternoon and I've already skipped the morning, and then I think, well, what's the point now. I know that doesn't sound like the best strategy.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: I'm glad you're being straight with me. Let's talk about something else that's come up—you mentioned your feet and the fatigue, but I also want to ask: have you noticed any increase in your thirst recently?
PATIENT: Actually, yes. There's been moderate increased thirst over the weekend, and I've been filling my water glass more often than usual. I thought maybe it was just the weather.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Let me check your most recent blood work here. Your hemoglobin a1c came back at 6.8 percent, which is actually pretty reasonable, but it tells me we need to look at your medication adherence more carefully and make sure you're properly supported. On top of that, the numbness in your feet—that concerns me given your history. Have you had any formal assessment for osteoarthritis in your lower extremities?
PATIENT: I've had osteoarthritis for years now, mostly in my knees and hips, gets worse on damp days. But the feet thing—no, I haven't been told that's arthritis.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: The numbness might be separate—could be a nerve-related issue. Here's what I want to do: I'd like to refer to endocrinology. They can help us get your metabolic control sorted and investigate the numbness more thoroughly. Does that sound okay to you?
PATIENT: Yeah, I'm willing to do that. Should help, I reckon. At my age, another specialist is just another card in the collection—might as well add the endocrinologist to the roster.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: How soon will that referral happen? And what should I be watching for in the meantime?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: The endocrinology referral will be sent out today, and I'd expect them to see you within 3 months. In that time, I want to schedule a follow-up visit in 3 months as well, so we can check in on your medications and see if we need to make any adjustments. In the meantime, can you both work on a system to help with the sitagliptin doses—maybe a pill organizer or a phone reminder?
PATIENT: I can try that. A pill organizer would probably help. And I'll keep taking the insulin aspart exactly as it is.

NURSE: Okay, so I've got here that you were discharged three weeks ago with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and atrial fibrillation. How are you managing at home?
PATIENT: Um, honestly, I'm just... I'm really tired all the time. The fatigue is just relentless, and I can't sleep properly at night. It's been a couple weeks ago that this started getting really bad.
NURSE: The difficulty sleeping started a couple weeks ago—okay. And is it still as bad as when it first came on, or has that been improving at all?
PATIENT: No, it's actually getting better, thank God. It's moderate right now, not like before. But the fatigue is still there, you know?
NURSE: Sure, the fatigue is persisting. Let me just take your vitals real quick.
PATIENT: Yeah, go ahead.
NURSE: Okay, your oxygen saturation is 93, and your heart rate is 104. Both are reasonable for now, but the heart rate's something we'll want to keep tracking.
PATIENT: Is that... is that normal? The heart rate?
NURSE: For someone with atrial fibrillation, we see that kind of rate pretty often. What we're looking for is that it stays relatively steady, and it's not spiking further. Does that make sense?
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. That makes sense.
NURSE: Now, you mentioned the fatigue and the sleep trouble. Are you having any night sweats?
PATIENT: Not since the spring, no. I had that back then but not anymore.
NURSE: Good to know. How's your appetite been? Any changes there?
PATIENT: Mild, I guess. Just mild poor appetite, about a month ago I noticed it starting. But again, it's getting better. Some days I eat fine.
NURSE: Mild poor appetite about a month ago—and improving. That's helpful. Let's talk about your medications. You're on warfarin, and we've adjusted that dose downward. Are you taking it as prescribed?
PATIENT: Yes, every single day. I haven't missed a dose. But honestly, I was getting some side effects from the higher dose, and I'm glad it's coming down.
NURSE: That makes sense. The warfarin at 7.5 mg once daily is the new dose, and we made that change because of the side effects you were experiencing. You're staying compliant, and that's important.
PATIENT: Yeah, I get it. What about the tramadol? My pain—
NURSE: Right, the tramadol. We're actually increasing that. You'll be taking 50 mg as needed, and—
PATIENT: Wait, I'm not sure how I've been taking it, to be honest. I don't remember if I've been keeping track of the doses properly.
NURSE: Okay, that's important to clarify. The new plan is 50 mg as needed. We're bumping it up because you had some side effects on the lower dose, and this should help without causing the same reactions. Can you try to keep a little log of when you take it?
PATIENT: I can try, yeah. That'll help me remember better.
NURSE: And then there's the furosemide—the water pill at 40 mg. I see that you're not taking it anymore. Is that right?
PATIENT: Yeah, I stopped taking it about two weeks ago. I felt like it wasn't helping and I was just... I don't know, it wasn't working for me.
NURSE: Understood. You haven't been taking the furosemide. That's actually fine—we've made the decision to discontinue it. Just want to make sure we're on the same page about—
PATIENT: Yeah, we are. I'm not taking it.
NURSE: Good. Now, one more thing. I want to circle back to the alcohol. How's your drinking been since discharge?
PATIENT: I mean, I've had a glass of wine here and there, but nothing crazy. Though with the heart thing, I know I should probably be more careful.
NURSE: Exactly. We really do need to reduce alcohol, especially with the atrial fibrillation and the heart failure. Can you commit to cutting back further over the next month?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. I'll be more strict about it.
NURSE: Excellent. And I'd like to schedule a follow-up visit in 4 weeks so we can recheck everything, make sure the medication adjustments are working—oh, one second.
PATIENT: Sure.
NURSE: Sorry about that. Yes, so let's schedule a follow-up visit in 4 weeks. Does that work with your schedule?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's fine. Four weeks sounds good.
NURSE: Perfect. One last thing—I know your father had type 2 diabetes mellitus, right?
PATIENT: Yeah, he did. He's actually been managing it pretty well these days. Why, do you think I should be worried about that?
NURSE: Not worried, just wanting to keep it on our radar given the family history. We'll keep monitoring your glucose levels at your follow-ups. Sound fair?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds fair.

text:
NURSE: I'm so sorry I'm running a bit late today—there was a mix-up with the schedule. But let's get right into it. You're in for your respiratory followup, is that right?
PATIENT: Yes, that's right. I've been having some trouble, especially at night.
NURSE: Okay, let's talk about that. What's been happening?
PATIENT: Well, the night sweats started three days ago. They were really bad at first—I mean severe—but I have to say they're getting better now. Still waking up all clammy though.
NURSE: That sounds miserable. And how often are you waking up?
PATIENT: Maybe once or twice a night. Last night wasn't as bad, so like I said, it does seem to be improving.
NURSE: Good to hear that's settling down. What about your cough?
PATIENT: Oh, the cough is worse. It started yesterday and it's been moderate, really, maybe getting a bit worse as the day goes on. This morning wasn't too bad, but by afternoon it picks up.
NURSE: Is it a dry cough, or are you bringing anything up?
PATIENT: Mostly dry. Sometimes a little mucus, but mostly just irritating.
NURSE: And have you noticed any chest pain at all with it?
PATIENT: No, thank goodness, no chest pain. I was a bit worried about that, but nothing like that has happened, so I'm relieved.
NURSE: That's good. But you have had some tightness in the chest, haven't you?
PATIENT: Oh yes, the chest tightness. It started a couple weeks ago. It's mild, really—doesn't bother me much. It's just sort of there, you know, about the same as it has been.
NURSE: Is it worse with activity, or does it come and go?
PATIENT: It comes and goes. Mostly when I'm worrying about things. I do have generalized anxiety disorder, as you know, and when my mind gets going, that's usually when I feel it.
NURSE: That makes sense. The anxiety can definitely contribute to that sensation. Well, given your asthma and everything, let's get a peak flow reading. Let me get you set up with the device here.
PATIENT: Okay, I remember how to do it, I think. Blow hard, right?
NURSE: That's it. Nice and hard. Alright, let me check... that reads 320 L/min. That's actually quite respectable.
PATIENT: Is that good?
NURSE: It's solid for you, yes. Now let's talk about your medications. How are you getting on with the azithromycin? We've actually been adjusting your dose down because of some side effects, haven't we?
PATIENT: Right, the antibiotic. I haven't been the best at taking it, to be honest. I've missed some doses. But I'm willing to do better.
NURSE: That's okay. Hopefully the lower dose will help with the side effects. So we'll do adjust azithromycin dose to bring that down further. You should be taking 250 mg once daily now. And the prednisone—how are you managing that?
PATIENT: The prednisone? I'm not sure if I've been taking it regularly. Some days I remember, some days I don't remember. I take so many pills...
NURSE: That's a common one. Well, we're going to keep you on the same dose. You're at 20 mg once daily, and I'm going to keep it exactly as-is for now, okay?
PATIENT: Okay, so no changes to that one?
NURSE: That's right. Now, I want to have you monitor blood pressure at home. Do you have a cuff?
PATIENT: Yes, my daughter got me one last year. I can do that.
NURSE: Great. Take it a couple times a week and just write down the numbers. And one more thing—I'm going to refer you to nephrology. I want them to take a look at your kidney function, especially given everything going on. Is that alright?
PATIENT: Nephrology? What's that again?
NURSE: Kidney doctors. They specialize in kidney problems and can make sure your kidneys are doing okay, especially with the medications you're on.
PATIENT: Oh, I see. Yes, that sounds fine. Whatever you think is necessary.

PHYSICIAN: So the waiting room was— did you have to wait very long, or did we...
PATIENT: Oh, maybe ten minutes? It was fine. The music was nice, actually.
PHYSICIAN: Good, good. Well, let's get into things. You're here for a post-discharge check-in, and I see the ER sent over notes about a couple of concerns. Tell me what's been happening since you got out.
PATIENT: Yeah, so the main thing is I've had a severe headache. Like, pretty much every day, and it's not going away. And then there's this dizziness I've got going on—it's mild, nothing crazy, but it's been there since my last visit, and honestly it's getting worse.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. And the headache—when exactly did that start, do you remember?
PATIENT: Um, I think it was like three weeks ago? Maybe four? I'm not... the days kind of blur together.
PHYSICIAN: That's fair. Let me just check the discharge summary—looks like you were admitted on the fifteenth, and you got out on the twentieth. So we're talking about just this past week, maybe.
PATIENT: Oh! Okay, yeah, that sounds right. I thought it was longer. So this week, yeah.
PHYSICIAN: Right. So the severe headache—is it constant, or does it come and go?
PATIENT: It's pretty much always there. Worse in the morning, a little better as the day goes on, but it never really leaves.
PHYSICIAN: And you mentioned the mild dizziness since your last visit is getting worse. Have you felt faint, or is it more of a spinning sensation?
PATIENT: It's like the room spins a little when I turn my head too fast. Not like I'm going to pass out, but it's definitely there.
PHYSICIAN: Mm-hmm. I'm also seeing here that you reported severe heartburn this morning. How's that been?
PATIENT: Yeah, this morning was rough. I had that for sure. But it's kind of stayed the same—hasn't gotten worse, hasn't gotten better. Just there.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. So I want to go through your medications with you, because some of these things might be connected. You have type 2 diabetes mellitus, which we're managing, and you also have gout, which is active. We sent you home with some new prescriptions. Walk me through—are you taking the colchicine?
PATIENT: Um, the colchicine... I'm not entirely sure, honestly. Like, I have it, and I know I'm supposed to take 0.6 mg once daily, but I can't quite remember if I've been doing that every day or... I don't remember exactly.
PHYSICIAN: That's actually pretty common when you're just starting something. No judgment. So you might be taking it, might not be—you just couldn't say for sure.
PATIENT: Right, exactly. I feel bad about that, but yeah.
PHYSICIAN: Don't feel bad. Let's nail that down. And what about the hydralazine for blood pressure? That's 25 mg, three times daily.
PATIENT: Oh, that one I'm pretty on top of. I take it as prescribed—I haven't missed a single dose since I got home. Three times, every single day.
PHYSICIAN: Excellent. And the losartan, 25 mg, once daily—how's that going?
PATIENT: That one... I've probably missed a dose or two. Maybe more. I keep forgetting, to be honest. I'm not always great about remembering the once-a-day thing.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. That's important information. So we're looking at some blood pressure variability potentially, which could be contributing to your headache and dizziness. I want to do a few things. First, we need to adjust colchicine dose—we can work that out with our care coordinator and get you sorted before your next visit.
PATIENT: Okay... is that going to make the headache go away?
PHYSICIAN: The headache is more likely related to your blood pressure right now, so that's where we need to focus. But adjusting the colchicine dose should help with the gout, which is its own problem. And I'd like you to monitor blood pressure at home. That means getting a cuff if you don't have one, and taking readings a few times a week. We'll review those at your next visit.
PATIENT: I can do that. I have my sister's cuff actually, so I can borrow that.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. One more thing—given the dizziness since your last visit that's getting worse, and just to be thorough, I'm going to refer to pulmonology. I know that might sound unrelated, but we want to make sure there's nothing going on with your breathing or your heart that we're missing.
PATIENT: Hmm. I mean... I'm not sure I have a lung problem. Do you think something's wrong?
PHYSICIAN: I don't think something's wrong, but we'd rather see you and check than miss something. It's just part of being thorough. Does that sound okay?
PATIENT: Yeah, okay. I trust you. I'll do it.

CARE_COORDINATOR: So we've got you down for a cardiometabolic followup today—looks like medication adherence is what we're focusing on. Is that tracking with what you understood when you called to schedule?
PATIENT: Yeah, I think so. I mean, there's a couple of things going on. My vision's been doing something weird the last few days, so I wanted to get that checked out, and also I'm pretty sure I've lost some weight, which is... I don't know, that seemed off.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. Let's start with the vision. You said a few days—can you be more specific?
PATIENT: Three days ago. Just woke up one morning and everything was kind of blurry—well, blurred vision is what I'd call it. Not terrible, like I can still function, but it's definitely there. Moderate blurring, I guess is the right way to describe it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Has it gotten worse, stayed the same, or actually improved at all since three days ago?
PATIENT: It's been about the same, yeah. Not really changing.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I've noticed it too. He squints a lot more when he's on his phone, and he mentioned it first thing when I picked him up yesterday.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Thanks for that context. And the weight loss you mentioned—when did you first notice that?
PATIENT: Yesterday, I think. I stepped on the scale and was just like, huh, that's not right. It's mild, though. Just a couple pounds maybe.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Have you been trying to lose weight, or is this unintentional?
PATIENT: Totally unintentional. I haven't changed anything about what I eat. Actually, speaking of which—my buddy Marcus from the warehouse where I used to work, he had a stroke last month. Pretty bad one. He's still in recovery. It had me thinking about all this stuff, you know, health and how fast things can change. Anyway, that's not really relevant, but it's just been on my mind.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: Yeah, Kajetan mentioned that. It was rough hearing about it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I'm sorry to hear about your friend. That kind of thing does put things in perspective. Let me ask—have you noticed increased thirst lately? Like needing more water than usual?
PATIENT: Actually, yeah, now that you mention it. It's been... well, it's getting worse, I think. Yeah, definitely getting worse over the past few days.
CARE_COORDINATOR: So the thirst is actually decreasing, then? Getting better?
PATIENT: No, wait—no, I said it wrong. It's not getting better. It's getting worse. I'm thirstier than I've been in a long time.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Got it. That's important to track. Any leg swelling at all? Puffiness in the ankles or calves?
PATIENT: No. Nothing like that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Alright. Let me pull up your current medications and let's talk through how things are going with those. You're on canagliflozin 300 mg once daily—how have you been taking that?
PATIENT: Um, honestly I'm not sure. I know I'm supposed to take it, but I couldn't say if I've been taking it exactly right. I've had some side effects from it, and I think the dose was adjusted because of that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: What kind of side effects are we talking about?
PATIENT: Genital yeast infections, and it's just... it's uncomfortable. I mentioned it at the last visit.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Right. So the plan had been to keep an eye on those while adjusting up to 300 mg once daily. You're also on metformin 850 mg once daily—how's that going?
PATIENT: That one I've been taking as prescribed. Every single day, no issues. Though I think they mentioned bringing the dose down because of some GI side effects, haven't missed a single day of the lower dose.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. And the insulin aspart—6 units with meals. How are you getting on with the injections?
PATIENT: I've... I mean, I've been taking them, mostly. But I'll admit I've missed some doses. Some mornings I just forget, or I'm in a rush and I skip it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: We'll keep you at 6 units with meals for now, but I want to loop back to that. Your fasting glucose this morning was 156 mg/dL, which is higher than where we'd like to see you. I think we should order follow-up bloodwork in 3 months to see how these adjustments are tracking, and I'd also like to refer to endocrinology in 3 months so they can do a more detailed review. Does that sound okay to you?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. Three months from now, so we check everything again then?
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I think that makes sense. I can help him keep track of the appointments and remind him about the insulin injections too.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's really helpful. And we do need to address the obstructive sleep apnea as part of this picture—have you been using your CPAP machine?
PATIENT: Most nights, yeah. Not every night, but probably five or six times a week.

PHYSICIAN: Hi Teresita, this is Dr. Chen calling—do you have a few minutes to go over how things have been going since we sent you home?
PATIENT: Yes, I have time. Is everything okay? You're not calling because something went wrong, are you?
PHYSICIAN: No, no, this is just our routine follow-up. You were discharged with community-acquired pneumonia, and I want to make sure you're managing okay. How's the appetite been?
PATIENT: Well, that's actually one of the things bothering me. It's been mild, to be honest. I'm just... I'm not interested in food the way I normally am. Since Monday it's been like that, and honestly it hasn't gotten any better or worse.
PHYSICIAN: Mild poor appetite since Monday, and it's stayed about the same—okay. And the dizziness you mentioned at discharge, how's that been?
PATIENT: Oh, the severe dizziness has been there since my last visit, but actually, I think it's getting better. I was scared at first that it was going to stick around, but these past couple days I notice it when I stand up, and then it passes. So... I think I'm on the right track.
PHYSICIAN: That's good to hear. Let me pull up your vitals from today. Your temperature is 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit, and your heart rate is 92. Both look reasonable. Let me ask you something else—have you had any nausea at all?
PATIENT: No, thank goodness. I was worried about that, honestly, but it hasn't happened. I'm relieved it hasn't been an issue.
PHYSICIAN: Good. And the night sweats—have you been having those?
PATIENT: No, I haven't had night sweats. It's been fine that way.
PHYSICIAN: Alright. I want to circle back to something. Given your history of chronic kidney disease stage 3, and the way you've been feeling, I want to rule out... I'm wondering if we should be thinking about heart failure with reduced ejection fraction here. I'm not convinced yet that that's what we're dealing with, but I'd like to explore it a bit more with you. Does that concern you?
PATIENT: Heart failure? I mean... that sounds serious. But honestly, I'm not sure that makes sense. I'm breathing fine now. The pneumonia thing was bad, but it's getting better. Do you really think that's something we need to worry about?
PHYSICIAN: It's one of the things I want to rule out, especially with your kidney disease. Sometimes they go hand in hand. We don't have a definite answer yet, but it's worth keeping an eye on. Now, let's talk about your medications. You're on ibuprofen 600 mg as needed—how are you taking that?
PATIENT: Oh, the ibuprofen—I've been taking it as prescribed. I haven't missed a dose when I need it. Usually I take it a couple times a day for the pain, but I'm not... I'm not overusing it or anything.
PHYSICIAN: Good. We'll get that refilled for you. Now, one thing I'm noticing—you mentioned pain. Where's that coming from? Is this incision pain?
PATIENT: Yeah, the incision. It's... well, it's moderate, and it actually started this morning. And honestly, it seems to be getting worse as the day goes on.
PHYSICIAN: Getting worse since this morning. That's something we should keep an eye on. Let me look into—hold on, I'm just pulling up your discharge summary here—
PHYSICIAN: Okay. So you were also discharged on dabigatran 110 mg twice daily. How have you been managing with that one?
PATIENT: The dabigatran... I'm not sure, honestly. I think I'm taking it, but I don't remember exactly how often or... I mean, I couldn't say for certain that I've gotten the schedule right. I know it's important, but...
PHYSICIAN: Okay, let's not worry too much about it right now. We're just reviewing. I'm not making any changes to that today. And you're also on naproxen 250 mg twice daily?
PATIENT: Yes, that one I'm taking—I take it every single day, morning and night. That's the one I have down pretty clearly.
PHYSICIAN: Good, so naproxen 250 mg twice daily you're staying consistent with. No changes there either. But I am concerned about this incision pain that's worsening. I'd like the nurse to reach out in about 4 weeks, and we're going to adjust ibuprofen dose with you to see if we can get better control.
PATIENT: Adjust the ibuprofen? I guess that makes sense if it's not helping enough. Yeah, okay, I can work with that.
PHYSICIAN: And here's the other thing I want to make sure we're doing—given everything going on, I'd like you to monitor blood pressure at home. Can you do that? You have a cuff?
PATIENT: I do, actually. My daughter left hers here. So I can... I can take readings at home, you want me to keep track of them?
PHYSICIAN: Yes, exactly. Let's monitor blood pressure at home starting now, and we'll check back in about 4 weeks to see what the pattern looks like. Does that work for you?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's... that's fine. I can do that. Should I be worried if the numbers are high?
PHYSICIAN: Call us if you're seeing consistent readings above 180 systolic. Otherwise, just keep a log and we'll review it together. One more thing—with the community-acquired pneumonia, make sure you're finishing any antibiotics you have left, and if the cough gets worse or you develop a fever, that's when you call right away. Sound good?
PATIENT: Okay, I'll do that. So to—to recap, I'm watching my blood pressure, adjusting the pain medication, and... what else am I missing? Oh, keep finishing the antibiotics. Got it.
PHYSICIAN: That's the main things. We're going to see you back in about 4 weeks, and hopefully by then we'll have a better picture of whether we need to worry about that heart failure concern or not. But I'm not convinced yet that that's your problem. In the meantime, if anything changes—especially with that dizziness or the incision—don't hesitate to call.
PATIENT: Alright. Thank you, doctor. I appreciate you following up.

text:
NURSE: So your legs started swelling over the weekend, and you came in because of that, or is there something else that made you decide to call?
PATIENT: Well, yeah, the leg swelling is the main thing. But I've also been having this chest pain, like, for a couple weeks ago now. It's been bothering me more than I expected it would.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Let me get the full picture here. Tell me more about this chest pain—when you say it's been going on for a couple weeks ago, is it getting worse, or is it about the same?
PATIENT: No, it's about the same. It's not like... getting worse or anything. Still there, but not changing really.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And is it severe?
PATIENT: I mean, yeah. It is. It's severe, especially when I'm trying to move around or doing anything physical.
NURSE: Have you noticed any other symptoms? Any dizziness, shortness of breath, anything like that?

PATIENT: Pretty much the same, honestly. I'm lying awake thinking about everything that's gone wrong, and then during the day I'm just exhausted.
NURSE: That must be really tough, especially recovering from the surgery. Tell me about the nausea—the notes mention some nausea.
PATIENT: Yeah, it's mild, but it's been there for the past few days now. When I wake up mostly, and sometimes after meals. Nothing dramatic, just sort of... there.
NURSE: Is it worse, better, or staying about the same?
PATIENT: About the same. I can eat, it doesn't stop me from eating, it's just there in the background.
NURSE: And you mentioned incision pain. Where are we with that?
PATIENT: That's actually getting better. It's more of a tenderness now when I touch it or reach. Nothing sharp like the first week.
NURSE: Good. Now let me ask you about leg swelling—I want to know if you've noticed any puffiness or tightness in your legs at all.
PATIENT: No, no leg swelling. I've been keeping an eye out for that specifically because the surgeon mentioned it as a warning sign, so I check every morning. Nothing there.
NURSE: Good. Now, the medications—let's walk through what you're actually taking. Let's start with the furosemide, the 80 mg.
PATIENT: The water pill? Well, we're kind of holding off on that for now, aren't we? I'm not sure if I've been taking it or not, to be honest. I couldn't say exactly what I've been doing with that one.
NURSE: That's fair—we did talk about holding it for a bit. What about the ibuprofen—the 400 mg that you were supposed to take as needed for pain?
PATIENT: I've stopped taking that. After the lab results came back, we talked about bringing that down, and I haven't been taking it. I figure the pain is manageable enough without it now anyway.
NURSE: Good decision. And the clopidogrel, the blood thinner—75 mg once daily—how's that going?
PATIENT: I'm not taking that anymore either. I thought you all said to stop it? I've stopped taking the clopidogrel.
NURSE: Yes, that's—
PATIENT: —actually, wait, am I supposed to still be on it? I got confused about that one.
NURSE: No, you're right, we discontinued it. You're doing fine. So let me ask you this: with the difficulty sleeping and everything else, have you thought about whether you want to pursue any support for the major depressive disorder? That's something we can certainly address.
PATIENT: I know it's there, the depression, but I'm not sure. My neighbor—you know, the man who cuts my lawn—he has this thing called psoriasis on his hands, and he's been telling me how much it messes with him, and it made me think about how one thing affects everything else. I don't know if talking to someone would help.
NURSE: Those are two totally different situations, but I hear what you're saying about things being connected. What I'm thinking is we should order follow-up bloodwork in 4 weeks to see how your heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is responding to the changes we've made. Does that sound reasonable?
PATIENT: Yeah, that makes sense. You want to check the numbers.
NURSE: Exactly. And we'll also adjust ibuprofen dose at that point, so in 4 weeks we can figure out the right level of pain management once you're healing up a bit more. We can settle on that plan. Okay?
PATIENT: Okay, that's fine. So the bloodwork and the ibuprofen adjustment in a month.
NURSE: Right. And I want to mention—there's also the possibility of a referral to pulmonology if we see anything on the bloodwork that suggests you might benefit from that.
PATIENT: Pulmonology? Like the lungs? I don't know about that yet. Let me think about it.
NURSE: No pressure. We can revisit it in 4 weeks when we get the labs back and see where we stand. For now, just keep monitoring that incision, no leg swelling like you're already doing—
PATIENT: There's a call for nursing—line three. Sorry, one second.
NURSE: No problem. Anyway, we're in good shape. You've got the follow-up set for 4 weeks out. Any questions before you head out?
PATIENT: I think I'm good. Thank you for walking through all this.
