text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So we've got you down for the nebivolol refill, but I want to check—did we book your next labs yet, or is that still floating out there?
PATIENT: I'm not sure, honestly. I got the text reminder about coming in today and figured I'd just come by the pharmacy window to grab the bottles, but then they said I needed to see someone first. Which, fair enough, I understand why.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Right. Well, while we're here, I want to touch base on a few things. You mentioned on the phone that you've been noticing some leg swelling—is that still happening?
PATIENT: Yeah, so that started yesterday, actually. I remember because I was doing yard work, it was hot, I came inside, took my socks off, and my ankles just looked... puffy. My wife was like, 'That doesn't look right.' But then I drank a ton of water, elevated my legs while we watched TV, and this morning it was already better. So I don't know if it's just one of those things or what.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's mild leg swelling and it came on yesterday, and you're saying it's getting better already?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's right. I mean, it's still a little there if I look, but definitely not like last night.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. And have you been keeping up with the nebivolol like we talked about?
PATIENT: Every single day, 10 mg once daily, no skipping. I haven't missed it once. I actually set a phone reminder so there's no chance of forgetting.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's excellent. And the dabigatran—
PATIENT: Same thing. Twice daily, 110 mg each time, as prescribed. I take it morning and night with meals.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Perfect. I'm going to have a quick word with our front desk about getting that refill ordered for you on the nebivolol. But first, I do want to circle back on the swelling and your breathing, because I know you mentioned feeling a bit winded when you called.
PATIENT: Well, I wouldn't say I feel winded exactly. I mean, I notice it more when I'm climbing stairs or something. Like, two flights and I have to catch my breath. But I've never been super athletic, so I'm not sure if that's normal for me or if it's new. And it's not like I'm gasping or anything dramatic.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Right, so exertion-related, stairs especially. That's worth paying attention to, especially given your hypertension history. We need to make sure we're managing that well.
PATIENT: I know I've got hypertension, but I mean, I feel okay most days. My numbers have been okay when I check them, haven't they?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: They've been reasonable, yes. Your LDL cholesterol came back at 102 mg/dL last quarter, which is—
PATIENT: Is that good or bad? I never know what those numbers actually mean.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's in a decent range. Not ideal, but not alarming. That said, with the exertional breathing you're describing and the swelling, even though it's mild and getting better, I think we should at least float the idea of—oh, sorry, one second.
PATIENT: Sure.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: —getting you in to see cardiology next week. Just as a precaution, to rule out anything we're missing. You don't have to commit to it right now, but it might be worth considering a referral to cardiology while we keep an eye on things.
PATIENT: Cardiology? Isn't that a bit much if it's just my ankles being puffy for one night?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's the combination—the swelling, the breathing with stairs, your existing hypertension. It's probably nothing, but given that we're managing your heart health anyway, a cardiology opinion next week would give us more clarity and maybe help us optimize your medications if needed. And we might want to also think about cutting back on salt next week, as you're making dietary adjustments and see if that helps with the swelling.
PATIENT: I guess that makes sense. I'll think about the cardiology thing and let you know.

CARE_COORDINATOR: So we've got you down for a medication adherence follow-up today, and you mentioned when you called that you've been having some weight loss and things have been off with your urination. Is that still what you're experiencing?
PATIENT: Yeah, both of those things are definitely happening. The urination part is, uh—honestly it's getting worse. It started since Monday, and I'm just—I can barely make it through work without having to run to the bathroom. I work in IT, so I'm at a desk all day, but even so, it's severe. It's really severe.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That sounds really disruptive. Walk me through a typical day for you—how often are we talking about?
PATIENT: I mean, it's gotten to where I'm going maybe every fifteen, twenty minutes? And at night too, which is keeping me up. My sister actually brought it up last week—she's a nurse, works over at the hospital—and she was like, 'That's not normal, you should mention that to your doctor.'
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He texted me about it too. I told him the same thing, to make sure he brings it up at this visit. It's been going on for almost a week now.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I'm glad he did. And you mentioned weight loss as well. How much, and over what timeframe?
PATIENT: I've dropped maybe eight pounds in the last month or so. I haven't been trying to lose weight. I mean, I could stand to lose some, but not like this—it's just happening.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay. Any other symptoms we should know about? Shortness of breath, for instance?
PATIENT: No, no shortness of breath. I've been wondering if I should be worried about that, but I'm not having that at all.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. What about vision—any changes there?
PATIENT: There's a little blurred vision, but it's mild. It started since my last visit, I think, and it hasn't gotten any worse. Just kind of there.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Let me pull up your lab work and your current medications, because I want to make sure we're addressing all of this together. Your hemoglobin a1c came back at 8.6 percent, and your fasting glucose was 141 mg/dL.
PATIENT: So is that—is that bad? Like, where should those numbers be?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We want to see a1c below 7 for most people, ideally, so there's room for improvement. Your fasting glucose in the 140s is higher than we'd like as well. This is part of why we need to talk about your medications and make sure everything is working the way it should be.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah. I've been stressed about a lot of things, if I'm being honest. I have generalized anxiety disorder, and work has been crazy, and I think the anxiety makes everything feel worse. I notice I'm more anxious about my health when things pile up.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's really helpful context. Stress and anxiety can definitely affect glucose levels too. Let's look at what you're taking right now. You're on ezetimibe—are you taking that exactly as prescribed?
PATIENT: Yeah, every single day. 10 mg once daily, morning with breakfast.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Great. We're going to increase that dose for better blood pressure control. Same frequency, but we'll bump the dose up, and I'll get you updated on what that looks like before you leave. Now, dapagliflozin—how are you managing with that one?
PATIENT: Honestly, I haven't been taking the dapagliflozin. I stopped taking it about two weeks ago because I was worried about side effects, and then your labs came back, so—I don't know, I just haven't restarted it.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay, I appreciate you being straight with me. The lab results actually show we need to come down on that one anyway, so we're going to adjust your dose based on what we're seeing. But we do need you on a medication regimen that works for you. What was the side effect concern?
PATIENT: I was just—worried about urinary tract stuff, and with everything else going on, I got in my head about it. Probably not my smartest move.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He should have called and asked about it instead of just stopping. I kept telling him that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's fair feedback. For the future, yes—give us a call before you make changes. But I want to address this head-on. Your severe frequent urination since Monday might actually be connected to your glucose levels, not the medication. That's why these labs matter. Now, semaglutide—1 mg once weekly. How are you with that one?
PATIENT: I'm taking that exactly as prescribed. Haven't missed an injection. That one's been okay.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Good. We're going to keep that exactly where it is. Here's what I'd like to do: I'm going to refer to endocrinology to help us get a more complete picture and optimize your regimen. We can set that up for our next visit. And at home, I want you to monitor blood pressure at home starting now, and we'll check in on those readings in 3 months. Does that make sense?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds good. I can do that. I'll get a cuff.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect. And one more thing—let's make sure you understand what you're taking and why. You still have questions, or does this land for you?
PATIENT: I think so. I'm taking the ezetimibe at a higher dose, stopping the dapagliflozin for now or changing it, keeping the semaglutide the same, monitoring my blood pressure, and seeing endocrinology next time. And I should call if anything doesn't make sense instead of just stopping things.

ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So last time we saw you, you'd been having some trouble with your breathing, and I think we started you on an antibiotic for what looked like a chest infection. How's that been going?
PATIENT: Well, the cough is still there, if I'm honest. It's moderate, and it started last week. Maybe a bit worse, actually.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Worse — so it's not improving as we'd hoped?
PATIENT: No, it's getting worse, yeah. And I've got this wheezing too, which is new or at least more noticeable.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Okay. And your breathing overall — how's that been? Any shortness of breath?
PATIENT: Yes, I've got severe shortness of breath. It came on for the past few days, and it seems to be getting worse, I'd say.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: So you're saying it's getting worse, the severe shortness of breath?
PATIENT: Well, actually no — I misspoke. It is getting better, thank goodness. I was worried it would linger, but it's improving.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good to hear that's trending the right way. Let me just check your medications with you. Are you still on your fluticasone-salmeterol?
PATIENT: No, I stopped taking that. I wasn't sure if I should be, so I just stopped. The instructions seemed complicated — 2 puffs twice daily was what it said, but I kept forgetting.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's helpful to know. We should probably adjust fluticasone-salmeterol dose given that you've stopped it and the wheezing's come back. We can find something that works better for you.
PATIENT: Okay, yes. If that'll help with the wheezing, I'm willing to give it another go.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: And your diabetes medication, the canagliflozin — 300 mg once daily, are you managing that one?
PATIENT: No, I haven't been taking that either. I ran out and just never refilled it. I wasn't sure if I still needed it.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: We'll arrange a refill for you. It's important to keep that going.
PATIENT: All right. What exactly does it do? I know it's for my blood sugar, but how?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It helps your kidneys clear out excess sugar in your urine, which keeps your blood sugar down and also takes a bit of pressure off your heart. You've got chronic kidney disease stage 3 — so managing that is part of looking after them.
PATIENT: Kidney disease? I didn't know I had that. Is it serious?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: It's something we're monitoring. Stage 3 means your kidneys are working at about 30 to 59 percent of normal, but it's not immediately dangerous if we keep an eye on it. That's actually something I want to address — I'd like to refer you to nephrology, a kidney specialist, so they can check in with you too.
PATIENT: A specialist for my kidneys. Okay, I think that makes sense.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Good. Now, the doxycycline you were prescribed — 100 mg twice daily. How's that going?
PATIENT: I've been taking that as prescribed. Every single day, no missed doses.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Excellent. That's exactly what we need for the community-acquired pneumonia. Let's keep you on that.
PATIENT: Is that what this is? Pneumonia?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: That's what we've been treating you for, yes. The community-acquired pneumonia showed up on your last visit.
PATIENT: Right. It's scary to say it out loud. My friend Barbara from my volunteer shift got a migraine last week and I thought she was going to have to sit out, but at least it wasn't anything like that.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Migraines can be rough, but they're a different thing entirely. Now, one more thing — we should probably think about monitoring your blood pressure at home next week, just to keep tabs on things while we're adjusting your medications.
PATIENT: I don't have a monitor at home, actually.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Well, it's something to consider if you can get one. No pressure though — we can talk about it when you come back.
PATIENT: Okay, I'll think about it.

PATIENT: Oh gosh, I'm so sorry—I forgot to fill out that blood pressure log you gave me. I meant to do it, I really did, but then I got sidetracked with my sister visiting and just... didn't get to it.
NURSE: That's okay, Izabela. We'll grab one before you leave today. But let's focus on how you've been managing since you came home from the hospital. What's been going on?
PATIENT: Well, the main thing is I've just been so tired. Not like my normal tired—I mean, I'm always a bit worn out, but this is different. It started... let me think... it was three days ago, and honestly, it's getting worse. Like I can barely get through the afternoon.
NURSE: Three days ago—that would have been Tuesday, wouldn't it? And this moderate fatigue has been picking up since then?
PATIENT: Yes, Tuesday sounds right. And yeah, every day it's a bit more. Yesterday I also had trouble getting to sleep, and again last night. It's mild, nothing terrible, but I just... can't seem to drop off like I used to.
NURSE: When did the difficulty sleeping start exactly?
PATIENT: Yesterday. And it's about the same—not getting better, not getting worse. Just there.
NURSE: Okay. And the nausea you mentioned on the phone—how's that sitting now?
PATIENT: It's mild, thankfully. I don't feel like I'm going to be sick, just kind of queasy if I eat too much at once. It's more annoying than anything.
NURSE: Got it. Let me ask you about your breathing. Have you noticed any shortness of breath? Any trouble catching your breath when you're walking around?
PATIENT: No, not really. I mean, my legs have been sore—the swelling, you know, from the deep vein thrombosis—but my breathing's been fine.
NURSE: Just to make sure—you're saying you haven't had any shortness of breath at all?
PATIENT: No, no, I haven't. I'm breathing fine.
NURSE: Good. That's reassuring. Now, with your deep vein thrombosis and everything, we want to make sure we're not missing anything else. I want to rule out something like coronary artery disease, just to be thorough. Have you had any chest discomfort or pressure?
PATIENT: Not really. My chest feels okay. Why—do you think I have that?
NURSE: I'm not convinced yet, but with your fatigue coming on this suddenly and your history, it's something we want to make sure we're not missing. It's just precaution.
PATIENT: That's... that's a little scary to hear, honestly.
NURSE: I know it sounds that way, but we're working it up carefully. Let's talk about your medications and make sure we've got those right. You're on aspirin—are you taking that like you're supposed to?
PATIENT: Yes, I take it every single day. 81 mg once daily. Haven't missed a single dose.
NURSE: Perfect. Actually, we're going to bump that up for you—increase the dose for better blood pressure control. So you'll be taking a higher aspirin dose, and I'll send that new prescription through today.
PATIENT: Okay, if you think that's best. Just... a higher dose won't make me bleeding too much or anything, right?
NURSE: No, we monitor for that. You're safe at the higher dose. Now, the tramadol—the pain medication—how are you doing with that?
PATIENT: I've been... I'll be honest, I've missed some doses. I meant to take it as prescribed, but sometimes I just forget, especially in the morning. And the swelling in my leg isn't as bad now, so I don't feel like I need it every time.
NURSE: That's actually helpful to know. Your labs came back, and we're going to bring that down—lower the dose of tramadol to 50 mg as needed. So you can take it when you really need it, not on a schedule.
PATIENT: Oh, okay, that makes sense. Thank goodness, because I was worried about getting too dependent on it.
NURSE: That's very understandable. And the torsemide—the water pill—are you taking that every day?
PATIENT: I stopped taking that one a couple weeks ago. It was making me run to the bathroom constantly, and I just... I haven't been taking it.
NURSE: I hear you on the inconvenience. But I want to keep it at 20 mg once daily. It's helping with your fluid balance. Why don't we stick with it for now?
PATIENT: I mean... if it's really important, I guess I can try again. I'm not thrilled about it, but I understand.
NURSE: It is important, especially with your deep vein thrombosis and your psoriasis potentially affecting fluid retention. And we're also going to refer you to nephrology—to a kidney specialist—to make sure everything's working right. That'll happen in about three months, and you'll hear from them to schedule.
PATIENT: A kidney specialist? Is there something wrong with my kidneys?
NURSE: Nothing we've found yet, but remember when you had those kidney stones a while back? We want to make sure everything's clear now and that your kidneys are handling everything well. It's routine.
PATIENT: Oh, right, when I had that terrible pain... that was resolved, though. It went away.
NURSE: It did. But we still want the specialist to check in. And one more thing—we need you to monitor blood pressure at home. We'll send you a new log. Take it once a day, same time if you can, and bring those readings back in three months when you come see us again.
PATIENT: I can do that. I promise I won't forget this time.

PHYSICIAN: Alright, so I'm looking at your chart here and I see we have your address down as Maple Street still—is that current, or did you move?
PATIENT: Oh no, we did move about two years ago. We're on Oak now, over on the east side. That should probably get fixed.
PHYSICIAN: We'll get that updated. Thanks for catching that. So today I wanted to go through your medications with you and also hear about what's been going on. I see in the notes there's been some numbness and you've been feeling pretty tired?
PATIENT: Yeah, that's right. The numbness in the feet started a couple weeks ago and it was pretty bad at first—severe, really. But honestly it's getting better now, which is nice. And then the fatigue, that's been going on about a month ago, maybe a little longer. It's moderate, you know, not like I can't get out of bed, but I'm definitely dragging.
PHYSICIAN: And when you say the numbness is getting better, what does that look like day to day? Is it improving consistently or does it come and go?
PATIENT: It's been pretty steady improvement. Started in both feet, sort of that pins and needles thing, and now it's mostly just the tips of my toes, maybe a little in the soles. I can actually feel more stuff than I could a week ago.
PHYSICIAN: Good to hear. And the fatigue—how is that affecting what you're able to do during the day?
PATIENT: Well, I'm still working part-time, and some days I make it through okay, but other days I just hit a wall by mid-afternoon. My wife has to basically drag me off the couch. I'm also getting some muscle aches along with it, you know, general achiness, which I think might be from the osteoarthritis catching up with me, but I'm not entirely sure.
PHYSICIAN: That makes sense. The osteoarthritis definitely can contribute to that. Let me just check your temperature real quick.
PATIENT: Okay.
PHYSICIAN: Alright, it's 97.8. So that's normal. Now let's talk through your medications. I want to make sure we're on the same page about what you're taking and how. You're on amitriptyline—that's for the nerve pain from your migraine condition—are you taking that regularly?
PATIENT: Yes, I'm taking the amitriptyline 10 mg at bedtime every single day, haven't missed a dose. That one's actually helping with sleep too, so I'm definitely sticking with it.
PHYSICIAN: Great, I'm glad that's working. We'll get that refilled. And then you're also on empagliflozin, which is for metabolic support. How have you been doing with that one?
PATIENT: Um, honestly I'm not sure. I know I have it, but I'm not entirely sure if I'm taking it every day or... I don't remember if it's supposed to be every day. I think it's supposed to be 25 mg once daily, but I couldn't say for certain how regularly I'm actually on it.
PHYSICIAN: Okay, so it sounds like that one may have gotten a little loose in the routine. Do you have it at home? Are you thinking you're taking it most days or...
PATIENT: I have the bottle, yeah. Probably most days? But I really couldn't tell you a percentage. Some weeks I'm more on top of it than others, you know?
PHYSICIAN: I hear you. Given that, we'll leave the empagliflozin 25 mg once daily as is for now and just review it in a couple of weeks. Actually, I wanted to ask—any family history of things like high cholesterol or heart stuff that you're aware of?
PATIENT: My grandmother on my mother's side had hyperlipidemia, I think that's what they called it? High cholesterol. She had some issues with that when she was older. Other than that, not a whole lot I know about.
PHYSICIAN: That's helpful to know. So we're mindful of that. Now, before we wrap up, I want to make sure we have a plan. I'd like you to monitor blood pressure at home, if you're able to do that—do you have a cuff there?
PATIENT: We have one somewhere, yeah. I think my wife used to check hers. But honestly with the insurance and all that, I'm not sure if I should be buying new equipment or...
PHYSICIAN: No, if you've got one that works, use what you have. Just a couple times a week would be great, and we'll want to look at those numbers in about 4 weeks. Can you do that?
PATIENT: Yeah, I can do that. A couple times a week for 4 weeks, got it.
PHYSICIAN: Perfect. And then the nurse will order follow-up bloodwork for you—we'll want that in 4 weeks as well, just to check in on where things are. That okay with you?
PATIENT: Sure, that sounds fine. So same timeframe, 4 weeks?
PHYSICIAN: Exactly. By the way, circling back to the numbness for a moment—is there anything else that's changed? Any weakness along with it, or any pain?
PATIENT: No weakness that I can tell, and the pain's minimal now. Like I said, it was severe a couple weeks ago, but it's really settling down. I'm hopeful it just keeps going that way.

PHYSICIAN: So the schedule's got you down for three weeks out—that works, right? Before we lock that in, let me just catch up on how you've been doing since you got home.
PATIENT: Yeah, three weeks is fine. But honestly, I've been struggling. The incision pain has been severe, and it started over the weekend, and it's just—it's not getting better, you know?
PHYSICIAN: Severe pain over the weekend. And where are we now—is it still about the same, or has it changed at all?
PATIENT: Same. Pretty much the same since it started. Some days I think maybe it's a tiny bit less, but I don't think I'm fooling myself—it's still there, same level.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. Have you had any fever along with that?
PATIENT: No, I haven't had a fever, no.
PHYSICIAN: And your breathing—anything going on there? Any trouble catching your breath?
PATIENT: Oh, no—I mean, you know my neighbour down the hall, she's got cellulitis in her leg, poor thing, and she was telling me about how exhausting it's been, but me, I'm breathing fine. No shortness of breath or anything.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Now, the other thing you mentioned—how's your appetite been?
PATIENT: Poor appetite, really. It's mild, really. Since Monday I just haven't been that interested in eating. But it's been the same since then, not worse.
PHYSICIAN: Since Monday. And that's staying steady?
PATIENT: Yeah, same every day. Not getting better, not getting worse.
PHYSICIAN: All right. Let's talk about what you're taking. You're on the warfarin now—tell me how that's been going.
PATIENT: Oh, the warfarin. Um. I think I'm taking 2.5 mg—wait, no. Actually, I'm not sure. Is it 2.5? I couldn't say for certain. Let me think—no, the bottle says 7.5 mg, so it's 7.5 mg once daily. I just started it, so I'm still getting used to it all.
PHYSICIAN: So 7.5 mg once daily—that's the one. And how are you remembering to take it?
PATIENT: I'm trying. I mean, I'm not sure if I've been taking it exactly right. Some days I remember in the morning, some days I think I took it the night before. I don't remember, honestly.
PHYSICIAN: Okay. We'll keep an eye on that. What about the naproxen—that refill came through, right?
PATIENT: Yes, I picked that up yesterday. But I have to admit I'm not totally sure how I'm supposed to be taking it. Is it the 250 mg twice daily? I mean, I think that's what it says, but I don't remember if I've been doing that right.
PHYSICIAN: The 250 mg twice daily, yes. So you've got a refill now—let's make sure that keeps going and we'll just monitor how you're doing. And the ibuprofen, 200 mg as needed?
PATIENT: Yeah, that one I've been taking as prescribed. I haven't missed it, every single day when the pain is really bad I take it.
PHYSICIAN: Good. Now, I'm going to take your temperature just to make sure everything's baseline.
PATIENT: All right.

CARE_COORDINATOR: So we've got you down for a cardiometabolic follow-up today, and the note says you've been having some trouble with frequent urination. Is that still the main thing that's been bothering you?
